The entire surface of this page is adorned with a dense, repeating **dendritic pattern** <term>dendritic pattern: A branching design that resembles the structure of a tree, coral, or seaweed.</term>. The motif consists of organic, branching, **coral-like shapes** printed in a rich red ink. This intricate design is set against a warm tan or ochre-colored background, a color palette often used in historical institutional bindings.

The design is a hallmark of high-quality **endpapers** <term>endpaper: The sheets of paper used by bookbinders to attach the text block of a book to its cover.</term> or decorative book covers from the late 19th century. # FOREWORD

*René* | *DESCARTES’S* | *MEDITATIONS* | *ON FIRST* | *PHILOSOPHY*, | *in which the existence of God* | *and the immortality of the soul* | *are demonstrated* <note>original Latin: "Renati DES-CARTES MEDITATIONES DE PRIMA PHILOSOPHIA, in qua Dei existentia et Animæ immortalitas demonstratur"</note>: such is the complete title of the first edition of the work that we will call quite simply, in English, the *Meditations* of Descartes. This first edition was published in Paris, by Michel Soly, in 1641 (printing completed on August 28, 1641), *with the Privilege and Approval of the Doctors* <note>original Latin: "cum Privilegio et Approbatione Doctorum"</note>. The "privilege"—the legal authorization to print—is found, in fact, at the end of the volume, or rather an *Extract from the King’s Privilege* <note>original French: "Extraict du Privilege du Roy"</note>, which we have reproduced in the present volume on page 448. However, the announced approval is missing; we know from Descartes's correspondence, and we will see in the *Life of the Philosopher*—specifically in the chapter regarding the history of this publication—all the attempts made to obtain it, which were ultimately in vain. Regarding this matter, there remains the Letter to the Dean and the Doctors of the Sorbonne: *To the Most Wise and Distinguished Men, the Dean and Doctors of the Sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris, René Descartes sends greetings* <note>original Latin: "Sapientissimis Clarissimisque Viris Sacræ Facultatis Theologiæ Parisiensis Decano et Doctoribus, Renatus Des-Cartes S. D."</note>, printed at the beginning of the edition. Following this are three preliminary pieces: a Preface, *Preface to the Reader* <note>original Latin: "Præfatio ad Lectorem"</note>, an Index, and a plan or overview, the *Synopsis*, which is the only part paginated as pages 1–7. Then, in succession, come the six *Meditations*, which form the body of the work, even though physically they occupy only about one-fifth of it, from pages 7–116. The Objections follow, along with the philosopher's Replies: the *first Objections*, by a Theologian <note>Johannes Caterus</note>, pages 117–131, and *Replies*, pages 132–160; the *second Objections*, by various Theologians and Philosophers, pages 161–172, and *Replies*, followed by an *Abridgment in the Geometric Style* <note>A formal proof using definitions, postulates, and axioms</note>, pages 172–232;

<keywords>René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy, Michel Soly, 1641 edition, Sorbonne, printing privilege, Objections and Replies, bibliography</keywords>

<note>original Latin title: "Renati Des-Cartes Meditationes de Prima Philosophia, In quibus Dei existentia, et animæ humanæ a corpore distinctio, demonstrantur. His adjunctæ sunt variæ objectiones doctorum virorum in istas de Deo et anima demonstrationes; cum Responsionibus Authoris. Secunda editio septimis objectionibus antehac non visis aucta"</note>

such is the complete title of the second edition, published in Amsterdam, at the house of Louis Elzevier, in 1642. Format, small duodecimo. Printer's mark: *Minerva* <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom; this was a famous trademark for the Elzevier publishing house</note>; this is even one of the first works where this mark appears, with the motto *Do not stray beyond the olive trees* <note>original Latin: "Ne extra oleas"—a classical Greek proverb advising one to stay within the boundaries of the racetrack, or more broadly, to stay focused and not wander from the subject</note>. The title, as one can see, is slightly changed: *in which* <note>Latin: "in quibus" (plural)</note>, instead of *in which* <note>Latin: "in qua" (singular)</note> <note>The grammar was adjusted so that "in which" refers to the "Meditations" (plural) rather than to "Philosophy" (singular)</note>; and especially, instead of *immortality of the soul*, this significant variation: *the distinction of the human soul from the body*. There is no longer any approval included, nor a privilege <note>The "privilege" was a legal monopoly granted by a monarch to a printer; the second edition, being published in the Netherlands, did not carry the French royal privilege</note>. However, we find, first of all, the same content as in the first edition, and in the same order, except however for the *Index*, which has disappeared (we have provided it in a note, p. 10-11). Here is the content: *Letter*, *Preface*, *Synopsis*, the latter on p. 1-6; the six *Meditations*, p. 7-95; *first Objections* and *Responses*, p. 96-131; *second*, p. 132-191; *third*, p. 192-224; *fourth*, p. 225-296; *fifth*, p. 297-454; and *sixth*, p. 455-496. But furthermore, as the title of the whole work announces, the sixth Objections are no longer the last, *ultimæ*, as they were in 1641; in the edition of 1642, they are followed by the *seventh Objections with the Author’s Notes* <note>These seventh objections were written by the Jesuit Father Pierre Bourdin</note>. And this important addition forms something of a new volume, following the first, with its own specific frontispiece: *Seventh Objections | In | Medi-*

# FOREWORD

*[Medi]tations | on First Philosophy with | the Author's notes. | (Amsterdam, | at the house of Louis Elzevier, 1642. | With the Author's consent)* <note>original Latin: "Meditationes de prima Philosophia cum notis Authoris. (Amstelodami, Apud Ludovicum Elzevirium, 1642. Cum Authoris consensu)"</note>, and with a separate pagination, p. 1-138; the frontispiece and its reverse side counting as pages 1 and 2. The typefaces remain at first the same as for all the preceding Objections, Responses, and Meditations. However, the second edition follows these seventh Objections, where Descartes's notes are interspersed, with another very important piece: Descartes’s Letter to Father Dinet, titled: *To the Very Reverend Father | Father Dinet | of the Society of Jesus | Provincial Superior | for France, | René Descartes sends greetings.* <note>original Latin: "Admodum Reverendo Patri Patri Dinet Societatis Jesu Præposito provinciali per Franciam, Renatus Des Cartes S. D." The abbreviation "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a formal Latin greeting.</note> This Letter is printed in a larger typeface and runs from page 139 to 212; it thus continues the pagination of the seventh Objections and forms a whole with them. This is because, in part at least, it completes them: the seventh Objections were written by Father Bourdin, a Jesuit, whose superior was Father Dinet. Descartes provides the latter with an account of his quarrels with Bourdin, as well as, on the same occasion, with a minister from Utrecht, Gisbert Voët <note>Voët was a powerful Dutch Calvinist theologian and a fierce opponent of Cartesian philosophy, eventually leading to Descartes being summoned by the city of Utrecht.</note>. Nevertheless, this new volume, although capable of being detached from the first, truly forms a single body with it, since the half-title of the first volume expressly mentions it: *Second edition... enlarged... by the seventh objections.*

These are the two sources from which we will draw for a new Latin edition of the *Meditations*. These were, however, reprinted once more during Descartes's lifetime, but without the accompanying Objections and Responses, without the Epistle or the Preface, though with the *Synopsis*; Descartes had no part in this reprint. It took place in 1644, in Amsterdam, *at the house of Johannes Blaeu*. A friend of Gassendi, Samuel Sorbière, then living in Holland, published Gassendi's objections—the fifth set—along with Descartes’s Responses and long Rebuttals or *Instances* by Gassendi as well, all under this title: *Pierre Gassendi’s | Metaphysical | Disquisition | Or | Doubts | and Instances:* <note>original Latin: "Petri Gassendi Disquisitio Metaphysica. Seu Dubitationes et Instantiæ"</note>

|against| *René Descartes's* | *Metaphysics and Responses*. <note>original Latin: "adversus Renati Cartesii Metaphysicam et Responsa."</note> The quarto <term>in-4º: A book format where each sheet of paper is folded twice, creating four leaves or eight pages.</term> volume contains no fewer than 319 pages (plus 14 unnumbered pages). At the end of the volume, for the reader's convenience, Sorbière added the text of the six Meditations, with a new pagination of 48 pages (the half-title counting as pages 1 and 2): *RENÉ DESCARTES'S* | *MEDITATIONS* | *ON FIRST* | *PHILOSOPHY*. | *In which the existence of God, and the distinction of the human soul from the body, are demonstrated*. In quibus Dei existentia, et Animæ humanæ a corpore distinctio, demonstrantur. (Amstelodami, Apud Iohannem Blaev, CIO IC XLIV.)" The date CIO IC XLIV is a typographic representation of 1644.</note> This addition, however, offers no textual interest.

The other editions of the *Meditations* in Latin did not appear until after Descartes's death. The Elzeviers of Amsterdam produced as many as five of them, not counting the 1642 edition; that one was a small duodecimo <term>in-12: A smaller, pocket-sized book format where each sheet is folded into twelve leaves.</term>, while the five others were in the quarto format. The first Elzevier quarto edition is from 1650; the four following are from 1654, 1663, 1670, and 1678. The title is the same, except that these last four bear the mention *final edition* <note>original Latin: "editio ultima"</note>, instead of *third edition* <note>original Latin: "tertia"</note> in 1650. Furthermore, the first two (1650 and 1654) bear the name of Louis Elzevier, the third (1663) those of Louis and Daniel, and the last two (1670 and 1678) that of Daniel alone. Here is the title common to all of them: *RENÉ DESCARTES'S* | *MEDITATIONS* | *ON FIRST* | *PHILOSOPHY. In which the existence of God, and the distinction of the human soul from the body, are demonstrated*. | *To these are added various objections by learned men regarding these demonstrations concerning God and the soul. With the Author's Responses*. | *Third edition (or Final edition) expanded and corrected relative to the previous ones*. (Printer's mark: Minerva.) <note>original Latin: "Renati Des Cartes Meditationes de Prima Philosophia... His adjunctæ sunt variæ objectiones doctorum virorum in istas de Deo et anima demonstrationes. Cum Responsionibus Authoris. Tertia editio (ou Editio ultima) prioribus auctior et emendatior." The "Minerva" refers to the emblem of the Roman goddess of wisdom used by the Elzevier printing house.</note> The pagination is also the same in these five quarto editions, namely: 6 preliminary leaves, — 191 pages for the 1st part, — 164 pages for the *Appendix* (dated 1649 in the 1650 edition), and 88 pages for the *Letter to Voetius* <note>original Latin: "Epistola ad Voetium." This was Descartes's public defense against the accusations of the Dutch theologian Gisbert Voetius.</note>. These 88 pages constitute a very important addition to the new edition. It naturally follows the Letter to Father Dinet, which concluded the 1642 edition; and above all, it completes a volume which, without that, would perhaps have seemed a bit slim, with 191 + 164

...or 355 pages only, while it actually contains 355 + 88, or 443 pages. Moreover, Louis Elzevier had himself already printed this letter to Voet <note>Gisbertus Voetius, a Dutch theologian and critic of Descartes.</note> separately in 1643. — Furthermore, the first part provides, after the sixth Objections and Responses, a piece that Louis Elzevier had also published separately in 1648: **RENÉ DESCARTES'S**, *Notes on a certain program published in the Netherlands toward the end of the year 1647, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Notæ in programma quoddam, sub finem anni 1647, in Belgio editum, etc."</note>, pages 169-191. On the other hand, the fifth set of Objections by Gassend <note>Pierre Gassendi, a philosopher and contemporary of Descartes who challenged his dualism.</note> do not appear in their usual place between the fourth and sixth. In that spot, Elzevier gives the Latin translation of two pieces inserted in 1647 into the French volume of the *Meditations*: namely, a *Foreword* by Descartes concerning Gassend's Objections, and a *Letter to Clerselier* <note>Claude Clerselier, the principal editor and translator of Descartes's works into French.</note> in response to some of the "Instances" <term>Instances: Rebuttals or counter-arguments, specifically those raised by Gassendi in response to Descartes's initial replies.</term> published in the *Metaphysical Disquisition* <note>original Latin: "Disquisitio Metaphysica"</note> in 1644. The first of these two pieces offers, in the 1650 edition, a very interesting peculiarity: while for everything else it is merely an exact translation of the original, one passage is completely changed. Regarding Gassend's Objections, Descartes had said in French:

> "When I learned that Mr. C. L. R. <note>Claude Clerselier.</note> was taking the trouble to translate the other objections, I asked him to omit these." (Volume of the *Meditations* in French, in the present edition, p. 109, l. 8-11.)

Here is the corresponding Latin sentence:

> "When I heard that Louis Elzevier, the industrious printer, had decided to submit my Meditations along with the other Objections to his press again, I asked him to omit the Fifth Objections." <note>original Latin: "Cùm audivi Ludovicum Elzevirium, industrium typographum, Meditationes meas unà cum aliis Objectionibus prælo suo iterum subjicere decrevisse, rogavi ipsum ut Quintas objectiones omitteret."</note> (Amsterdam Edition, Louis Elzevier, 1650, p. 141.)

Descartes would therefore have personally made express recommendations to Louis Elzevier so that the 1650 edition (which was actually begun in 1649, as evidenced by the date of the Appendix)—that is, the second to come from the Amsterdam presses—would differ from the 1642 edition, which was the first printed in Holland. However, Elzevier did not want to entirely exclude the fifth Objections and Responses from the volume: he was content to relegate them, along with the seventh...

> “Even though the Author of the *Meditations on First Philosophy* <note>original Latin: "Meditationes de Primâ Philosophiâ"</note> did not wish for the fifth Objections to be read in his book alongside the others anymore—as is clear from the Warning placed in their stead—nevertheless, because they were produced by a philosopher of great renown, I believed I would be doing something not unwelcome to curious minds if I restored them in this place, albeit out of their usual order, together with the Responses. Since this same reasoning applies also to the seventh Objections and Responses, I have added those as well after the Fifth, along with the letters to the Jesuit Dinet and to Gisbert Voetius, the theologian of Utrecht. And so as not to fail their wishes in any respect, I shall indicate here by the same effort that: the author of the First objections is a certain learned theologian of the United Netherlands <note>Referring to Johan de Kater, often called Caterus.</note>; the Second were collected in Paris <note>original Latin: "Lutetiæ"</note> by Marin Mersenne from the mouths of various philosophers and theologians; the Third are by Thomas Hobbes, the famous English philosopher; the Fourth by Antoine Arnauld, Doctor of Theology at the Sorbonne; the Fifth bear the name of their author, Pierre Gassendi; the Sixth were again collected by the same Mersenne from the mouths of others; and finally, the Seventh appear, from the Letter to Father Dinet, to be by a certain Jesuit <note>Father Pierre Bourdin, who was a sharp critic of Descartes's scientific and philosophical methods.</note>.”

Next came the editions by *Blaeu*, in Amsterdam, in 1685, 1698, etc., also in quarto format. These are reproductions of the Elzevir editions. They contain the same omission of the fifth Objections by *Gassendi* between the fourth and sixth; in their place, one finds the Latin translation of the same two pieces: the *Foreword by Descartes* from the 1647 French edition, and the *Letter to Clerselier*. There is also the same addition of the *Notes on a certain program, etc.*, after the sixth...

# FOREWORD

->NOTICE.<-

Objections. The same *Appendix* is composed in the same manner: the fifth Objections from Gassendi and Descartes's Responses, the seventh (by Father Bourdin) and the notes inserted by Descartes, and the latter’s Letter to Father Dinet. Finally, to conclude, the Letter to Voet <note>Gisbert Voetius, a Dutch theologian and critic of Descartes.</note>.

In what way is it now appropriate to use the old editions, whether for the content of the present volume or for the establishment of the text?

Regarding the content, the second edition—that of 1642—must obviously be the standard. The first edition is, in fact, incomplete: it lacks the seventh Objections, which had not been sent in time to appear there. Furthermore, these were produced not from a manuscript copy—as the others were, having been sent by Mersenne before any printing to the theologians or philosophers whose critiques he invited—but from the printed volume available from August 28, 1641. Father Bourdin, the author of the seventh Objections, studied this volume on his own for the sole purpose of criticizing it. Since Descartes also added to these seventh Objections (augmented by his own Notes) the Letter he subsequently wrote to Father Dinet, we shall not separate them in the present volume either. However, we will not include the Letter to Voet, as the Elzeviers did from 1650 to 1678, followed by Blaev. This addition on the part of the Dutch printers seems to have had no other cause than the need to enlarge a volume which, in the new <term>quarto</term> <note>original: "in-4"; a book size where each sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note> format, would have been a bit thin. Now, our present volume of the *Meditations* in Latin is quite large enough without it. Moreover, while a good half of the Letter to Father Dinet does indeed relate Descartes's quarrels in Utrecht with Voet—which explains why the Letter to Voet naturally follows—it would then also be necessary, to have a complete set, to print the *Apologetic Letter to the Magistrate of Utrecht* on the same subject, and furthermore, as the Dutch editions have done since 1650, the *Notes on a Program* <note>original Latin: "Notæ in programma etc."; these were Descartes's comments on a broadsheet or manifesto distributed at the University of Utrecht.</note>, the final piece...

->NOTICE.<-

the file of Descartes' relations with his former disciple and friend from Utrecht, Professor Henry de Roy <note>Also known by his Latinized name, Henricus Regius (1598–1679). On the other hand, we shall not imitate the Dutch publishers, who removed the Fifth Objections and Responses from their chronological place to make them a simple *Appendix* along with the Seventh, etc. They may well have justified this by citing Descartes' own *Foreword* in the 1647 French edition of the *Meditations*, and even precise instructions that the philosopher seems to have given to Louis Elzevier in 1649. However, in 1647, Descartes speaks only of the translation of these Fifth Objections, and he urges Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), a devoted friend and the primary editor of Descartes’ posthumous works.</note> not to undertake it; but when they were translated anyway, he did not object to them being printed at the end of the volume. Later, likewise, in 1649, despite his instructions to Louis Elzevier, he allowed the text to be reprinted, at least as an *Appendix*. Furthermore, he himself had already permitted—and likely seen to it—that this text of the Fifth Objections, with his own Responses in Latin, be printed between the Fourth and the Sixth, in the second edition produced under his supervision in Amsterdam by Louis Elzevier in 1642. 

We shall therefore be more faithful, it seems, to his original intention by keeping them, as he did, in their proper place within the body of the work, rather than listening too compliantly to a word that perhaps escaped him later in a moment of ill humor—and which, having said it, he did not wish to retract, except by half-closing his eyes to what his publishers might do. And he was far from remaining indifferent to the Objections of Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a major rival philosopher who challenged Descartes from an empiricist and materialist perspective.</note>, which he not only permitted to be printed in the end (even if following the others), both in the French translation of 1647 and the Latin text of 1649–1650, but he even wished...

# FOREWORD

<page-num>XIV</page-num>

“*...since these [pages] were sent to the press in the Author’s absence, and from a copy rather than from his own manuscript, no amount of diligence could prevent certain errors from creeping in, the principal of which will be corrected as follows.*” <note>original: "hæc absente Authore, atque ab exemplari, non ab eius manuscripto, typis mandata sunt, nulla diligentia potuit impedire, quin aliqui errores irrepserint, quorum præcipui sic corrigentur."</note>

It is not certain, however, that Descartes himself reviewed the proofs of the second edition. But it is likely, as the printing took place in Amsterdam, which is not so far (about eight leagues) from Endegeest <note>Endegeest: A manor house near Leiden where Descartes resided between 1641 and 1643, providing him with a quiet environment for his work.</note>, where Descartes lived throughout that year of 1642. We can therefore follow this text with full confidence, while not failing to carefully note all the variations from the first edition. Other variations still, and sometimes even successful corrections, have been provided to us for the text of the fifth Objections (those of Gassendi) by the *Metaphysical Inquiry* <note>original: "Disquisitio Metaphysica"</note> of 1644; we have noted each of these as they occur.

The spelling is also not the same in the two editions of 1641 and 1642. We will also adopt the Dutch spelling of 1642. It does, however, present several innovations: the distinction between *i* and *j* (except, however, for capital letters at the beginning of words, where one almost always finds *I*, and the specific cases of *ajo* [I say] and *ajebant* [they were saying]); and the distinction between *u* and *v*, both as initial letters and within the body of words, etc. The 1641 edition, by contrast, published in Paris, is more archaic: it makes no distinction between *j* and *i* (for example: *eius* [his], *coniicere* [to throw together], etc.); it uniformly prints *v* for *u* or *v* at the beginning of words (*vt* [as], *vnus* [one], etc.), and *u* for *v* or *u* in the body of words (*diuersus* [diverse], *viuunt* [they live], etc.). In this respect, it is certainly closer to Descartes' own spelling, and perhaps it was appropriate to adopt it. However, as the text printed in Paris was based not on the philosopher's manuscript but on a copy (*from a copy, not from his own manuscript* <note>original: "ab exemplari, non ab eius manuscripto"</note>), and as, on the other hand, Descartes allowed the spelling of the Elzeviers <note>Elzevier: A famous family of Dutch printers known for their high-quality editions of classical and contemporary works.</note> to stand in the 1642 edition, and consequently did not disapprove of it, we may therefore follow it without hesitation, as it is also more in keeping with our mo-

# FOREWORD

<page-num>XV</page-num>

modern authors. — Let us note an interesting peculiarity of the fifth set of Objections, which seems specific to Gassendi; for it is found not only in the text of these Objections, printed in 1641 and 1642, but in the *Metaphysical Inquiry* <note>original: "Disquisitio Metaphysica"</note> of 1644, and in general in all the works of this philosopher (*Works of Gassendi* <note>original: "GASSENDI Opera"</note>, 1658 edition). Almost always, *ei* is used in place of *e* in words like *omneis* <note>all</note>, *plureis* <note>several/many</note>, etc., and even for *i* in *heic* <note>here</note>, *heinc* <note>hence</note>, etc. We will reproduce this peculiarity.

A difficulty gave us pause for some time. The Latin text of the *Meditations* is printed, in both 1641 and 1642, as a continuous flow, with almost no paragraph breaks, which makes reading it quite exhausting. No doubt one receives a somewhat physical impression of a line of reasoning that holds together from beginning to end, forming a compact whole, like a single block. However, Descartes' reasoning also has a certain flexibility and something like "articulations": it resembles a developing organism, or perhaps a body of troops on the march, with its companies and squads following one another at regular intervals. This is why the early editors, at least for the French translation, did not hesitate to start a new paragraph as often as the matter seemed to allow. We have done the same, with all the less hesitation because a careful study of Descartes' text seems to provide some indications on this subject. By carving the philosopher’s thought into slices—acting as a "skillful cook," as <term>Plato</term> <note>In the *Phaedrus*, Plato describes the "art of division" as carving a subject at its natural joints, rather than breaking it like a clumsy butcher.</note> used to say—we did not believe we were betraying his intentions, but, on the contrary, respecting and following them more faithfully.

Indeed, the sixth Meditation and even the fifth do not resemble the four that precede them in this regard, as if the editors themselves had grown tired of those long sentences placed end-to-end interminably, without a rest for the eyes or a pause for the reader’s attention. To be precise, the first two editions begin to divide the...

# FOREWORD

<page-num>XVI</page-num>

text of the paragraph breaks <note>The French term "alinéas" refers to starting a new line or paragraph.</note>, p. 68 of the present volume, l. 20. The text of the Sixth Meditation is broken into a new line up to *nineteen* times (2nd edition), and even *twenty-nine* times (1st edition), which is perhaps excessive; and the text of the fifth, four times already, which is not enough. Is this not an example to follow for printing the text of Meditations I, II, III and IV in the same way, even though, in neither 1642 nor 1641, is it *not once broken into a new line?*

But did Descartes intend it so? Or is it the fault of his editors, who might not have understood his instructions? In the original handwritten manuscripts <note>original: "autographes"</note> that we have from him, he does not often start a new line, it is true; but, from time to time, after a period, the following sentence, instead of resuming immediately, leaves a small white space, very distinct, and which, let us note, is not found before every sentence, but only before those that pass to another order of ideas. This small white space corresponds, therefore, quite well to a new paragraph, and it seems we are being faithful to Descartes by interpreting it this way typographically, as we have done many times in the five volumes of the *Correspondence*. On the contrary, to ignore it and skip over this little interval would be to build a bridge where there is a ditch, and to unduly link to what precedes a new development that the philosopher clearly intended to detach. Whether the manuscript of the *Meditations* featured this peculiarity, we cannot know, and we must even doubt it, since it was not Descartes’ own manuscript, but a copy, as we saw above, *from a copy, not from his own manuscript* <note>original: "ab exemplari, non ab eius manuscripto"</note>; unless the copy—which is improbable—reproduced the smallest details of the original as if by tracing. Nevertheless, at least in the 1642 edition, one quite often notices small white spaces at the end of sentences. One would not dare to say that this is in conformity with the manuscript, especially if one is not sure that the latter gave such indications. Perhaps these are

<page-num>XVII</page-num>

# FOREWORD

<sig>WORKS. II. c</sig>

...simple negligence on the part of the typographer, especially since these intervals sometimes—though not always—correspond to a change in ideas. In such cases, even doubt can be interpreted in our favor. We see no reason why we should maintain a superstitious respect for a typographical layout that even the original editors themselves did not strictly observe (at least in Meditations V and VI), and which we have no reason to attribute to Descartes; in fact, the opposite is more likely.

One might, however, object that if Descartes had wanted more frequent paragraph breaks <note>original: "mît davantage à la ligne"</note>, he would have corrected the 1642 edition in that regard, since it was printed so close to him in Amsterdam. But first, it is possible—even probable—that this edition was produced not from a new manuscript (which no one would have taken the trouble to recopy for that purpose), but from the 1641 edition, a copy of which would have been sacrificed for the task. Consequently, the original divisions were likely followed most of the time. Furthermore, it is not absolutely certain that Descartes reviewed all the proofs, especially from this perspective. In the seventeenth century, people did not attach the same importance to purely typographical layout as we do today. It is quite possible that the philosopher, entirely focused on the logical order of his work, neglected to rectify the printer’s layout—a mere question of form, after all, and a matter of relative indifference to one primarily attentive to the substance. Therefore, no consequences or obligations can be drawn from this fact, and we maintain our full and complete freedom in this regard.

We have used this freedom for the best. We have, therefore, not hesitated to start a new line <note>The French term "alinéa" refers to a new paragraph or indented line.</note> whenever the meaning seemed not only to authorize it, but to require it. Indeed, Descartes' reasoning is so clear that very little room for error is left for an attentive interpretation. One can almost certainly point to the precise spot where one argument ends and another begins. We have divided the text of each Meditation into as many paragraphs as we judged necessary for the...

Furthermore, there is a difference in this respect: in **Geometry**, since everyone is convinced that nothing is usually written for which a certain demonstration <term>demonstration: in 17th-century logic, this refers to a rigorous proof that moves from self-evident truths to an inescapable conclusion</term> is not held, the unskilled more often err by approving false things—desiring to seem as if they understand them—rather than by refuting true ones. And therefore, whatever my arguments may be, because they nevertheless belong to **Philosophy**, I do not hope that I will achieve a great result by their means unless you assist me with your patronage <note>original: "patrocinio"; Descartes is seeking the formal "imprimatur" or approval of the Sorbonne to protect his work from charges of heresy</note>. # PREFACE TO THE READER

I have already touched upon the questions concerning **God** and the **human mind** <margin>5</margin> briefly some time ago in my *Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One’s Reason and Seeking Truth in the Sciences* <note>original: "Dissertatione de Methodo..." This refers to Descartes' famous 1637 work, originally published in French.</note>, published in French in the year 1637. I did so not because I intended to treat them with precision there, but only to offer a foretaste <note>original: "delibarem" — to sip or taste; Descartes implies he was only sampling the topics</note> and to learn from the judgments of readers how they ought to be treated later. These matters seemed to me of such great importance that I judged they should be dealt with more than once; and the path I follow to explain them is so little trodden and so remote from common <margin>10</margin> usage, that I did not think it useful to teach it more extensively in a French work that might be read by everyone everywhere. I feared that even weaker minds might believe they should also set out upon it <gloss>a</gloss>.

However, since I had requested everyone there who might find anything in my writings worthy of reproach to deign to point it out to me <gloss>b</gloss>, <margin>15</margin> no objections worthy of note were raised regarding these questions, except for two. I will respond to these briefly here before I begin a more precise explanation of those same matters. The first is that, from the fact that the human mind, when turned inward upon <margin>20</margin> itself...

b. See *Discourse on the Method*, p. 75, l. 22, of this edition.

<meta>This page continues Descartes' response to the two primary objections raised against his preliminary philosophical sketches in the Discourse on Method. He is refining his definitions of the "thinking thing" and the "idea" of God to prepare the reader for the more rigorous proofs that follow in the Meditations.</meta>

->OEUVRES DE DESCARTES.<-

<page-num>8</page-num>

...itself, does not perceive itself to be anything other than a **thinking thing** <term>res cogitans: Descartes' term for the mind, defined by the act of consciousness</term>, it does not follow that its nature or **essence** <term>essentia: the fundamental qualities that make a thing what it is</term> consists only in its being a thinking thing, such that the word *only* excludes all other things which might perhaps also be said to <margin>5</margin> belong to the nature of the soul. To this objection I reply that I did not intend to exclude those other things in relation to the actual truth of the matter (which I was not dealing with at the time), but only in relation to my perception; my meaning was that I knew of nothing clearly that I knew to belong to <margin>10</margin> my essence, except that I was a thinking thing, or a thing having in itself the faculty of thinking. In the following pages, however <margin>(3)</margin> <note>These numbers in parentheses refer to the page numbers of the original 1641 edition.</note>, I will show how it follows that nothing else truly belongs to my essence, based on the fact that I recognize nothing else belonging to it. <margin>15</margin>

The second objection is this: from the fact that I have within me an idea of a thing more perfect than myself, it does not follow that the idea itself is more perfect than I am, and much less that the thing represented by that idea actually exists. But I reply here that there is an <margin>20</margin> ambiguity in the word **idea**: for it can be taken either *materially*, for the operation of the **intellect** <term>intellectus: the faculty of understanding</term> (in which sense it cannot be said to be more perfect than me), or *objectively*, for the thing represented by that operation. This thing <note>original: "res," referring to the content or object of the thought</note>, even if it is not <margin>25</margin> assumed to exist outside the intellect, can nonetheless be more perfect than me by reason of its essence. How it follows that the thing truly exists, from the sole fact that the idea of a thing more perfect than me is in me, will be explained at length in what follows.

I have also seen two other fairly long writings, <margin>30</margin> but in these, it was not so much my reasons regarding these matters that were attacked, but rather my conclusions, using arguments drawn from the commonplaces of the **Atheists** <term>atheus: in the 17th century, this term was used for anyone denying the existence of a providential God</term>...

<summary>Descartes clarifies his definitions of the mind as a "thinking thing" and explains the dual nature of "ideas"—distinguishing between the act of thinking and the object being thought of—to counter early critics.</summary>

...were attacked with common arguments <margin>(4)</margin> borrowed from others <note>original: "communibus mutuatis impugnabantur"</note> <sup>a</sup>. And since arguments of that kind can have no force among those who understand my reasoning, and the judgments of many are so backwards and weak that they are more easily <margin>5</margin> persuaded by first-received opinions—however false and contrary to reason—than by a true and firm, but later-heard refutation of them, I do not wish to respond to them here, lest I should first have to repeat them. I will only say generally that all those things commonly <margin>10</margin> boasted by **Atheists** <term>Atheis: literally "those without God," referring here to those who deny God's existence</term> to attack the **existence of God** <term>existentiam Dei</term> always depend on this: either that human affections are attributed to God, or that our minds are claimed to have such power and wisdom that we attempt to determine and comprehend what God can and ought to <margin>15</margin> do. Thus, provided we only remember that our minds are to be considered as **finite**, but God as **incomprehensible** and **infinite**, these arguments will cause us no difficulty.

But now, after I have once experienced how men judge, <margin>20</margin> I here approach the same questions regarding God and the human mind once more, while at the same time treating the principles of all **First Philosophy** <term>prima Philosophia: the study of the fundamental principles of reality, including the nature of existence and the soul</term>; but in such a way that I expect no <margin>(5)</margin> applause from the common crowd, nor a great number of readers. Indeed, I advise no one to read these things <margin>25</margin> except those who are able and willing to meditate seriously with me, and to withdraw their minds from the senses as well as from all **prejudices** <term>præjudiciis: preconceived notions or biases formed before rational investigation</term>; and I know well enough that only very few such people are to be found. But as for those who do not care to understand the <margin>30</margin> series and connection of my reasons, but merely strive against individual clauses, as...

is the habit of many <note>original: "multis in more est"</note>, and they will strive to **quibble** <term>argutari: to engage in subtle, often petty or sophistical, arguments</term>; they are not going to receive much fruit from reading this writing. » **Second objections** by several **Theologians and Philosophers**, from page 161 to 172. — Responses, at the conclusion of which the preceding Meditations are reduced to a **Geometric fashion** <term>morem Geometricum: a method of formal demonstration using definitions, postulates, and proofs, similar to the style used in Euclid’s geometry</term>, from page 172 to 232.
» **Third objections** by a **Philosopher** <note>These were submitted by the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes.</note>, with Responses, from page 233 to 271.
» **Fourth objections** by a most **subtle Theologian** <note>The "subtle theologian" refers to Antoine Arnauld, a prominent Jansenist thinker.</note>, from page 272 to 304. — Responses, from page 305 to 354.
» **Fifth objections** by **Pierre Gassendi**, Provost of the Church of Digne and a most acute philosopher, from page 355 to 492. — Responses, from page 493 to 551.
» **Sixth**, or final, **objections**, from page 552 to 566. — Response, from page 556 to 602.

*In the first [Meditation], the reasons are explained for which we can doubt all things, especially material things; so long, that is, as we have no foundations for the sciences other than those we have had until now. ### WORKS OF DESCARTES.

...so that it may be known that all substances whatsoever—that is, things that must be created by God in order to exist—are by their nature <term>incorruptible: incapable of being destroyed or decaying by natural means</term>, and can never cease to exist unless they are reduced to nothing by that same God withholding His concurrence from them. <note>original: "concursum suum iis denegante"; in Scholastic philosophy, God must "concur" or actively support the existence of all things at every moment.</note> And then, so that it may be noticed that "body," taken in a general sense, is a substance, and therefore also never perishes. But the human body, insofar as it differs from other bodies, is composed only of a certain configuration of members and other such <term>accidents: non-essential properties, like shape or position, that can change without the object itself ceasing to be what it is</term>. The human mind, however, does not consist of any such accidents in this way, but is a pure <term>substance: an independent thing that does not need another thing to exist</term>. For even if all its accidents were changed—such as if it understands different things, wills different things, or perceives different things—the mind itself does not therefore become something else. On the other hand, the human body becomes something different simply because the shape of some of its parts is changed. From these things it follows that the body indeed perishes very easily, but the mind is by its nature immortal.

<margin>5</margin>In the third Meditation, I have explained my primary argument for proving the existence of God at sufficient length, as it seems to me. Nevertheless, because I wanted to lead the minds of readers as far as possible away from the senses, I did not wish to use any comparisons drawn from physical things; therefore, many obscurities perhaps remained. These, I hope, will later be completely removed in the responses to objections. Among these obscurities is the question of how the idea of a supremely perfect being, which is in us, has so much <term>objective reality: the degree of "being" or perfection contained within an idea</term> that it cannot but come from a supremely perfect cause. This is illustrated there by the comparison of a highly perfect machine, the idea of which is in the mind of some craftsman; for just as the <term>objective craftsmanship: the design or complexity as it exists in the mind's eye</term> of this idea must have some cause—namely, the knowledge of this craftsman, or of someone else from whom he received it—so...

<summary>Descartes explains that while the human body is a temporary configuration of parts that can "die," the human mind is a pure substance that is naturally immortal. He also introduces his argument for God's existence, comparing the idea of a perfect God to a craftsman's mental blueprint of a complex machine.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, substance, accidents, objective reality, existence of God, craftsmanship analogy, Descartes, metaphysics</keywords>

->### 4-5. MEDITATIONS. — SYNOPSIS.<-

...the idea of God which is within us cannot fail to have God himself as its cause.

In the *fourth* [Meditation], it is proven that everything we perceive clearly and distinctly is true; at the same time, the nature of error <note>original: "ratio falsitatis"</note> is explained. This knowledge is necessary both to confirm what came before and to understand what follows <margin>a.</margin>. (But meanwhile, it should be noted that this in no way concerns sin, or the error committed in the pursuit of good and evil, but only <margin>6</margin> that which happens in the judgment of truth and falsehood. Nor are those things considered which pertain to faith or the conduct of life, but only speculative truths known through the aid of the <term>natural light: the innate human capacity for reason, independent of divine revelation</term>.)

In the *fifth* [Meditation], besides explaining <term>corporeal nature: the essence of physical things, characterized primarily by having extension in space</term> taken in general, the existence of God is demonstrated by a new argument. However, some difficulties might arise here again, which will later be resolved in the Response to Objections. Finally, it is shown in what way it is true that the certainty of even geometrical demonstrations depends on the knowledge of God.

Finally, in the *sixth* [Meditation], <term>intellection: the act of pure understanding by the mind alone</term> is distinguished from imagination; the signs of these distinctions are described; it is proven that the mind is really distinct from the body, yet is shown to be so closely joined to it that it forms a single unit with it. All errors typically arising from the senses are reviewed, and the ways they can be avoided are set forth. Finally, all the reasons from which the existence of material things <margin>7</margin> can be concluded are provided—not because I thought they were very useful for proving that very thing...

->*Concerning those things which can be called into doubt. ᵇ*<-

I realized several years ago how many false things I accepted as true in my youth, and how <margin>8</margin> doubtful | are all the things I subsequently built upon them. <margin>5</margin> Therefore, I concluded that once in a lifetime I must completely demolish everything and begin again from the first foundations, if I ever desire to establish anything firm and lasting in the sciences <note>In the 17th century, "sciences" referred to all organized knowledge, including philosophy and physics.</note>. However, this seemed a massive task, and I waited until I reached an age so mature that no better time for undertaking these studies would follow. <margin>10</margin> For this reason, I have delayed so long that from now on I would be at fault if I spent the time remaining for action in mere deliberation. Appropriately, therefore, today I have [cleared] my mind of all cares...

WORKS OF DESCARTES. 7-9.

[freed] from all [cares], I have procured for myself a secure <term>leisure</term> <note>original: "otium". This refers to a state of being free from business or public duties, allowing for philosophical contemplation.</note>, I withdraw alone; at last, I will apply myself seriously and freely to this general destruction of my opinions.

<margin>5</margin>
For this purpose, it will not be necessary to show that they are all false, which I might never be able to achieve; but since reason now persuades me that I should withhold my assent no less carefully from things that are not plainly certain and indubitable than from those that are obviously false, it will be sufficient to reject all of them if I find in each some reason for doubt. <margin>10 9</margin> Nor, therefore, must each one be examined individually, which | would be an infinite task; but because, once the foundations are undermined <gloss>a</gloss>, whatever is built upon them collapses of its own accord, I will immediately attack those very principles upon which everything I once believed rested.

<margin>15</margin>
Surely, whatever I have accepted until now as most true, I have received either from the senses or through the senses <gloss>b</gloss>; but I have discovered that these sometimes deceive, and it is a point of prudence never to trust completely those who have deceived us even once.

But perhaps, although the senses sometimes deceive us regarding certain <margin>20</margin> minute and distant objects, there are many other things about which one plainly cannot doubt, even though they are derived from those same senses: for example, that I am now here, sitting by the fire, wearing a winter dressing gown, touching this paper with my hands, and similar things. <meta>This page continues Descartes’s radical doubt. Having just questioned the reliability of the senses for perceiving distant or small objects, he now moves to a more unsettling possibility: that even our most immediate experiences—like sitting by a fire or having a body—could be illusions similar to those experienced by the mentally ill or by anyone who dreams.</meta>

### MEDITATIONS. — FIRST.

...[those] whose brains are so undermined by a persistent vapor from <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atrâ bile". According to the medical theories of the time, an excess of this substance was believed to cause "melancholy" or various forms of insanity.</note> that they constantly assert they are kings, when they are impoverished; or that they are dressed in purple, when they are naked; or that they have a clay head; or that they are entirely made of <term>pumpkins</term> <note>original: "cucurbitas". This refers to a known delusion of the era where people believed their bodies or heads were as fragile as gourds.</note>, or composed of glass. But these people are <margin>5</margin> insane, and I would seem no <margin>10</margin>| less mad if I took them as an example for myself.

<margin>10</margin> This is all very well, except I am a man who is accustomed to sleep at night and to experience in my dreams all the same things—and sometimes even less likely things—than those people do while awake. How often does my nightly rest convince me of these familiar things: that I am here, wearing a <term>gown</term> <note>original: "togâ". Referring to a scholar’s dressing gown or robe.</note>, sitting by the fire, <margin>15</margin> when in fact I am lying stripped of my clothes between the sheets! Yet now I certainly look at this paper with wakeful eyes; this head that I move is not heavy with sleep; I extend this hand intentionally and knowingly, and I feel it. These things would not happen so distinctly to someone dreaming. As if I did not recall that I have been deceived by similar thoughts in my sleep before! <margin>20</margin> As I consider this more attentively, I see so plainly that there are no certain signs by which <term>wakefulness</term> <note>original: "vigiliam"</note> can be distinguished from sleep, that I am quite astonished; and this very astonishment almost confirms the idea that I am dreaming.

Let us assume then that we are dreaming, and that these particular actions are not true: that we open our eyes, move our head, or <margin>25</margin> extend our hands; and perhaps even that we do not have such hands or such a whole body. Nonetheless, it must <margin>11</margin>| surely be admitted that the things we see in sleep are like <term>painted images</term> <note>original: "pictas imagines". Descartes uses the analogy of art to suggest that even the most fantastic dreams are composed of "colors" or elements borrowed from reality.</note>, which could only have been formed in the likeness of real things. Therefore, at least these general things—eyes, head, hands, <margin>30</margin> and the whole body—exist not as imaginary things, but as real ones. For even painters themselves, even when...

<summary>Descartes introduces his famous "Dream Argument," observing that the sensations of being awake are often indistinguishable from those in dreams. He concludes that while specific details (like having hands) might be illusions, the basic "components" of our thoughts must be derived from something real.</summary>

<keywords>madness, black bile, dream argument, wakefulness vs. sleep, reality of the body, mental illusions, Descartes</keywords>

--- Page 50 ---
<meta>This page continues Descartes's "Dream Argument." Having suggested that our senses might deceive us even about our own bodies (thinking we are sitting by a fire when we are actually in bed), he now considers whether there are "building blocks" of reality—like shape and number—that remain true even in dreams.</meta>

### WORKS OF DESCARTES. 10-11.

...indeed, when <term>painters</term> <note>Descartes uses the analogy of an artist to explain how our minds construct illusions from real components.</note> strive to create <term>Sirens</term> <note>original: "Sirenas". Mythological creatures, typically half-woman and half-bird or fish.</note> and <term>Satyrs</term> <note>original: "Satyriſcos". Mythological Greek spirits of the woods, half-man and half-goat.</note> with the most unusual forms, they cannot assign to them natures that are new in every respect, but can only mix together the limbs of different animals; or if by chance they devise something so new that nothing at all like it has ever been seen, and is thus completely fictional and false, at least the colors from which they compose it must be real. In no different way, although even these general things—eyes, head, hands, and the like—could be <margin>10</margin> imaginary, one must still necessarily admit that certain other even more simple and universal things are true, from which all those images of things—whether true or false—that are in our thought are formed, just as if from true colors.

<margin>12</margin> To this class of things seem to belong <term>corporeal nature</term> <note>original: "natura corporea". This refers to the fundamental "stuff" that physical objects are made of.</note> in <margin>15</margin> general, and its <term>extension</term> <note>original: "extensio". For Descartes, this is the defining characteristic of physical matter: the fact that it takes up space in length, width, and depth.</note>; likewise the shape of extended things; likewise quantity, or their magnitude and number; likewise the place in which they exist, the time through which they endure, and similar things.

Because of this, we might not be wrong to conclude <margin>20</margin> that <term>Physics</term>, <term>Astronomy</term>, <term>Medicine</term>, and all other disciplines which depend on the consideration of composite things, are indeed doubtful; but <term>Arithmetic</term>, <term>Geometry</term>, and others of this kind, which treat only the simplest and most general things, <margin>25</margin> and care little whether those things exist in nature or not, contain something certain and indubitable. For whether I am awake or whether I sleep, two and three joined together are five, and a square has no more sides than four; and it does not seem possible that such <margin>30</margin> transparent truths could fall under the suspicion of falsehood.

<summary>Descartes argues that while our complex experiences might be illusions, the basic building blocks of reality—extension, shape, and mathematical truths—remain certain even in dreams.</summary>
<keywords>extension, corporeal nature, dream argument, mathematics, geometry, arithmetic, physics, sirens, satyrs, certainty</keywords>

--- Page 51 ---
<meta>This page continues from Descartes’s exploration of the "building blocks" of reality. Having previously argued that even if we are dreaming, basic concepts like shape and number seem certain, he now introduces one of his most famous and radical doubts: the possibility of a "deceiving God" or a flaw in our very nature that makes even simple math unreliable.</meta>

## MEDITATIONS. — FIRST.

<sig>*</sig>

<margin>11-12.</margin> Nevertheless, there is a certain long-standing opinion fixed in my mind: that there is a <term>God</term> <note>original: "Deum". Descartes is referring to the traditional concept of an all-powerful creator.</note> who can do all things, and by whom I was created as the kind of being I exist as. But how do I know that He has not brought it about that there is no earth at all, no sky, no <margin>5</margin> <term>extended thing</term> <note>original: "res extensa". For Descartes, this is the fundamental nature of physical matter—anything that takes up space.</note>, no shape, no size, no |<margin>13</margin> place, and yet all these things seem to me to exist exactly as they do now? Furthermore, just as I judge that others sometimes err regarding those things they think they know most perfectly, might I not be deceived whenever I add <margin>10</margin> two and three together, or count the sides of a square, or if anything even easier can be imagined? But perhaps God did not wish me to be so deceived, for He is said to be <term>supremely good</term> <note>original: "summe bonus". A central tenet of the theology of Descartes's time was that God's nature is purely good and cannot involve deception.</note>; yet, if it were repugnant to His goodness to have created me such that I am always <margin>15</margin> deceived, it would seem equally foreign to that same goodness to allow me to be deceived even sometimes; and yet, it cannot be said that He does not allow this.

There would be some, perhaps, who would prefer to deny such a powerful God rather than believe that all other things are uncertain. But let us not <margin>20</margin> oppose them, and let us grant that this whole idea of God is a fiction; regardless of whether they suppose I have reached my current state by fate, or by chance, or by a continuous chain of events, or by any other means; since being deceived and erring seems to be a certain imperfection, the <margin>25</margin> less powerful they make the author of my origin, the more probable it will be that I am so imperfect that I am always deceived. To these arguments I certainly have no |<margin>14</margin> answer, but I am finally forced to admit that there is nothing among those things I once thought were true which it is not permitted to <margin>30</margin> doubt, and this not out of thoughtlessness or levity, but because of powerful and well-considered reasons; therefore, from these things as well, no less than from those that are openly false,

<summary>Descartes introduces the possibility that an all-powerful God (or a flaw in his own origin) could cause him to be deceived even about basic mathematical truths like 2+3=5. He concludes that there is nothing he formerly believed that is not now subject to doubt.</summary>
<keywords>God, deception, mathematics, doubt, res extensa, imperfection, certainty</keywords>

--- Page 52 ---
<meta>This page continues Descartes’s systematic process of doubt. In the preceding lines, he explored the possibility that even mathematical truths could be deceptive if a powerful creator allowed it. He now transitions from theoretical doubt to a deliberate, practical exercise of withholding belief to avoid falling back into old habits of thought.</meta>

### WORKS OF DESCARTES.
<meta>12-13.</meta>

...that from now on, I must carefully withhold my <term>assent</term> <note>original: "assensionem". In Descartes's philosophy, this is the act of the will agreeing to a perception or thought.</note>, if I wish to find anything certain.

<margin>5</margin>
But it is not enough to have noticed these things; I must take care to remember them. For my habitual opinions constantly return, and they seize my belief as if bound to them by long use and the right of familiarity, almost even against my will. I shall never lose the habit of <margin>10</margin> assenting to and trusting them as long as I suppose them to be such as they truly are—namely, in some way doubtful, as has just been shown, but nonetheless highly probable, and which it is much more consistent with reason to believe than to deny. Therefore, I think I will not act wrongly if, by turning my will entirely in the opposite direction, I <margin>15</margin> deceive myself and pretend for a time that they are completely false and imaginary, until finally, as if the weights of <term>prejudice</term> <note>original: "praejudiciorum". These are the "pre-judgments" or unexamined beliefs we have held since childhood.</note> were equalized on both sides, no further <margin>15</margin> | bad habit may twist my judgment away from the correct perception of things. For I know that no danger or error will follow from this in the meantime, and that I cannot indulge in more distrust than is fair, since I am now <margin>20</margin> occupied not with acting, but only with knowing.

I will suppose, therefore, <gloss>a</gloss> not a <term>best God</term> <note>original: "optimum Deum". ...having fallen unexpectedly into a deep whirlpool, I am so disturbed that I can neither fix my foot on the bottom nor <margin>17</margin> swim up to the surface. I will strive, however, and I will attempt once more the same path which I entered upon yesterday, by removing, namely, everything that admits of even the slightest doubt, no less than if I had found it to be entirely false; and I will continue further until I know something certain, or, if nothing else, at least this very thing for certain: that nothing is certain. Archimedes <note>A Greek mathematician (c. 287–212 BC) who famously claimed that with a lever and a fixed fulcrum, he could move the Earth.</note> asked for nothing but a point that was firm and immovable, in order to move the entire earth from its place; great things are also to be hoped for, if I find even the smallest thing that is certain and unshakable <gloss>a. I suppose, therefore, that all things I see are false; I believe that nothing has ever existed of those things which my deceitful memory represents; I have no senses at all; body, shape, extension, movement, and place are chimeras <note>In this context, "chimeras" refers to mere figments of the imagination or impossible fictions.</note>. What, then, will be true? Perhaps this one thing: that nothing is certain.

But how do I know there is nothing different from all these things I have just reviewed, concerning which there is not even the slightest occasion for doubting? Is there not some God, or whatever name I might call him, who puts these very thoughts into me? But why <margin>18</margin> should I think this, since perhaps I myself could be the author of them? Am I not, then, at least something? But I have already denied that I have any senses and any body. Yet I hesitate; for what...

<margin>10</margin>Let us take, for example, this piece of wax: it has just been taken from the honeycomb; it has not yet lost all the taste of its honey; it retains something of the scent of the flowers from which it was gathered; its color, 
<margin>26</margin>shape, and size are obvious; it is 
<margin>15</margin>hard, cold, easily handled, and if you strike it with your knuckle, it will emit a sound; in short, everything is present in it that seems necessary for a body to be known as distinctly as possible. <margin>20</margin>the color changes, the shape is destroyed, its size increases, it becomes liquid, it becomes hot, it can hardly be touched, and now, if you strike it, it will not emit a sound. Does the same wax still remain? We must admit it does; no one denies it, no one thinks otherwise. 
<margin>25</margin>What was it, then, in the wax that was so distinctly understood? Certainly, it was nothing that I reached through the senses; for everything that fell under the senses of taste, smell, sight, touch, or hearing has now changed: and yet the wax remains.

<margin>30</margin>Perhaps it was what I am now thinking: namely, that the wax itself was not really that sweetness of honey, nor that fragrance of flowers, nor that 
<margin>27</margin>whiteness, nor that shape, nor that sound, but was a body that appeared to me a moment ago in those forms, and now appears in different ones. But what precisely is this thing that I imagine in this way? Let us pay attention—

...[let us] see, and, having removed those things that do not belong to the wax, let us see what remains: namely, nothing other than something extended, flexible, and changeable. But what is this flexible, changeable thing? Is it what I imagine—that this wax can be turned from a round shape into a square one, or from that into a triangle? 
<margin>5</margin>By no means; for I understand that it is capable of countless such changes, yet I cannot run through these countless changes by imagining them; therefore, this understanding <note>original: *comprehensio*</note> is not achieved by the faculty of imagination. What is "extended" <term>extension: in Cartesian philosophy, "extension" is the essential property of matter—the fact that it occupies space (length, breadth, and depth)</term>? <margin>10</margin>For in melting wax, the extension becomes larger; larger still in boiling wax, and larger again if the heat is increased; and I would not be judging correctly what the wax is, unless I thought that it was capable of more variations in extension than I have ever encompassed in my imagination. 

It remains, therefore, that I must grant that I do not even imagine what 
<margin>15</margin>this wax is, but perceive it with the mind alone; I say "this wax" in particular, for it is clearer regarding wax in general. But what is this wax which is only perceived by the mind? It is surely the same one that I see, 
<margin>20</margin>that I touch, that I imagine; the same one, finally, <margin>28</margin> that I thought it was from the beginning. However, what must be noted is that its perception is not vision, not touch, not imagination, nor was it ever, although it previously seemed so; but it is an inspection of the mind alone <note>original: *solius mentis inspectio*</note>, which 
<margin>25</margin>can be either imperfect and confused, as it was before, or clear and distinct, as it is now, depending on how much or how little I attend to those things of which it consists.

If I consider this by speaking out loud, I am still caught by the words themselves, and I am almost deceived by the very usage of ordinary speech. For we say that we *see* the wax itself, if it is present, and not that we *judge* it to be present from its color or shape. From this I would immediately conclude: 
<margin>5</margin> therefore, the wax is recognized by the sight of the eye, and not by the mind’s inspection <note>original: *inspectione*</note> alone; unless I happened to look out from a window at men passing in the street, whom I also say I *see* just as commonly as I say I see the wax. <margin>10</margin> robots <term>automata: Descartes was fascinated by the mechanical moving statues found in 17th-century royal gardens, using them as a metaphor for bodies without souls</term> could be hidden? Yet I *judge* them to be men.
<margin>29</margin> And so, what I thought I saw with my eyes, I actually comprehend solely by the faculty of judging, which is in my mind.

But I should be ashamed, as one who wishes to be wiser than the common crowd, to have sought doubt in the forms of speech that the common crowd invented; let us proceed instead by paying attention to whether I 
<margin>15</margin> perceived what the wax was more perfectly and evidently when I first looked at it—and believed I knew it by the external sense itself, or at least by the "common sense" <note>original: *sensus communis*; in historical philosophy, this was the faculty thought to unite the five different senses</note> as they call it, that is, by the power of imagination—or whether I perceive it more perfectly 
<margin>20</margin> now, after I have more diligently investigated both what it is <gloss>a</gloss> and how it is known? Certainly, it would be foolish to doubt this; for what was distinct in that first perception? What was there that even any animal might not seem to have? But truly, when 
<margin>24</margin> I distinguish the wax from its external forms, and consider it as if its "clothes" had been taken off and it were 
<margin>25</margin> naked, then, even though there might still be an error in my judgment, I truly cannot perceive it in this way without a human mind.

But what shall I say about this mind itself, or about myself? For I do not yet admit that anything else exists in me except a mind <note>original: *mentem*</note>. <margin>30</margin> What, I ask, of me—I who seem to perceive this wax so distinctly? Do I not know myself not only much <margin>5</margin> more truly and certainly, but also much more distinctly and evidently? For, if I judge that the wax exists because I see it, it is certainly much more evident that I myself also exist, from the very fact that I see it. For it is possible that what <margin>10</margin> I see is not truly wax; it is possible that I do not even have eyes with which anything might be seen; but it is clearly impossible, when I see, or (which I no longer distinguish) when I think <note>original: *cogitem*</note> I see, that I myself who am thinking am not something. By a similar logic, if I judge the wax to be there <margin>15</margin> because I touch it, the same thing will follow: namely, that I exist. If I judge it because I imagine it, or for any other reason, it is plainly the same. Moreover, what I observe about the wax can be applied to all other things situated outside of me. Furthermore, if the <margin>20</margin> perception of the wax seemed more distinct after it became known to me from many causes—not just from sight or touch—how much more distinctly must it be admitted that I now know myself! <margin>31</margin> Since no reasons can assist in the perception of wax or any other body without those same reasons proving the nature <margin>25</margin> of my mind even better! But there are so many other things in the mind itself from which its knowledge can be made more distinct, that those things which flow to it from the body seem hardly worth counting.
<margin>30</margin> And look, I have finally returned of my own accord to where <note>The text cuts off here, leading into the conclusion that the mind is easier to know than the body.</note>

<meta>This page continues Descartes’s "Third Meditation," specifically the section where he develops his causal argument for the existence of God. This page introduces the "Causal Adequacy Principle": the idea that there must be at least as much reality in the cause as there is in the effect.</meta>

And this is not only clearly true of those effects whose reality is actual or formal <term>formal reality: "realitas formalis," meaning the reality a thing has in the actual world, independent of our thoughts.</term>, but also of ideas, in which only objective reality <term>objective reality: "realitas objectiva," the reality of the content represented within an idea.</term> is considered. For <margin>15</margin> although that cause transfers nothing of its actual or formal reality into my idea, one must not therefore think that the cause must be less real; rather, such is the nature of the idea itself that it requires no other formal reality of itself, except that which it borrows from my thought <margin>20</margin>, of which it is a mode <term>mode: "modus," a specific state or modification of the mind, like a single thought or feeling.</term>. However, that this idea contains this or that objective reality rather than another, this it must surely have from some cause in which there is at least as much formal reality as the idea contains objective [reality]. For if <margin>25</margin> we suppose that something is found in the idea that was not in <margin>43</margin> its cause, it therefore has this from nothing; and however imperfect this mode of being is—by which a thing is objectively in the intellect through an idea—it is certainly not plainly nothing, and therefore cannot come from nothing. <margin>30</margin> Nor should I suspect that, since the reality I consider in my ideas is only objective, there is no need...

...is that the same reality must be formally <term>formal reality: "realitas formalis," the actual, mind-independent existence of a thing.</term> in the causes of those ideas, but that it is sufficient if it is in them even objectively <term>objective reality: "realitas objectiva," the reality of the content represented within an idea.</term>. And although perhaps one <margin>5</margin> idea can be born from another, there is not, however, an infinite regress <note>original: "progressus in infinitum"</note> here; instead, one must eventually reach some first idea, whose cause is like an archetype <term>archetype: "instar archetypi," a primary model or original from which others are derived.</term>, in <margin>10</margin> | which all the reality is contained formally that is only in the idea objectively. And the longer and more carefully I examine all these things, the more clearly and distinctly I recognize them to be true. But what finally should I conclude from this? Namely, if the objective reality of any of my ideas is so great that I am certain <margin>20</margin> the same is not in me either formally or eminently <term>eminently: "eminenter," possessing a quality in a higher, more superior form than the effect it produces.</term>, and therefore that I myself cannot be the cause of that idea, it follows necessarily that I am not alone in the world, but that some other thing, which is the cause of that idea, also exists. If, however, no such idea is found in me, I <margin>25</margin> will have no <gloss>a</gloss> argument at all to make me certain of the existence of any thing different from myself; for I have looked around most diligently at everything, and so far I have been able to find no other.

<meta>This page continues Descartes’s "Third Meditation," where he categorizes the ideas in his mind to determine their origin. Having established that an idea's cause must have as much reality as the idea represents, he now tests whether he, the thinker, could be the author of his own ideas about other people, animals, angels, and the physical world. He specifically breaks down physical objects into "clear and distinct" mathematical properties (like size and shape) and "confused" sensory qualities (like color and heat).</meta>

-># MEDITATIONS. — THIRD.<-

<margin>5</margin> And as for the ideas <term>ideas: "ideas."</term> that display other men, or <margin>45</margin> animals, or Angels, I easily understand that those can be composed from the ideas I have of myself, of corporeal things <term>corporeal things: "rerum corporalium," physical or bodily objects.</term>, and of God, even if no other men, nor animals, nor Angels existed in the world.

<margin>10</margin> However, as for the ideas of corporeal things, nothing occurs in them that is so great that it does not seem possible for it to have originated from myself; for if I look more closely and examine each one in the way I examined the idea of wax yesterday <note>A reference to the famous "wax argument" in the Second Meditation, where Descartes concludes that the essence of wax is not its smell or color, but its "extension."</note>, I notice that there are only very few things that <margin>15</margin> I perceive clearly and distinctly in them: namely, magnitude, or extension <term>extension: "extensio," the property of taking up space in three dimensions.</term> in length, breadth, and depth; shape, which arises from the termination of that extension; position, which differently shaped things maintain among themselves; and motion, or the change of that position; to <margin>20</margin> which can be added substance <term>substance: "substantia," that which exists independently.</term>, duration <term>duration: "duratio."</term>, and number <term>number: "numerus."</term>. <summary>Descartes argues that his ideas of other people, animals, and angels could be constructed from his own thoughts, and that physical objects are primarily defined by mathematical properties like extension and shape. He introduces "material falsity" to describe confused sensory perceptions like heat or color, which might not represent anything real at all.</summary>

<summary>Descartes argues that "confused" sensory ideas like heat and cold might be "materially false" and originate from his own imperfections. However, he notes that his clear ideas of physical objects—such as substance and number—might be derived from his own self-conception as a "thinking substance."</summary>

# MEDITATION IV.

## Concerning the True and the False.

And indeed, I have a much more distinct idea of the human mind, insofar as it is a **thinking thing** <term>thinking thing: *res cogitans*; Descartes’ famous definition of the soul or mind as a substance that lacks physical extension but possesses the capacity for thought, doubt, and will.</term>, not extended in length, breadth, or depth, nor having anything of the body, <margin>60</margin> than I have of any bodily thing. And now I seem to see a path by which we may move from this <margin>15</margin> contemplation of the true God—in whom, indeed, are hidden all the treasures of the sciences and of wisdom—to the knowledge of other things. <margin>20</margin>

For in the first place, I recognize that it is impossible that He should ever deceive me; for in every fraud or deception some imperfection is found; and although being able to deceive might seem to be <margin>25</margin> some proof of cleverness or power, undoubtedly the will to deceive testifies to malice or weakness, and therefore does not apply to God <margin>61</margin>.

Next, I experience that there is in me a certain faculty of judgment, <margin>30</margin> which certainly, like everything else that is in me...
