[...all that is in me], I received from God; and since He does not wish to deceive me, He certainly did not give me a faculty <note>original: "talem [facultatem]"; referring to the ability to judge or reason.</note> such that, as long as I use it correctly, I could ever fall into error.

<margin>5</margin>
Nor would any doubt remain on this matter, were it not for the fact that it seems to follow that I can therefore never err. For if everything that is in me I have from God, and if He gave me no faculty for making mistakes, it would seem that I could never go wrong. And indeed, as long as I think only of God and turn myself entirely toward <margin>10</margin> Him, I find no cause for error or falsehood; yet, when I return my focus to myself, I experience that I am nonetheless subject to countless errors. In seeking the cause of these, I notice that I have not only a real and positive idea of God—that is, of a supremely perfect <margin>15</margin> being—but also, so to speak, a certain negative idea of **nothingness** <term>nothingness: *nihil*; in Descartes' system, this represents the absolute absence of perfection, the opposite pole to God’s total perfection.</term>, or of that which is furthest removed from all perfection. I see that I <margin>**62**</margin> am constituted as a kind of middle ground between God and nothingness, or between the highest being and non-being. Insofar as I was created by the highest being, there is nothing in me <margin>20</margin> that would cause me to be deceived or led into error; but insofar as I also participate, in a way, in nothingness or non-being—that is, insofar as I am not myself the supreme being and lack many things—it is not surprising that I fall into error. Thus I certainly understand that error, as <margin>25</margin> such, is not something real that depends upon God, but is merely a **defect** <term>defect: *defectus*; an absence of a capacity that should be there, or a limitation of a finite being.</term>. Consequently, I do not require a specific faculty granted by God for the purpose of making mistakes; rather, I happen to err because the faculty of judging the truth, which I received from Him, <margin>30</margin> is not infinite within me.

Nonetheless, this is not yet entirely satisfactory; for...

<summary>Descartes reasons that since God is not a deceiver, human error must not come from a faculty God provided, but rather from the fact that humans are finite beings positioned between perfect "Being" (God) and "non-being."</summary>

[...nothingness,] for error is not a pure **negation** <term>negation: *negatio*; the simple absence of a thing that was never intended to be there in the first place.</term>, but a **privation** <term>privation: *privatio*; the lack of a quality or knowledge that a being ought naturally to possess.</term>, or the lack of some knowledge that somehow ought to be in me; and to one who considers the nature of God, it does not seem possible that He should have placed any faculty in me <margin>5</margin> which is not perfect in its kind, or which is deprived of any perfection due to it. <margin>63</margin> For if, the more skilled the craftsman is, the more perfect the works produced by him, what could have been made by that supreme creator of all things that is not complete in every respect <note>original: "omnibus numeris absolutum"; a Latin idiom meaning "perfect in every detail."</note>? <margin>10</margin> Nor is there any doubt that God could have created me such that I would never be deceived; nor is there any doubt that He always wills what is best: is it therefore better for me to be deceived than not to be? 

While I weigh these things more carefully, it first occurs to <margin>15</margin> me that I should not wonder if some things are done by God whose reasons I do not understand; nor should His existence be doubted for the reason that I perhaps experience some other things to exist, though I do not comprehend why or how they were made by Him. From these things, I perceive that neither the power of **willing** <gloss>the will</gloss>, which I have from God, viewed by itself, is the cause of my errors—for it is most ample and perfect in its kind—nor even the power of understanding. For whatever I understand, since I have from God the capacity to understand it, I undoubtedly understand it correctly, and it is impossible for me to be deceived in that. Whence, then, do my errors arise? Truly, from this one thing: that since the **will** <gloss>voluntas</gloss> extends further than the **intellect** <gloss>intellectus</gloss>, I do not contain it within the same limits, but also extend it to those things which I do not understand. Since the will is indifferent to these things, it easily turns away from the true and the good; in this way, I am both deceived and I sin.

For example, when I was examining these past few days whether anything existed in the world, and I noticed that from the very fact that I was examining it, it evidently followed that I existed, I could not help but judge that what I understood so clearly was true; not that I was [forced] by some ex- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "externa" (external), which will be completed on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ examination of the will and the intellect. On the previous page, he defined "indifference" as the lowest grade of freedom, occurring when the mind lacks clear evidence. ### MEDITATIONS. — FOURTH.

...not that I was compelled to it by any external force, but because a **great light in the intellect** <note>original: "ex magnâ luce in intellectu"; a metaphor for clear and distinct rational intuition</note> was followed by a great inclination in the **will** <gloss>voluntas</gloss>, and thus I believed it all the more spontaneously and freely, the more I was <margin>69</margin> far from being **indifferent** <term>indifferent: *indifferens*; the state of being undecided because no reason pulls the mind one way or the other</term> toward it. 

<margin>5</margin> But now, I do not only know that I exist, insofar as I am a certain **thinking thing** <term>thinking thing: *res cogitans*; the essence of the self in Descartes’ philosophy, defined by mental activity rather than physical extension</term>, but moreover a certain idea of corporeal nature presents itself to me. It <margin>10</margin> happens that I doubt whether the thinking nature which is in me—or rather, which I myself am—is different from that corporeal nature, or whether both are the same; and I suppose that no reason has yet occurred to my intellect that persuades me of one more than the other. Certainly, from this very fact, I am **indifferent** as to whether I should affirm or <margin>15</margin> deny it, or even whether I should make no judgment at all on the matter.

Indeed, this indifference does not extend only to those things of which the intellect knows nothing at all, but generally to all things which are not clearly enough perceived by it at the very time <margin>20</margin> when the will deliberates upon them. For however much probable conjectures may pull me toward one side, the mere knowledge that they are only conjectures, and not certain and indubitable reasons, is enough to push my assent <margin>70</margin> in the opposite direction. I have had enough experience of this in recent days, when I assumed that all those things which I had previously believed to be <margin>25</margin> most true were plainly false, for the simple reason that I had discovered they could be doubted in some way.

However, when I do not perceive what the truth is with sufficient clarity and distinctness, if I simply abstain from making a judgment, it <margin>30</margin> is clear that I act rightly and am not deceived. But if I either affirm or deny, then I am not using my **freedom of choice** <gloss>libertas arbitrii</gloss> correctly; and...

<summary>Descartes explains that clear intellectual perception naturally moves the will to believe, while "indifference" arises from a lack of evidence. He concludes that the most certain way to avoid error is to withhold judgment on any matter that is not perfectly clear and distinct.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Meditation IV, where Descartes investigates the source of human error. He has established that error arises not from God, nor from the intellect (which simply perceives ideas), nor from the will (which is perfect in its own kind), but from the will outstripping the intellect and judging things it does not clearly understand. This page concludes that God is not responsible for the finite nature of human understanding.</meta>

### WORKS OF DESCARTES

If I turn toward the side that is false, I shall be plainly deceived; if, however, I embrace the other side, I may happen upon the truth by chance, but I will not be free of blame, because it is manifest by the **natural light** <note>original: "lumine naturali"; the innate power of human reason to recognize self-evident truths</note> that the perception of the **intellect** <gloss>intellectus</gloss> must always precede the determination of the **will** <gloss>voluntatis</gloss>. 

<margin>5</margin> And it is in this incorrect use of **free will** <term>free will: *liberi arbitrii*; the faculty of choosing or judging freely</term> that the **privation** <term>privation: *privatio*; the absence of a perfection or quality that should normally be present</term> exists which constitutes the form of error. This privation, I say, is in the operation itself, insofar as it proceeds from me; but it is not in the faculty which I received from God, nor even in the <margin>10</margin> operation insofar as it depends on Him. 

For I have no cause to complain that God did not give me a greater power of understanding, or a greater **natural light** than He did; for it is the <margin>71</margin> nature of a **finite intellect** <note>original: "intellectûs finiti"</note> not to understand many things, and it is the <margin>15</margin> nature of a created intellect to be finite. Rather, I should give thanks to Him, who never owed me anything, for what He has bestowed, instead of thinking that I have been deprived by Him, or that He has taken away from me those things which He never gave. 

<margin>20</margin> Nor do I have cause to complain that He gave me a **will** that is wider in scope than my intellect. Since the will consists in only one thing, and is, as it were, something **indivisible** <note>original: "indivisibili"; Descartes views the will as a "yes/no" faculty that cannot be divided into parts</note>, its nature does not seem to allow for anything to be taken away from it; and truly, the more ample it is, the <margin>25</margin> greater the thanks I owe to its giver. 

Finally, I should not complain that God concurs with me in performing those acts of the will, or those judgments, in which I am deceived. For those acts are entirely true and good insofar as they depend on God, and it is, in a <margin>30</margin> way, a greater perfection in me that I can perform them than if I could not. However, the **privation**, in which alone the essence <note>Text cuts off at "ratio" (reason/essence)</note>...

He concludes that humans have no right to complain about their finite intellect or their expansive will, as both are gifts rather than entitlements.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Meditation, in which Descartes analyzes the nature of human error. Having established that error is a "privation"—a lack of knowledge rather than a positive "thing" created by God—he now argues that God is not to blame for human fallibility, as a universe with diverse parts (some more perfect than others) is more perfect than one where everything is identical.</meta>

### 60-61. MEDITATIONS. — FOURTH.

<margin>72</margin> [In this] the **formal falsity** <term>formal falsity: *formalis falsitatis*; the essential nature of an error as it exists in the mind's judgment</term> and fault consists, it requires no **concurrence** <note>original: "concursu"; in Scholastic philosophy, this refers to God's "cooperation" or sustaining power required for any action to occur</note> from God, because it is not a "thing," nor should it be called a **privation** <term>privation: *privatio*; the absence of a quality that ought to be present by nature</term> relative to Him as its cause, but only a **negation** <term>negation: *negatio*; a simple absence or lack of something that is not necessarily required for a being's nature</term>. For certainly there is no imperfection in God for having given me the liberty to assent or not to assent to certain things of which He did not place a **clear and distinct perception** <note>original: "claram & distinctam perceptionem"; for Descartes, the gold standard of truth</note> in my **intellect** <gloss>intellectus</gloss>; but without doubt there is an imperfection in me, that I do not use this liberty well, and that I pass judgment on things that I do not correctly understand. 

However, I see that it could easily have been brought about by God that, even though I remained free and possessed **finite knowledge** <note>original: "cognitionis finitæ"</note>, I would never err: namely, if He had either bestowed upon my intellect a clear and distinct perception of everything I was ever to deliberate upon; or if He had only so firmly impressed it upon my memory—that I should never judge anything I did not clearly and distinctly understand—that I could never forget it. And I easily understand that I, insofar as I am a part of a certain whole, would have been more perfect than I am now, if I had been made so by God. 

<margin>73</margin> But I cannot for that reason | deny that it is in some way a greater perfection in the **entire universe** <gloss>tota rerum universitate</gloss> that some of its parts are not immune from error while others are, than if they were all | entirely alike. And I have no right to complain that God willed me to sustain that role in the world which is not the most principal and most perfect of all.

Furthermore, even if I cannot abstain from errors in that first way, which depends on the evident perception of all those things upon which one must deliberate, I can nevertheless do so in that other way <gloss>a</gloss> which depends only on...

<summary>Descartes argues that while God could have created humans who never err, the presence of fallible beings contributes to the overall perfection of a diverse universe. He distinguishes between 'negation' (a simple lack) and 'privation' (a lack of what one should have) to absolve God of responsibility for human mistakes.</summary>

--- Page 92 ---
<meta>This page concludes the Fourth Meditation. Descartes transitions from discussing the nature of error as a "privation" to the practical solution: how a human being, despite having a finite intellect, can avoid falling into falsehood by exercising the will correctly.</meta>

### WORKS OF DESCARTES.
#### 62

...that I remember, whenever the truth of a matter is not clear, I must abstain from passing judgment. For, although I experience a certain weakness in my nature such that I cannot always remain fixed upon one and the same piece of knowledge, I can nonetheless, through attentive and frequently repeated **meditation** <note>original: "meditatione"; here Descartes refers to the disciplined mental exercise he is currently practicing</note>, ensure that I remember this rule whenever the need arises, and in this way I may acquire a certain **habit of not erring** <note>For Descartes, virtue and truth are not just about single moments of insight, but about training the mind to behave reliably over time.</note>.

<margin>74</margin> Since the greatest and most important perfection of man consists in this ability, I believe I have gained no small amount from today’s meditation, having investigated the cause of error and falsity. And truly, there can be no cause other than the one I have explained; for as often as I restrain my **will** <gloss>voluntas</gloss> in making judgments so that it extends only to those things which are **clearly and distinctly** <note>original: "clare & diſtincte"; the Cartesian standard for truth—information that is so present to the mind and so precise that it cannot be doubted.</note> presented to it by the **intellect** <gloss>intellectus</gloss>, it is absolutely impossible for me to err. This is because every clear and distinct perception is undoubtedly "something," and therefore cannot come from nothing; instead, it necessarily has God as its author—God, I say, that **supremely perfect being** <note>original: "ſumme perfectum"</note>, whom it is contradictory to call a deceiver; and therefore, such a perception is undoubtedly true.

Today I have learned not only what I must avoid so that I am never deceived, but also what I must do to attain the truth. For I will surely attain it if I only pay enough attention to all the things that I **perfectly understand**, and separate them from the rest, which I apprehend more confusedly and obscurely. To this task I will diligently apply myself hereafter.

<summary>Descartes concludes that error is avoided by restraining the will to judge only what the intellect perceives clearly and distinctly. He establishes that clear perceptions must be true because they originate from God, who is not a deceiver.</summary>
<keywords>will, intellect, clear and distinct perception, habit of mind, divine perfection, certainty, method of doubt</keywords>

### MEDITATION VI.

->*Of the existence of material things, and the real distinction*<-
->*between the mind and the body.*<-

...I notice that a certain peculiar effort of mind is required for the act of imagining, which I do not employ for understanding <note>original: "intelligendum"; here referring to pure intellection or abstract thought</note>. This new effort of mind clearly shows the difference between imagination and pure intellection.

<margin>90</margin>
Furthermore, I consider that this power of imagining which is in me, insofar as it differs from the power of understanding, is not a necessary part of my essence—that is, the essence of my mind. For even if I lacked that power, I would without doubt remain the same person I am now; from which it seems to follow that the power of imagination depends upon something different from myself. And I easily understand that, if some body exists to which the mind is so joined that it can apply itself to look into it <note>original: "inspiciendum"</note> at will, it might be possible that through this very means I imagine corporeal things. Thus, this mode of thinking differs from pure intellection only in this: that the mind, when it understands, turns in a way toward itself and looks at one of the ideas inherent in it; but when it imagines, it turns toward the body and beholds something in it conforming to an idea either understood by itself or perceived by the sense. I easily understand, I say, that imagination could be performed in this way, provided that a body exists; and because no other equally convenient way of explaining it occurs to me, I therefore conjecture with probability that the body exists. But this is only a probability; and although I investigate everything accurately, I do not yet see how any argument can be drawn from that distinct idea of corporeal nature which I find in my imagination that necessarily concludes that any body exists.

<margin>102</margin>Nature also teaches me, by these sensations of pain, hunger, thirst and so on, that I am not merely present in my body as a sailor is present in a ship <note>original: "ut nauta adest navigio"; a famous metaphor Descartes uses to distinguish his view from a simple pilot-machine relationship</note>, but that I am very closely joined and, as it were, intermingled with it <insert>a</insert>, so much so that I and the body form a unit. If this were not the case, when my body is hurt, I, who am nothing but a thinking thing, would not feel pain because of that; instead, I would perceive that wound by the pure intellect, just as a sailor perceives by sight if anything in the ship is broken. And when the body needs food or drink, I would explicitly understand this very fact, rather than having confused sensations of hunger and thirst. For certainly these sensations of thirst, hunger, pain, etc., are nothing other than certain confused modes of thinking arising from the union and, as it were, intermingling of the mind with the body.

Moreover, I am also taught by nature that various other bodies exist around my body, some of which are to be sought after and others avoided. And certainly, from the fact that I perceive widely different colors, sounds, smells, tastes, heat, hardness, and the like, I rightly conclude that there are, in the bodies from which these various sensory perceptions arrive,
<margin>103</margin>variations corresponding to them, even if perhaps they are not similar to them. And because some of these perceptions are pleasant to me while others are unpleasant, it is plainly certain that my body—or rather my whole self, insofar as I am composed of body and mind—can be affected by various benefits and inconveniences from the surrounding bodies.

# WORKS OF DESCARTES. 85-86.

There are, however, many other things which, although I seem to have been taught them by nature, I did not actually receive from nature itself, but from a certain habit of judging inconsiderately; therefore, it easily happens that these things are false. Examples include the belief that any space in which nothing occurs that moves my senses is empty; that in a body which is hot, for instance, there is something exactly similar to the idea of heat which is in me; that in a white or green body there is the same whiteness or greenness that I feel; that in a bitter or sweet body there is the same taste, and so on for the rest. Other examples are that stars, towers, and any other distant bodies have only that size and shape which they present to my senses, and other such notions. 

But, lest I perceive anything in this matter without sufficient clarity, I ought to define more accurately what I properly mean when I say that I am "taught something by nature." <margin>104</margin> Truly, I am taking "nature" here in a stricter sense than as the combination of all things bestowed upon me by God. For in this combination many things are included that pertain to the mind alone—such as my perception that what has been done cannot be undone <note>original: "factum est infectum esse non posse"</note>, and all other things known by the natural light <note>The "natural light" (lumen naturale) refers to the God-given faculty of reason or intuition that reveals self-evident truths.</note>, which are not under discussion here. Many things are also included that relate only to the body, such as its tendency to move downward <note>Descartes refers to the contemporary understanding of gravity as a physical tendency of bodies.</note>, and similar things, which I am also not dealing with. Instead, I am speaking only of those things bestowed by God upon me as a composite of mind and body. 

Therefore, this nature does indeed teach me to flee from those things that bring a sense of pain, and to pursue those that bring a sense of pleasure, and so forth. But it does not appear that nature teaches us that we should conclude anything from these sensory perceptions regarding things placed outside of us without a prior examination by the intellect; because knowing the truth about such things <insert>seems to belong to the mind alone, not to the composite of mind and body.</insert>

# 89-90. MEDITATIONS. — SIXTH.

The dryness of the throat moves the body to take a drink that is useful to it. And although, looking at the preconceived use of a clock, I might say that it deviates from its nature when it does not indicate the hours correctly; and in the same way, <margin>5</margin> considering the machinery of the human body as being built for the movements that usually occur in it, I might think that it also wanders from its nature if its throat is dry when drink is not beneficial for its preservation; I nevertheless realize well enough that this last sense of "nature" <note>original: "naturae acceptionem"</note> differs greatly from the other. For this is nothing other than a label <term>denominatio: a name or classification applied by the mind rather than an inherent property</term> depending on my thought, which compares a sick man and a poorly made clock with the idea of a healthy man and a well-made clock, and is extrinsic to the things of which it is said; but by the other sense, I understand something that is truly found in things, and therefore possesses some truth.

And certainly, although in respect to a body suffering from dropsy <note>original: "hydrope laborans"; dropsy (edema) is a condition where fluid builds up in the body, causing the patient to feel thirsty even though drinking more fluid is harmful</note>, it is only an extrinsic label <margin>109</margin> <margin>20</margin> when its nature is said to be "corrupted" because it has a dry throat and yet does not need drink; nevertheless, in respect to the composite—that is, to the mind united to such a body—it is not a mere label, but a true error of nature, that it should feel thirst when drink is going to be harmful to it. <margin>25</margin> Therefore, it remains to be investigated here how the goodness of God does not prevent nature, understood in this way, from being deceptive.

Namely, I first notice here that there is a great difference between the mind and the body, in that the body by its nature is always divisible, while the mind is plainly <margin>30</margin> indivisible.

Nor can the faculties of willing, sensing, understanding, etc., be called its "parts," because it is one and the same mind that wills, that senses, and that understands. On the other hand, no corporeal or extended thing can be thought of by me which I cannot easily divide into parts in my thought, and by this very fact I understand it to be divisible. Next, I notice that the mind is not immediately affected by all parts of the body, but only by the brain, or perhaps even by only one small part of it—namely, by that part in which the "common sense" <note>original: "sensus communis." I notice, furthermore, that the nature of the body is such that no part of it can be moved by another part some distance away, without it being possible for it to be moved in the same way by any of the parts that lie between them, even if that more distant part does nothing. And the same must be thought regarding any other sense.

I notice, finally, that since each of the motions occurring in that part of the brain which immediately <margin>112</margin> affects the mind produces only one specific sensation in it, nothing better can be devised in this matter than that it should produce the one which, of all those it could produce, is most especially and most frequently conducive to the preservation of a healthy human being. Experience, moreover, testifies that all the senses given to us by nature are of this sort; and therefore, nothing at all is found in them that does not testify to the <term>power and goodness of God</term><note>original: "Dei potentiam bonitatemque"</note>. When the nerves in the foot are moved violently and beyond their usual manner, their motion passes through the marrow of the spinal cord <note>original: "spinæ dorsi medullam"</note> to the innermost parts of the brain. There, it gives a signal to the mind to feel something—namely, a pain as if existing in the foot. By this, the mind is stimulated to do its best to remove the cause of the pain as something harmful to the foot. Indeed, the nature of man could have been so constituted by God that this same motion in the brain presented something else entirely to the mind: perhaps the motion itself as it exists in the brain, or as it is in the foot, or in any of the <margin>413</margin> intermediate places, or finally, anything else at all. But nothing else would have contributed as well to the preservation of the body. In the same way, when we need a drink, a certain dryness arises in the throat, moving its nerves and, by their means, the interior of the brain; this motion affects the mind with the sensation of thirst, because in this whole matter nothing is more useful for us to know than that we need drink to maintain our health; and so it is with the rest.

From these facts it is entirely manifest that, notwithstanding the immense goodness of God, the nature of man—as a composite of mind and body—cannot help but sometimes be deceptive. For if any cause, not in the foot but in any other part through which the nerves extend from the foot to the brain, or even in the brain itself, excites the exact same motion which is usually excited by a foot in bad condition, pain will be felt as if in the foot, and the sense will be naturally deceived. This is because that same motion in the brain cannot help but always bring the same sensation to the mind; and since it usually arises much more frequently from a cause that harms the foot than from a cause existing elsewhere, it is consistent with reason <insert>that the sensation always represents a pain in the foot.</insert>

And if at any time a dryness of the throat arises, not as it usually does because a drink would be conducive to the body's health, but from some contrary cause, as happens in a person with dropsy <note>original: "hydropico"; a historical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid, which causes intense thirst even when drinking is harmful</note>, it is far better <gloss>a</gloss> that it should deceive the mind at that time than if, conversely, it were always to deceive when the body is well-constituted; and so it is with the rest.

And this consideration is greatly helpful, not only so that I may notice all the errors to which my nature is liable, but also so that I may easily be able to correct or avoid them. For indeed, since I know that all the senses indicate the truth much more frequently than the false regarding those things which concern the advantage of the body, and I can almost always use several of them to examine the same thing, and in addition, use memory, which connects present things with preceding ones, and the intellect, which has already perceived all the causes of error; I ought no longer to fear that those things which are daily presented to me by the senses are false. Rather, the hyperbolic <note>meaning "exaggerated" or "extreme"</note> doubts of the previous days are to be exploded <note>original: "explodendæ"; in the Latin sense of being hissed off a stage or rejected as ridiculous</note> as worthy of laughter. Especially that supreme doubt concerning sleep, which I did not distinguish from being awake; for now I notice that there is a very great difference between the two, in that dreams are never joined by memory with all the other actions of life, as those things which occur to a waking person are; for indeed, if someone, while I am awake, were suddenly to appear to me, and immediately afterwards disappear, as happens in dreams, such that I saw neither where he came from nor where he went, I would not without merit judge him to be a ghost...

### FIRST OBJECTIONS.

*Most Distinguished Gentlemen,*

As I saw that you were entirely of the mind that I should look more deeply into the writings of Master Descartes, I ought not to fail to comply with men who are in every way my friends: both so that you may see by this very act how much I value you, and also so that it may be clear how much my strength and talent fall short, so that in the future you may love me a little more if I am in need, and be less of a burden if I am not sufficient for the task.

If it is from itself, then it is God; for whatever exists from itself would easily have given itself all things.

-># FIRST OBJECTIONS.<-

## FIRST OBJECTIONS.

I ask and implore the man <note>Descartes</note> not to hide his meaning from the eager *Reader*, who perhaps understands less than he might. For the phrase "of itself" is taken in two ways. First, *positively*, namely from *itself as from a cause*; and in this sense, whatever would be of itself—giving itself its own being—if it gave itself what it wanted by *prior choice*, it would undoubtedly give itself everything, and thus would be God. Second, it is taken *negatively*, so that it is the same as "by itself," or "not from another"; and in this way, *as far as I remember*, it is understood by everyone.

Now, however, if something exists of itself (that is, not from another), how shall I prove that it encompasses all things and is infinite? For I no longer listen if you say: *if it is of itself, it would have easily given itself everything*. For it is not "of itself" as if from a cause, nor was it prior to itself so that it could choose beforehand what it would be afterward. I know I once heard Suarez <note>Francisco Suárez (1548–1617), a highly influential Jesuit philosopher and theologian</note> say this: *all limitation comes from a cause*; for a thing is limited and finite either because the cause could not give anything greater or more perfect, or because it did not wish to; if, therefore, something is of itself and not from a cause, it is surely unlimited and infinite.

I, however, do not entirely agree. For what if the limitation comes from *intrinsic constituent principles* <term>intrinsic constituent principles: the internal qualities or "ingredients" that make a thing what it is</term>, that is, from the *form and essence itself*, which you have not yet proved to be *infinite*, *however much it may be of itself (that is, not from another)*? Truly, *if you suppose that heat is heat, it will be hot and not cold because of its intrinsic constituent principles, even if you imagine that its very existence comes from no one*. I do not doubt that Mr. *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesio"</note> does not lack the reasons by which he might establish that which others perhaps have not presented clearly enough.

Finally, I agree with the man. He establishes this as a general rule: *whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly,*

*that is surely a true being*<gloss>a</gloss>. Indeed, *whatever* I think... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "cogito" (I think).</note>

<margin>127</margin> ...though I may be <note>original: "sim"</note>, I will nevertheless differ somewhat, which I cannot avoid. And in the first place, although we are not now acting by authority but by reason alone, nevertheless, lest I seem to resist a most great genius out of mere whim, listen rather to Saint Thomas himself. He poses this objection to himself: once it is understood what this name "God" signifies, it is immediately <margin>5</margin> held that God exists; for by this name is signified that than which nothing greater can be signified. Moreover, that which exists in reality and in the intellect is greater than that which is in the intellect alone; hence, since upon understanding this name "God," he is immediately in the intellect, it follows also that he is in reality. <margin>10</margin> <note>This is the famous "Ontological Argument" originally formulated by Anselm of Canterbury, which Aquinas famously critiqued.</note> I render this argument in formal logic as follows: God is that than which nothing greater can be signified; but that than which nothing greater can be signified includes existence; therefore God, by his very name or concept, includes existence, and accordingly can neither be conceived nor exist without existence. <margin>15</margin> Now, I ask you, is this not the very argument of Mr. Descartes? Saint Thomas defines God thus: *that than which nothing greater can be signified.* Mr. Descartes <note>original: "D. C." for Dominus Cartesius</note> calls him a *supremely perfect Being*; surely nothing greater than that can be signified. Saint Thomas assumes: that than which nothing <margin>128</margin> greater can be signified includes existence; otherwise <margin>20</margin> something greater than it could be signified, namely that which is also signified to include existence. But does not Mr. Descartes seem to assume the same? *God is a supremely perfect being, but a supremely perfect being includes existence, otherwise it would not be supremely perfect.* Saint Thomas infers: therefore, since <margin>25</margin> upon understanding this name "God," he is immediately in the intellect itself, it follows also that he is in reality; that is, by the very fact that existence is involved in the essential concept of a being than which nothing greater can be signified, it follows that this very being exists. From the fact that I cannot think of God except as existing, it follows that existence is inseparable from him, and therefore that he truly exists <note>original: "revera existere"</note>. <margin>129</margin> But now, let Saint *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and theologian.</note> respond both to himself and to Mr. *Descartes*: Even granted, he says, that everyone understands by this name *God* that which is signified—namely, that than which nothing greater can be thought—it does not follow from this that he understands that which is signified by the name to exist in the nature of things, but only in the apprehension of the intellect. Nor can it be argued that it exists in reality, unless it were granted that there is something in reality than which nothing greater can be thought; which is not granted by those who hold that God does not exist. <margin>130</margin> From which I also briefly respond: even if it is granted that a supremely perfect being implies existence by its very name, it still does not follow that this very existence is anything actual in the nature of things, but only that the concept of existence is inseparably joined with the concept of the highest being. From this you cannot infer that the existence of God is anything actual, unless you suppose that this highest being actually exists; for then it will actually include all perfections, including this one of real existence.

Forgive me, most distinguished men, I am tired; I shall play a little. This composite, *Existing Lion*, includes both, and indeed essentially: namely, the lion and the mode of existence. For if you take away either one, this same composite will not be. Now, however, has not *God* known this composite clearly and distinctly from eternity? And does not the idea of this composite, as a composite, essentially involve both of its parts? That is, does not existence belong to the essence of this...

### Most Distinguished Gentlemen<gloss>Descartes addresses his two friends, Bannius and Bloemaert, who acted as intermediaries between him and Caterus.</gloss>,

You have certainly stirred up a formidable adversary against me. His intellect and learning could have caused me a great deal of trouble, had this pious and most kind Theologian <note>Referring to Johan de Kater (Caterus), the author of the first objections.</note> not preferred to favor the cause of God—and even God's humble advocate—rather than to attack it in earnest. First, he summarized my principal argument for proving the existence of God in a few words, so that it might stick better in the readers' memory. And when the most learned Theologian <note>Referring to Johan de Kater, or Caterus, who wrote the First Objections to the Meditations.</note> says there is an **equivocation** <note>original: "æquivocationem"; a term used when a single word is used with different meanings, leading to confusion.</note> in those words, he seems to wish to warn me of the very point I just noted, lest I should perhaps be ignorant of it. But he adds nonetheless, **because it is only conceived, and is not in act** (that is, because it is only an idea, and not a thing positioned outside the intellect), it can indeed be conceived, **but it can by no means be caused** <note>original: "causari minime posse"</note>, that is, it does not require a **cause** in order to exist outside the intellect. This I grant, but it certainly requires a **cause** in order to be conceived, and the question is about this alone. Thus, if someone has in the intellect the idea of some **machine devised with the highest craftsmanship**, it can truly and deservedly be asked what the **cause** of that idea might be. Nor will it suffice if someone says that the idea is nothing outside the intellect, and therefore cannot be caused, but only conceived; for nothing else is sought here than what the **cause** is for its being conceived. Nor will he satisfy the question who says that the intellect itself is its **cause**, namely as the cause of its own operation; for there is no doubt about this matter, but only about the **cause** of the **objective craftsmanship** <note>original: "artificii objectivi"; the intricate design or "content" present within the idea itself.</note> which is in it. <margin>136</margin> If a machine contains such a specific objective craftsmanship <note>original: "artificium objectivum"; this refers to the design or structural complexity as it exists in the mind's eye</note> rather than another, it must surely derive this from some cause; and this objective craftsmanship is the same in relation to the machine as objective reality is in relation to the idea of God. Indeed, various causes for this craftsmanship can be assigned: it might be some real, physical machine seen previously, in whose likeness that idea was formed; or a great knowledge of Mechanics existing in that intellect; or perhaps a great subtlety of genius, by the help of which one could invent it even without prior knowledge. It must be noted that every bit of craftsmanship that exists only objectively in that idea must necessarily exist in its cause—whatever that cause may finally be—either formally or eminently <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "formally" means the cause has the property itself (a hot coal makes things hot); "eminently" means the cause possesses the property in a higher, more perfect form (God creating light without being light himself).</note>. And the same must be thought regarding the objective reality found in the idea of God. In whom, then, will this reality exist, unless in a God who really exists?

But the perceptive man <note>Referring to the author of the First Objections, the theologian Johannes Caterus.</note> saw all these points very well, and therefore admits it can be asked why this idea contains this specific objective reality rather than another; to this question he first responded: *regarding all ideas, the same holds true as what I wrote regarding the idea of a triangle; namely, even if perhaps a triangle exists nowhere in the world, there is nonetheless a certain determined nature, or essence, or immutable and eternal form of it.* <margin>137</margin> And he says that such a nature does not require a cause. Yet he saw that this did not quite satisfy the problem; for even if the nature of a triangle is immutable and eternal, one may nonetheless ask why its idea is within us. Therefore he added: *if, however, I were to stubbornly demand a reason, it would be the imperfection of our intellect, etc.* By which response he seems to have meant nothing other than that no likely answer can be given by those who wish to disagree with me on this matter.

Indeed, it is certainly no more probable that the cause of the idea of God being within us is the imperfection of our own intellect, than it is that a lack of mechanical skill is the cause of our imagining a highly ingenious machine rather than a more imperfect one. For quite to the contrary: if someone possesses the idea of a machine in which every conceivable artifice is contained, it is most rightly inferred that this idea flowed from some cause in which every conceivable artifice actually existed, even if it exists in that cause only objectively <note>original: "objective"; in Scholastic terms, this refers to the reality of an object as it exists in the mind as a representation.</note>. By the same reasoning, since we have within us the idea of God, in which every conceivable perfection is contained, it can be most evidently concluded from this that the idea depends on some cause in which all that perfection also exists—namely, in a God who truly exists.

<margin>138</margin>Truly, no greater difficulty would appear in the one case than in the other, if it were the case that—just as not everyone is a skilled mechanic and therefore cannot have ideas of highly ingenious machines—not everyone possessed the same faculty for conceiving the idea of God. But because that idea is implanted in the minds of all in the same way, and we never notice it coming to us from anywhere other than ourselves, we suppose it to belong to the very nature of our intellect. And indeed, this is not a wrong assumption, but we omit something else which must be especially considered, and upon which the entire force and light of this argument depends: namely, that this faculty of having the idea of God within itself could not be in our intellect if this ᵃ intellect were merely a finite being <note>original: "ens finitum"</note>.

Therefore, I preferred to use as the foundation of my reasoning my own existence, which does not depend on any series of causes and is so well known to me that nothing can be better known. Regarding myself, I did not ask so much by what cause I was produced in the past, as by what cause I am preserved in the present moment, so that I might thus free myself from any succession of causes.

Next, I did not ask what the cause of myself is insofar as I consist of mind and body, but precisely only insofar as I am a <term>thinking thing</term> <note>Latin: *res cogitans*; the core of Descartes' philosophy defining the self as a purely mental substance</note>. understand, when they say something exists *from itself* <note>original: "a se esse"; a central Scholastic and Cartesian concept regarding self-origination</note>, anything other than that it has no cause; yet if these same people would attend to the reality of the matter rather than the mere words, they would easily notice that the negative *acceptance* of the phrase "from oneself" proceeds only from the imperfection of the human intellect and has no foundation in reality. There is, however, another positive sense derived from the truth of things, and it is from this sense alone that my argument proceeded. For if, for example, someone thinks that some body exists *from itself*, perhaps they understand nothing more than that it has no cause; and they do not affirm this for any positive reason, but only negatively, because they recognize no cause for it. And yet <margin>145</margin> this is a certain imperfection in them, as they will easily experience later if they consider that the parts of time do not depend upon one another. Consequently, from the fact that this body is supposed to have existed *from itself* up to this time—that is, without a cause—it does not follow that this is sufficient for it to continue to exist in the future, unless there is some power in it that, as it were, continually reproduces it. For then, seeing that no such power is found in the idea of a body, they will immediately conclude that it does not exist *from itself*, taking this phrase *from itself* in a positive sense. In a similar way, when we say God exists *from itself*, we can indeed also understand this negatively, so that the meaning is merely that He has no cause; but if we have previously inquired into the cause of why He exists, or why He continues to exist, and attending to the immense and incomprehensible power contained in the idea of Him, we recognize that power to be so exuberant that it is clearly the cause why He continues to exist, and that there can be no other cause besides it, we then say God exists *from itself*, no longer negatively, but in the highest degree positively. To avoid a mere dispute over words regarding whether God is the <term>efficient cause</term><note>The agent or power that brings something into being.</note> of himself, we must recognize that we perceive his existence—being from himself or having no cause distinct from himself—not as coming from nothing, but from the real immensity of his power. Therefore, it is entirely permissible for us to think that he, in a certain sense, performs the same role toward himself that an efficient cause performs toward its effect, and consequently that he exists from himself in a positive sense. It is also permissible for each person to ask themselves whether they exist from themselves in that same sense; and when they find no power within themselves sufficient to preserve their own existence even for a single moment, they rightly conclude that they derive their being from another. Furthermore, this other must be from itself, because since the question concerns the present time—not the past or the future—one cannot proceed to infinity in a chain of causes. Indeed, I will add here what I have not written before: one cannot even stop at any secondary cause. Rather, whatever has so much power that it can preserve a thing placed outside itself must, all the more so, preserve itself by its own power <insert>a</insert>, and thus exist from itself <insert>b</insert>.

And indeed, here I distinguish between the *indefinite* and the *infinite*. I properly call only that *infinite* in which no limits can be found in any respect; in this sense, God alone is infinite. However, those things in which I simply do not recognize a limit under a certain respect—such as the extension of imaginary space, the multitude of numbers, the divisibility of the parts of quantity, and the like—I call *indefinite* indeed, but not *infinite*, because they are not without limits in every respect. <note>original: "indefinita... non autem infinita". Descartes uses this distinction to separate the mathematical potential for endlessness from the actual, perfect infinity of God.</note>

Furthermore, I distinguish between the *formal* reason <note>The "formal reason" or "formal concept" refers to the essential definition or nature of a thing.</note> of the infinite, or infinity, and the thing which is infinite. For as far as infinity is concerned, even if we understand it to be in the highest degree positive, we nevertheless only understand it in a certain negative way, namely from the fact that we perceive no limitation in the thing. But the thing itself which is infinite, we do indeed understand positively, but not adequately; that is, we do not comprehend everything in it that is intelligible. 

But, just as when we turn our eyes toward the sea, even if our vision does not reach the whole of it nor do we measure its immense vastness, we are still said to see it; and indeed, if we look from a distance so that we embrace the whole at once with our eyes, we see it only confusedly—just as we also confusedly imagine a chiliogon <note><term>chiliogon</term>: A polygon with 1,000 sides. Descartes often uses this example to show that while we can understand a mathematical concept, we cannot clearly visualize it in our mind's eye.</note> when we embrace all its sides at once. But if we fix our gaze closely upon some part of the sea, such a vision can be very clear and distinct, just as the imagination of a chiliogon can be if it extends only to one or two of its sides. In a similar way, God cannot be grasped by the human mind, since <margin>See volume III, page 273, line 27.</margin>

He here again compares one of my arguments with another from Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval philosopher and theologian.</note>, as if to force me to show what greater force is found in the one than in the other. And this I seem to be able to do without great ill-will, because neither did Saint Thomas use that argument as his own, nor does it conclude the same thing as mine, nor finally do I disagree in any matter here with the Angelic Doctor <note>A traditional title for St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>. For it is asked by him whether "God exists" is self-evident to us, that is, whether it is obvious to everyone; which he denies, and rightly so. However, the argument which he objects to himself can be proposed thus: *Once it is understood what this name "God" signifies, it is understood to be that than which nothing greater can be signified; but it is greater to exist in reality and in the intellect than to exist in the intellect alone; therefore, once it is understood what this name "God" signifies, it is understood that God exists in reality and in the intellect.*ᵇ <note>original: "Intellecto quid significet hoc nomen Deus..." It should be noted that in the concept or idea of all those things which are clearly and distinctly understood, possible existence is contained ^c, but necessary existence is found nowhere except in the idea of God alone. Even if we never understand other things except as existing, it does not follow from this that they actually exist, but only that they *can* exist. This is because we do not understand it to be necessary that actual existence is joined with their other properties. However, from the very fact that we understand actual existence to be necessarily and always joined with the rest of God's <term>attributes|The inherent qualities or characteristics of God, such as omnipotence or infinity</term>, it follows absolutely that God exists.

Next, to remove the other part of the difficulty, it must be noted that those ideas which do not contain true and immutable natures, but only fictitious ones composed by the intellect, can be divided by that same intellect—not merely by <term>abstraction|The mental process of considering a property or quality apart from the object it belongs to</term>, but through a clear and distinct operation. Thus, those things which the intellect cannot divide in this way were, without a doubt, not composed by it. 

For example, when I think of a winged horse, or a lion actually existing, or a triangle inscribed in a square, I easily understand that I can also think, conversely, of a horse without wings, a lion not existing, and a triangle without a square, and so on. <margin>155</margin> Therefore, these things do not have true and immutable natures. 

But if I think of a triangle or a square (I do not speak of a lion or a horse here, because their natures are not entirely clear to us), then certainly whatever I find to be contained in the idea of a triangle—such as that its three angles are equal to two right angles <note>A fundamental theorem in Euclidean geometry</note>, etc.—I will affirm with truth regarding the triangle; and whatever I find in the idea of a square, I will affirm of the square. <meta>This page continues the author's philosophical defense regarding the nature of God and existence, specifically responding to critiques of his ontological arguments. It maintains the formal, argumentative tone of a 17th-century metaphysical treatise.</meta>

# FIRST RESPONSES

<margin>5</margin>Whether existence should be numbered among the perfections that can exist together is something we might doubt at first glance; for since our mind, which is finite, is not accustomed to considering them except separately, it perhaps will not immediately notice how necessarily they are joined together. And yet, if we attentively examine whether existence belongs to a supremely powerful being, and what kind of existence, we will be able to perceive clearly and distinctly, first, that at least possible existence belongs to it, just as it does to all other things of which we have a distinct idea, even those composed by a <term>fiction of the intellect</term><note>Latin: *figmentum intellectus*; refers to a mental construct or imagined concept rather than a discovered truth.</note>. Next, because we cannot think that its existence is possible without also—when attending to its immense power—recognizing that it can exist by its own power<gloss>a</gloss><note>original: *propriâ suâ vi posse existere*</note>, we shall conclude from this that it actually exists and has existed from eternity; for it is very well known by the <term>natural light</term><note>The innate human capacity for reason and self-evident truths.</note> that what can exist by its own power always exists. And so we will understand that necessary existence is contained in the idea of a supremely powerful being, not by a fiction of the intellect, but because it belongs to the true and immutable nature of such a being to exist. Nor will we fail to perceive easily that this supremely powerful being cannot help but have in itself all the other perfections contained in the idea of God, so that those perfections, without any fiction of the intellect and by their own nature, are joined together and exist in God.

<margin>25</margin>All of these things are indeed manifest to those who attend diligently—

As far as pertains to the formal distinction <note>original: "distinctionem formalem"; a technical term in scholastic philosophy for a distinction that is more than mental but less than a real separation of things</note> which the most learned Theologian brings forward from Scotus <note>referring to Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher</note>, I say briefly that it does not differ from a modal distinction, nor does it extend except to incomplete beings, which I have accurately distinguished from complete ones; and it is indeed sufficient that one be conceived distinctly and separately from the other through an abstraction of the intellect conceiving the thing inadequately, but not so distinctly and separately that we understand each one as a being in itself <note>original: "ens per se"</note> and diverse from every other; rather, for this, a real distinction <note>original: "distinctionem realem"</note> is absolutely required. Thus, for example, between the motion and the figure <note>shape</note> of the same body, the distinction is formal, and I can very well understand motion without figure, and figure without motion, and both by abstracting them from the body: but I cannot, however, completely understand motion without the thing in which the motion occurs, nor even the figure

If I have not yet satisfied him by these remarks, I ask that he advise me of what is either still desired or where I have erred; if I obtain this from him through you, I shall count it as a great favor.

### I.
FIRST, you should remember that you have rejected all images <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> of bodies to the best of your ability—not indeed in actual fact and reality, but only by a fiction of the mind—so that you might conclude that you are only a thinking thing. ### SIXTH,
where you respond to the Theologian <note>Likely referring to Caterus, the author of the First Objections</note>, you seem to wander astray in the conclusion, which you propose as follows: that which we clearly and distinctly understand to belong to the true and immutable nature of any thing, etc., can be affirmed of that thing with truth; but (after we have sufficiently and accurately investigated what God is) we clearly and distinctly understand that it belongs to his nature to exist<gloss>a</gloss>. It would be necessary to conclude: therefore (after we have sufficiently and accurately investigated what God is) we can with truth affirm that it belongs to the nature of God to exist. From this it does not follow that God actually exists, but only that he ought to exist, if his nature is possible, or does not involve a contradiction; that is, the nature or essence of God cannot be conceived without existence, so that, if it exists, it actually exists. This is recalled in that argument which others bring forward in these words: if it does not imply a contradiction for God to be, it is certain that he exists; but it does not imply a contradiction for him to exist. But work is needed on the minor premise, which is: "but it does not imply a contradiction," a truth which your adversaries say they either doubt or deny. Furthermore, that clause of your reasoning (where we have sufficiently clearly and distinctly investigated what God is) is assumed as true, which not everyone yet believes, since you yourself admit that you only inadequately grasp the infinite being. And the same must plainly be said of any of his attributes: for since whatever is in God is utterly infinite, who—except in the most inadequate way, so to speak—can even for a moment grasp anything of God with the mind? How, therefore, have you sufficiently clearly and distinctly investigated what God is?

<margin>141-142.</margin> I recognize in these remarks your piety and your care for promoting the glory of God; and I cannot help but rejoice, not only because you have judged my arguments worthy of your examination, but also because you propose nothing against them to which I do not seem able to respond quite conveniently.

<margin>173</margin> FIRST, you warn me to *remember* that I have *rejected the phantasms of bodies* <note>original: "corporum phantafmata" — mental images or sensory perceptions of physical things</note> not *actually* and *in reality*, but *only by a fiction of the mind*, so that I might *conclude that I am a thinking thing*, lest perhaps I *think it follows from this that I am in reality nothing besides a mind* <insert>a</insert>. I have already testified that I was sufficiently mindful of this matter in the Second Meditation with these words: *But perhaps it happens that these very things, which I suppose to be nothing because they are unknown to me, do not in the truth of the matter differ from that "me" whom I know; I do not know, I am not yet disputing this matter* <insert>b</insert>, etc.; by which I expressly wished to warn the reader that I was not yet seeking there whether the mind was distinct from the body, but was only examining those properties of which I can have certain and evident knowledge. And because I noticed many such properties there, I cannot admit without qualification what you later add: that I *nevertheless do not know what a thinking thing is* <insert>c</insert>. For although I confess that I did not yet know whether that thinking thing was the same as the body or something different, I do not therefore confess that I did not know the thing itself: for who has ever known any thing so well as to know that there was absolutely nothing else in it than that very thing which he was perceiving? <margin>5</margin> But I see what you are hinting at: namely, that since I have written only six *Meditations on First Philosophy* <note>Latin: *Meditationes de primâ Philosophiâ*</note>, readers will be surprised that nothing except what I have just mentioned is concluded in the first two. <margin>10</margin> To these people I simply respond that I do not fear that those who read the rest of my writings with judgment will have any reason to suspect I lacked material. However, it seemed entirely reasonable to me that matters requiring singular attention, which must be considered separately from others, should be assigned to individual Meditations.

<margin>175</margin> Therefore, since nothing is more conducive to achieving a firm knowledge of things than first becoming accustomed to doubting all things—especially corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> things—I could not do otherwise than devote an entire Meditation to this. This is true even though I had long ago seen many books written on that subject by the Academics and Sceptics <note>The Academics and Sceptics were ancient schools of philosophy that questioned the possibility of certain knowledge.</note>, and I was reluctant to "serve up that twice-cooked cabbage" <note>original: *crambem... recoquere*; a Latin idiom for repeating a stale or tedious argument</note> with some distaste. I would wish for readers to spend not only the brief time required to read it, but several months, or at least weeks, in considering the matters it treats before progressing to the rest; for in this way, they would undoubtedly be able to derive far greater benefit from them.

mixed with the ideas of sensible things <note>original: "rerum sensibilium"; things perceived through the five senses</note>. This was the first and primary reason why none of those things said concerning the soul and God could be understood with sufficient clarity. I thought I would be doing something of great value if I could show in what way the properties or qualities of the mind are to be distinguished from the qualities of the body. For although many have said before now that the mind must be led away from the senses in order to understand metaphysical matters, no one yet, as far as I know, had shown by what method this could be done. The true way—and in my judgment the only way—to achieve this is contained in my **Second Meditation**. However, that method is of such a nature that it is not enough merely to have looked at it once; it must be practiced and repeated for a long time. This is so that the lifelong habit of confusing intellectual things with corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> things may be erased by a contrary habit, lasting at least a few days, of distinguishing between them. This seemed to me a most just cause for treating no other subject in that Second Meditation.

*of the body, insofar as it is an extended thing and not a thinking thing, it is certain that I (that is, the mind) am truly distinct from my body, and can exist without it.* To which may easily be added: *everything that can think is a mind, or is called a mind; but since the mind and the body are really distinguished, no body is a mind; therefore no body can think.* <note>original: "omne id quod potest cogitare est mens... nullum corpus potest cogitare." This is a central syllogism in Cartesian dualism.</note>

Nor indeed do I see what you could deny here; is it not sufficient that we clearly understand one thing without the other in order to recognize that they are really distinguished? Provide, then, some more certain sign of a real distinction; for I am confident that none can be given. For what will you say? That those things are really distinguished, either of which can exist without the other? But again, I would ask how you know that one thing can be without the other? For in order to serve as a sign of distinction, it must be known. Perhaps you will say this is obtained from the senses, <margin>178</margin> because you see or touch one thing while the other is absent, etc. But the faith of the senses is more uncertain than that of the intellect; and it can happen in many ways that one and the same thing appears under various forms, or in several places or modes, and thus is taken for two things. And finally, if you remember those things which were said at the end of the Second Meditation concerning the wax, <note>Descartes refers to his famous "wax argument" where he demonstrates that the essence of the wax is perceived by the mind alone, not the senses.</note> you will notice that not even bodies themselves are properly perceived by sense, but by the intellect alone, so that to perceive one thing without another is nothing else than to have an idea of one thing, and to understand that this idea is not the same as the idea of the other. Moreover, this cannot be understood from any other source...

<margin>181</margin>It is of no greater weight that you call the idea of God which is within us a *being of reason* <note>original: "ens rationis," a technical Scholastic term for something that exists only in the mind, like a chimera</note> <gloss>a. Page 124, line 1.</gloss>. In this same way, this entire world could be called a "being of the divine reason"—that is, a being created by a simple act of the divine mind. I have already emphasized in various places that I am dealing only with the objective perfection or reality of an idea <term>objective reality: the reality of the thing represented by an idea, as opposed to the "formal reality" of the idea as a mere thought</term>, which requires a cause no less than the objective craftsmanship found in the idea of a highly ingenious machine requires a cause.

It is also a primary notion that all reality or perfection which exists only <term>objectively</term> in ideas must exist either <term>formally</term><note>Existing in reality exactly as it is perceived.</note> or in a higher way in their causes. Every opinion we have ever held regarding the existence of things placed outside our mind rests solely on this principle. For from where did we suspect that those things exist, if not from the sole fact that ideas of them reached our mind through the senses?

Furthermore, that there is within us an idea of a being supremely powerful and perfect, and also that the objective reality of this idea is found in us neither formally nor in a higher way, will become clear to those who pay sufficient attention and meditate with me for a long time. I can do nothing better than to refer you back to my second Meditation, so that you may at least notice that it has some use. For what could I achieve here in one or two sentences, if I accomplished nothing there with a longer discourse, prepared for that one purpose, and into which I believe I put no less industry than into anything else I have ever written?

Nor does it stand in the way that in that Meditation I dealt only with the human mind; for I freely and willingly confess that the idea we have, for example, of the divine intellect <note>The capacity of God to know or understand</note>, does not differ from the idea we have of our own intellect, except in the same way that the idea of an infinite number differs from the idea of the number four or two; and the same is true of each of the attributes of God, of which we recognize some trace within ourselves.
<margin>185</margin> | But furthermore, in God we understand an absolute immensity, simplicity, and unity embracing all other attributes, which has no example at all [in us], but is, as I said before, *like the mark of the craftsman impressed upon his work*<note>original: "tanquam nota artificis operi suo impressa". See page 51, lines 16-17.</note>. By reason of this mark, we recognize that none of those things which we consider individually in God—just as we perceive them in ourselves—apply to Him and to us in the same sense <term>univocally: using a word in exactly the same way for two different things</term>, because of the limitation of our own intellect. And we also distinguish, from among many indefinite particulars of which we have ideas—such as indefinite or infinite knowledge, likewise power, number, length, etc.—that some of these are contained <term>formally: existing in a thing exactly as it is perceived</term> in the idea of God, such as knowledge and power, while others are contained only <term>eminently: existing in a higher or more excellent form than the human version</term>, such as number and length; which certainly would not happen [without that idea].

<margin>192</margin> **FOURTHLY**, when I deny that God lies, or is a deceiver, I believe I am in agreement with all Metaphysicians <note>scholars of the nature of reality</note> and Theologians who ever will be or ever have been. Nor do the points you have brought to the contrary stand in the way any more than if I had denied that God is angry, or subject to other disturbances of the mind <note>original: "animi commotionibus"</note>, and you were to object with passages of Scripture in which human affections are attributed to Him. For the distinction is known to everyone between the ways of speaking about God adapted to the grasp of the common people <note>original: "ad vulgi sensum"</note>—which contain some truth, but only as it relates to human beings, and which the Sacred Scriptures are accustomed to use—and other ways of speaking which express a more naked truth, not related to human beings. It is these latter ways of speaking that everyone ought to use when philosophizing, and which I especially had to use in my *Meditations*, since I did not even suppose at that point that any human beings were known to me, nor

Nevertheless, I would not wish to rebuke those who concede that God could utter some verbal lie through the Prophets (such as those used by physicians, with which they deceive the sick in order to cure them—that is, a lie in which all malice of deception is absent).

<margin>194</margin>
Furthermore, what is even more significant, we see that we are sometimes truly deceived by the very natural instinct given to us by God, as when a person with dropsy <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema or swelling, where the patient feels an intense but harmful thirst</term> feels thirsty; for then he is positively impelled toward drink by nature, which was given to him by God for the preservation of the body, even though this nature deceives him because the drink will be harmful to him. However, I explained in the sixth Meditation how this does not conflict with the goodness or truthfulness of God.

But in those matters which cannot be explained in this way—namely, in our most clear and accurate judgments, which, if...

## 158-160.

If these perceptions were false, they could not be corrected by any clearer perceptions nor by the help of any other natural faculty; I plainly affirm that in such a case we could not avoid being deceived. For since God is the supreme being, he cannot but be also the supreme good and the supreme truth, and therefore it is a contradiction <note>original: "repugnat"</note> that anything should proceed from him which positively tends toward falsehood. And yet, since nothing real can exist in us which was not given by him (as was demonstrated along with the proof of his existence), and we possess a real faculty for recognizing the truth and distinguishing it from the false (as is evident from the mere fact that the ideas of truth and falsehood are within us), unless this faculty tended toward the truth—at least when we use it correctly (that is, when we assent to nothing except what is clearly and distinctly perceived, for no other correct use of this faculty can be imagined)—then God, the giver of that faculty, would rightly be considered a deceiver.

<margin>105</margin> And so you see, after it has been recognized that God exists, it is necessary that we imagine him to be a deceiver if we wish to cast doubt upon those things which we perceive clearly and distinctly; and because a deceiver cannot be imagined <note>Descartes argues that deception is an imperfection, which is incompatible with the nature of a perfect being</note>, those things must be admitted as altogether true and certain.

But because I notice here that you are still stuck in the doubts which I proposed in the first Meditation—and which I thought had been sufficiently and accurately removed in the following sections—I will set forth here once more the foundation upon which all human certainty seems to me to rest.

First of all, as soon as we think we perceive something correctly, we are spontaneously persuaded that it is true. Now, if this persuasion is so firm that we can never have any cause to doubt that which we are so persuaded of, there is nothing further for us to seek; we have everything that can reasonably be desired.

<summary>Descartes argues that because God is the supreme truth and not a deceiver, our faculty of clear and distinct perception must be reliable. He asserts that once God's existence is known, any firm persuasion based on clear perception constitutes absolute certainty.</summary>

For what is it to us if someone should perhaps imagine that this very thing, of whose truth we are so firmly persuaded, appears false to God or an Angel, and is therefore, speaking absolutely, false? Why should we care about that absolute falsity <note>original: "falsitatem absolutam"</note>, since we by no means believe in it, nor have even the slightest suspicion of it? For we are assuming a conviction <note>original: "persuasionem"</note> so firm that it can in no way be removed; such a conviction is therefore exactly the same as *most perfect* certainty.

But it can be doubted whether any such certainty, or firm and immutable conviction, is actually possessed.

And indeed it is *evident* <note>original: "perspicuum"</note> that such certainty is not held regarding those things which we perceive even in the slightest degree obscurely or confusedly; for any such obscurity is cause enough for us to doubt them. Nor is it held regarding those things which, however clearly, are perceived by the senses alone; for we have often noted that error can be found in the senses, as when a person with dropsy <note>term: "hydropicus" - a medical condition involving swelling and extreme thirst</note> feels thirst, or when a person with jaundice <note>term: "ictericus" - a condition causing yellowing of the eyes and skin</note> sees snow as yellow; for he sees it no less clearly and distinctly as such than we see it as white. It remains, therefore, that if any such certainty is held, it is only regarding those things which are clearly perceived by the intellect.

Now, among these, some are so *evident*, and at the same time so simple, that we can never think of them without believing them to be true: for example, that I, while I think, exist; that those things which have once been done cannot be *undone* <note>original: "infecta"</note>; and similar things, concerning which it is manifest that this certainty is held. Nor is it an obstacle that we have often experienced others to have been deceived in those matters which *they believed they knew more clearly than the sun* <note>original: "sole clarius se scire credebant"</note>. For we have never noticed, nor can it be noticed by anyone, that this has happened to those who sought the clarity of their perception from the intellect alone, but only to those who took it either from the senses or from some false prejudice.

Nor is it an obstacle even if someone were to imagine that those things appear false to God or to an Angel, because the evidence of our perception will not allow us to listen to anyone imagining such things.

There are other things which are indeed also perceived very clearly by our intellect, when we attend to the reasons from which they depend; <margin>198</margin> and at that time we cannot doubt them. But because we can forget those reasons, and meanwhile remember the conclusions deduced from them, the question arises whether there is also a firm and immutable persuasion regarding these conclusions, as long as we remember that they were deduced from evident principles; for this memory must be assumed so that they can be called "conclusions." And I respond that such persuasion is indeed held by those who know God in such a way that they understand it to be impossible that the faculty of understanding given to them by Him should not tend toward the truth; but it is not held by others.

And this was explained so clearly at the end of the fifth Meditation <note>Descartes refers here to his "Meditations on First Philosophy," where he argues that the certainty of all science depends on the knowledge of the true God.</note>, that nothing further seems necessary to be added here.
