FIFTHLY, I am surprised that you deny that the **will** <note>Latin: *voluntatem*; the faculty of choice</note> exposes itself to danger if it follows a conception of the **intellect** <note>Latin: *intellectus*; the faculty of understanding</note> that is not at all clear and **distinct** <margin>See page 126, lines 21-24</margin>. For what makes the will certain, if that which it follows has not been clearly perceived? And who has ever—whether a Philosopher, a Theologian, or simply a person using their reason—not confessed that we are in so much less danger of wandering into error the more clearly we understand something before we give our assent to it, and that those who pass judgment while the cause is unknown are at fault? Moreover, no concept is called obscure or confused except because it contains something within it that is unknown.

Nor, therefore, does what you object regarding the **embracing of faith** <margin>See page 126, lines 25-28</margin> have any more force against me than against all others who have ever cultivated human reason; indeed, it has no force against anyone at all. For even if faith is said to concern obscure matters, nevertheless, the reason for which we embrace it is not obscure, but is more illustrious than any natural light. Truly, a distinction must be made between the matter or the thing itself to which we assent, and the formal reason <note>The underlying logical or divine justification</note> which moves the will to assent. For it is in this reason alone that we require **perspicuity** <note>Clarity or transparency of thought</note>. And as for the matter, no one has ever denied that it can be obscure—indeed, that it can be **obscurity** itself; for when I judge that obscurity must be removed from our concepts so that we may assent to them without any danger of error, I form a clear judgment about this very obscurity. Instead, he would be sinning by not using his reason correctly. Nor do I think any orthodox theologian has ever felt otherwise on these matters. For as far as the conduct of life is concerned, I am so far from thinking that we should only assent to things clearly perceived, that on the contrary, I do not even think we should always wait for probabilities. Instead, we must sometimes choose one option from many completely unknown ones and, once chosen, hold to it no less firmly—as long as no reasons to the contrary appear—than if it had been chosen for very clear reasons. I explained this on page 26 of the *Discourse on Method* <note>original: "Dissertatione de Methodo"</note>. However, when the subject is solely the contemplation of truth, who has ever denied that assent should be withheld from obscure things that are not sufficiently and distinctly perceived? That I was dealing only with this latter case in my *Meditations* is shown by the subject matter itself, and I also declared it in express words at the end of the First Meditation, saying: *that I could not indulge in too much distrust there, since I was not occupied with practical action, but only with the acquisition of knowledge* <note>original: "non rebus agendis, sed cognoscendis tantùm incumbabam"</note>.

Referring to page 127, lines 17-18 of the original manuscript.</note> etc. This is indeed materially true, but formally it is a sophism <note>A "sophism" is an argument that seems plausible but is logically fallacious.</note>. This is clear from the fact that, if the major premise is denied, it must be proved thus: *if God does not yet exist, it implies a contradiction that He should exist, because no sufficient cause can be given to produce Him; but it does not imply a contradiction that He exists, as has been assumed; therefore* etc. If, however, the <margin>206</margin> minor premise is denied, it must be said thus: *that does not imply a contradiction in whose formal concept there is nothing involving a contradiction; but in the formal concept of the divine existence or nature there is nothing involving a contradiction; therefore* etc. These two are

And although we conceive of God only inadequately, or, if you prefer, <margin>207</margin> most inadequately <note>original: "inadæquatiſſime"; Descartes is responding to the objection that a finite mind cannot fully grasp an infinite God.</note>, this does not prevent it from being certain that his nature is possible, or does not involve a contradiction; nor does it prevent us from being able to truly affirm that we have investigated it clearly enough (namely, as much as suffices for knowing this, and also for knowing that necessary existence belongs to that same nature of God). For all contradiction or impossibility consists solely in our own concept, when we wrongly join together ideas that are mutually opposed to one another; it cannot exist in any thing <note>original: "re"</note> positioned outside the intellect, because by the very fact that something is outside the intellect, it is manifest that it does not involve a contradiction, but is possible. Moreover, contradiction arises in our concepts only from the fact that they are obscure and confused, and it can never exist in clear and distinct ones. And therefore it is enough that we clearly and distinctly understand those few things which we perceive concerning God, even if in no way adequately; and that among other things we notice that necessary existence is contained in this concept of him, however inadequate it may be, in order for us to affirm that we have investigated his nature clearly enough, and that it does not involve a contradiction.

SEVENTHLY, as to why I have written nothing concerning the immortality of the soul <note>original: "immortalitate animæ"</note>, I have already explained this in the Synopsis of my Meditations. I have shown above that I have sufficiently proved its distinction from every body. However, regarding your further point—that *the immortality of the soul does not follow from its distinction from the body*, because *it can nonetheless be said that it was created by God with such a nature that its duration ends at the same time as the duration of the corporeal life*—I confess that I cannot refute this. For I do not take it upon myself to attempt to determine anything by the power of human reason concerning those things which depend upon the free will of God. Natural knowledge <note>The light of reason or "natural light," as opposed to divine revelation.</note> teaches that the mind is diverse from the body, and that the mind is a substance; whereas the human body, insofar as it differs from other bodies, consists only of the configuration of its members and other such accidents; and finally, that the death of the body depends solely upon some division or change of shape. We have no argument, nor any example, to persuade us that the death—or rather the annihilation of a substance such as the mind—ought to follow from so slight a cause as a change of shape, which is nothing other than a mode <note>A "mode" is a specific state or quality of a substance, like the shape of a piece of wax.</note>, and indeed not a mode of the mind, but of the body which is really distinct from the mind. Nor indeed do we even have any argument or example to persuade us that any substance can perish. This is sufficient for us to conclude that the mind,

Finally, as for your advice regarding the presentation of my arguments *in a geometric fashion* <note>original: "more geometrico"; referring to the formal style of proofs used by mathematicians like Euclid</note>, so that they might be perceived by the reader as if in a single glance<gloss>a</gloss>, it is worthwhile for me to explain here to what extent I have already followed that advice, and to what extent I think it should be followed hereafter. I distinguish two things in the geometric manner of writing: namely, the order, and the method of demonstration.

The order consists solely in this: that those things which are proposed first must be known without any help from those that follow, and all the rest must then be so arranged that they are demonstrated solely from what precedes them. And indeed, I endeavored to follow this order as accurately as possible in my Meditations; and the observance of this was the reason why I treated the distinction between the mind and the body not in the second, but only in the sixth Meditation, and why I knowingly and willingly omitted many other things because they required the explanation of many more matters.
<margin>211</margin>

The method of demonstration, however, is twofold: one is by analysis, the other by synthesis.

Analysis shows the true way by which a thing was discovered methodically and, as it were, *prior to experience* <note>original: "a priori"</note>, so that if the reader is willing to follow it and attend sufficiently to everything, they will understand the matter no less perfectly and make it their own than if they themselves had discovered it. However, it contains nothing to compel a reader who is less attentive or resistant to be-

Often he barely touches upon many things because they are sufficiently clear to an attentive person, yet these are the very things that especially need to be noticed.

<margin>212</margin> **Synthesis**, on the other hand, proceeds by the opposite path and, as it were, "from the effect" <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>—even though the proof itself is often more "from the cause" <note>original: "a priori"</note> in this method than in the former. It clearly demonstrates that which has been concluded and employs a long series of definitions, postulates, axioms, theorems, and problems, so that if anything in the consequences is denied, it may immediately show that it is contained in the antecedents. In this way, it wrests assent from the reader, however reluctant or stubborn they may be. But it does not satisfy the mind as the other method does, nor does it fulfill the desires of those wishing to learn, because it does not teach the method by which the thing was discovered.

The ancient Geometers <note>Descartes refers here to classical Greek mathematicians like Euclid or Archimedes</note> were accustomed to use only this method in their writings—not because they were entirely ignorant of the other, but, as I judge, because they valued it so highly that they reserved it for themselves as a kind of secret.

I, however, have followed only **Analysis** in my *Meditations*, which is the true and best way for teaching. But as for **Synthesis**, which is undoubtedly what you require of me here, although it is most aptly placed after Analysis in Geometric matters, it cannot be so conveniently applied to these Metaphysical ones.

# REASONS
## PROVING THE EXISTENCE OF GOD
## & THE DISTINCTION OF THE SOUL FROM THE BODY
## ARRANGED IN A GEOMETRIC MANNER
<note>original: "More Geometrico Dispositæ." This refers to the method of presenting philosophy through definitions, postulates, and axioms, similar to a mathematical proof.</note>

->DEFINITIONS.<-

I. By the name *Thought*, I include everything that is within us in such a way that we are immediately conscious of it. Thus, all operations of the will, the intellect, the imagination, and the senses are thoughts. But I have added <margin>10</margin> *immediately*, in order to exclude those things which follow from them; for example, voluntary motion has thought as its principle <note>or "starting point"</note>, but the motion itself is not a thought.

II. By the name *Idea*, I understand that form of any thought through the immediate perception of which <margin>15</column-break/> I am conscious of that very same thought; so much so that I can express nothing in words, while understanding what I say, without it being certain from this very fact that there is in me an idea of that which is signified by those words. And thus, I do not call "ideas" only those images depicted in the fantasy <note>the "phantasia" or the faculty of the mind that deals with sensory images</note>; indeed, <margin>20</margin> I do not call them ideas here at all, insofar as they are in the fantasy

<margin>218</margin>
...corporeal <note>original: "corporeâ"</note>, that is, depicted in some part of the brain, but only insofar as they inform the mind itself when it is directed toward that part of the brain.

III. By the *objective reality of an idea*, I understand the being <note>original: "entitatem"</note> of the thing represented by the idea, insofar as it is in the idea; and in the same way one can speak of *objective perfection*, or *objective craftsmanship*, etc. For whatever we perceive as being in the objects of our ideas, those things are in the ideas themselves objectively.

IV. These same things are said to be *formally* in the objects of the ideas when they are in them exactly as we perceive them; and *eminently* <note>A scholastic term meaning that a cause possesses a quality in a higher or more excellent form than its effect, even if not in the same way.</note> when they are not indeed such as we perceive, but are so great that they can take the place of such things.

<margin>219</margin>
V. Every thing in which there inheres <gloss>a</gloss> immediately, as in a subject, or through which something exists that we perceive—that is, some property, or quality, or attribute, of which there is a real idea in us—is called *Substance*. For we have no other idea of substance itself, strictly taken, than that it is a thing in which that something we perceive (or which exists objectively in one of our ideas) exists formally or eminently; for it is known by the natural light <note>The innate human capacity for reason, independent of sensory experience.</note> that there can be no real attribute of nothingness.

VI. The substance in which thought inheres immediately is called *Mind*; I speak here of the mind rather than the soul, because the name "soul" is equivocal <note>Having multiple or uncertain meanings.</note> and is often used for a corporeal thing.

VII. The substance which is the immediate subject of local extension, and of the accidents <note>Non-essential properties that can change without the substance ceasing to exist.</note> which presuppose extension, such as shape, position, local motion, etc.

->|| POSTULATES ||<-

I ask, FIRST, that readers notice how weak the reasons are for which they have hitherto trusted their senses, and how uncertain all the judgments are that they have built upon them; and that they revolve this in their minds so long and so often that they finally acquire the habit of no longer trusting them too much. ### II.
The present time does not depend upon the time immediately preceding it; therefore, no less a cause is required to preserve a thing than was required to produce it in the first place. <note>This is the doctrine of "continuous creation," suggesting that the universe would vanish if God did not actively keep it in existence at every moment.</note>

But that vision does not reach the mind except insofar as it is an idea: an idea, I say, inherent in the mind itself, and not an image depicted in the <term>phantasia</term> <note>the "imagination" or the physical faculty of the brain that processes sensory images</note>. Nor can we judge from this idea that the sky exists, except because every idea must have a really existing cause of its objective reality; which cause we judge to be the sky itself, and so on for other things.

But because it is not easy to arrive at such great perspicacity <note>Clarity of insight or mental sharpness.</note>, we shall seek the same thing by other means.

### PROPOSITION II.
THE EXISTENCE OF GOD IS DEMONSTRATED FROM THE SOLE FACT THAT THE IDEA OF HIM IS IN US, REASONING FROM EFFECT TO CAUSE. <note>original: "A POSTERIORI DEMONSTRATUR". In logic, "a posteriori" refers to knowledge derived from experience or effects rather than first principles.</note>

*Demonstration.*

The objective reality <note>The reality of the thing represented by an idea, as opposed to the reality of the thought itself.</note> of any of our ideas requires a cause in which that same reality is contained—not only objectively, but formally or eminently (by Axiom 5). However, we possess the idea of God (by Definitions 2 and 8), and the objective reality of this idea is contained in us neither formally nor eminently (by Axiom 6), nor can it be contained in any other besides God Himself (by Definition 8). Therefore, this idea of God which is in us requires God as its cause; and consequently, God exists (by Axiom 3).

<summary>Descartes presents a formal proof for God's existence, arguing that the idea of an infinite being within the human mind must have been caused by an actual infinite being, as the effect cannot exceed the cause.</summary>

### PROPOSITION III.

GOD'S EXISTENCE IS ALSO DEMONSTRATED FROM THE FACT THAT WE OURSELVES, POSSESSING THE IDEA OF HIM, EXIST.

*Demonstration.*

<margin>5</margin>If I had the power of preserving myself, I would have all the more power to give myself the perfections that I lack (by axioms 8 & 9 <note>Axiom 8 states that a thing able to perform the greater can perform the lesser; Axiom 9 states it is greater to create/preserve a substance than its attributes.</note>); for those perfections are merely attributes of a substance, whereas I am a substance. But I do <margin>10</margin>not have the power to give myself these perfections; for otherwise I would already possess them (by axiom 7 <note>Axiom 7 suggests that whatever can do the greater would not deny itself the lesser.</note>). Therefore, I do not have the power of preserving myself.

Furthermore, I cannot exist without being preserved as long as I exist, whether by myself—if indeed I have that power—<margin>229</margin>or by another | who possesses it (by axioms 1 & 2 <note>These axioms establish that the present moment does not follow from the past without a cause of preservation.</note>). And yet <margin>15</margin>I exist, and nevertheless I do not have the power of preserving myself, as has just been proven. Therefore, I am preserved by another.

Moreover, he by whom I am preserved possesses in himself, either formally or eminently <term>Formally or Eminently: "Formally" means possessing a quality in the same way we perceive it; "eminently" means possessing it in a higher, more perfect form that can cause the lesser version.</term>, everything that is in me (by axiom 4). But within me there is the perception of many perfections <margin>20</margin>which I lack, and at the same time the idea of God (by definitions 2 & 8). Therefore, there is also in him, by whom I am preserved, a perception of those same perfections.

Finally, that same being cannot have a perception of any perfections which he lacks, or which he does not possess in himself formally or eminently (by axiom 7). For <margin>25</margin>since he has the power of preserving me, as has already been said, he would have all the more power to give those perfections to himself, if they were lacking,

## COROLLARY.

### *Demonstration.*

GOD CREATED THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH, AND ALL THINGS THAT ARE IN THEM; AND FURTHERMORE, HE IS ABLE TO BRING ABOUT EVERYTHING THAT WE CLEARLY PERCEIVE, EXACTLY AS WE PERCEIVE IT.

All these things follow clearly from the preceding proposition. For in that proposition, the existence of God was proven from the fact that someone must exist in whom all the perfections of which we have an idea are present, either formally or eminently. However, there is within us an idea of a power so great that by him alone, in whom this power resides, the heavens and the earth, etc., were created; and also that all other things understood by me as possible can be made by the same being. Therefore, along with the existence of God, all these attributes have been proven of him at the same time.

THE WORKS OF DESCARTES.

<margin>238</margin> ...it seems it should rather be inferred that the thinking thing is material rather than immaterial.

## REPLY.

Where I said *this is the mind, the soul, the intellect, the reason, etc.*,
<margin>5</margin> I did not mean by these names the faculties alone, but the things endowed with the faculty of thinking. This is how the first two terms <note>mind and soul</note> are commonly understood by everyone, and how the latter two <note>intellect and reason</note> are frequently understood; and I explained this so explicitly and in so many places that there seems to have been no reason for doubt.

<margin>10</margin> Nor is there an equivalence here between walking and thinking: because "walking" is usually only understood as the act itself; whereas "thinking" <note>original Latin: *cogitatio*</note> is sometimes taken for the act, sometimes for the faculty, and sometimes for the thing in which that faculty exists.

I do not say that the thing that understands and the act of understanding are the same; nor even that the thinking thing and the intellect are the same, if
<margin>15</margin> "intellect" is taken as a faculty; I only say they are the same when "intellect" is taken as the thing itself which understands. Furthermore, I freely admit that to signify the thing, or substance <note>original Latin: *substantia*; the underlying reality or essence of a thing</note>, which I wished to strip [Margin 239] of all things [Margin 20] that do not belong to it, I used the most abstract words possible. By contrast, this Philosopher <note>referring to Thomas Hobbes</note> uses the most concrete terms possible—namely, *subject, matter, and body*—to describe this thinking thing, so that he might prevent it from being separated from the body.

<margin>25</margin> I am not concerned that his method of grouping many things together will appear more suited to finding the truth than my own method, by which I distinguish each thing as clearly as possible. But let us leave the words aside and speak of the matter itself.

<summary>Descartes defends his definition of the mind against Thomas Hobbes, arguing that while "thinking" can refer to an act, it also refers to the substance of the mind itself, which he maintains is distinct from the physical body.</summary>

# Third Objections.

<margin>175</margin> *“It is possible,”* he says, *“that the thinking thing is something corporeal; the contrary of which is assumed, but not proved.”*<sup>a</sup> On the contrary, I did not assume it, nor did I use it in any way as a foundation; rather, I left it entirely undecided until the Sixth Meditation, in which it is finally proven.

<margin>5</margin> Next, he correctly says that we cannot conceive of any act without its subject,<sup>b</sup> such as a thought without a thinking thing <term>res cogitans: Descartes’s term for the mind or the underlying "stuff" that performs the act of thinking</term>, because that which thinks is not nothing. But without any reason, and against all common usage and all 
<margin>10</margin> logic, he adds that from this it seems to follow that the thinking thing is something corporeal. <margin>240</margin> For the subjects of all acts are indeed understood under the category of substance<sup>c</sup> (or even, if you like, under the category of matter—specifically metaphysical matter <note>original Latin: *materia Metaphysica*. In philosophy, "matter" can sometimes refer to the underlying "substrate" of a thing rather than physical "stuff" like wood or stone.</note>), but they are not necessarily understood to be bodies.

<margin>15</margin> Both logicians and people in general are accustomed to saying that substances are either spiritual or corporeal. Nor did I prove anything else by my example of the wax <note>In his Second Meditation, Descartes describes how wax changes its shape, color, and smell when melted, yet we still know it is the same wax through the mind's understanding rather than the senses.</note>, except only that color, hardness, and shape do not belong to the formal nature <term>ratio formalis: the essential definition or "form" that makes a thing what it is</term> of the wax itself. I was not dealing there with the formal nature 
<margin>20</margin> of the mind, nor even the formal nature of the body.

Nor is it relevant when this Philosopher <note>Descartes is referring to Thomas Hobbes here.</note> says that one thought cannot be the subject of another thought. For who, besides himself, ever 
<margin>25</margin> imagined such a thing? To explain the matter briefly: it is certain that a thought cannot exist without a thinking thing, nor can any act or any accident <term>accidens: a philosophical term for a quality or property that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist (like the color of a shirt)</term> exist without a substance...

<meta>198-199.</meta>

...the substance in which it inheres. Since, however, we do not know substance itself immediately through itself, but only through the fact that it is the subject of certain acts, it is highly reasonable, and custom dictates, that we call those substances which we recognize to be the subjects of clearly different acts 
<margin>241</margin> or accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property or quality that a thing has, but which is not essential to its existence (like the color of a shirt).</note> by different names. We then later examine whether those
<margin>5</margin> different names signify different things or one and the same thing.

Now, there are certain acts which we call corporeal <note>relating to physical bodies</note>, such as size, shape, | motion, and all other things that <margin>10</margin> cannot be thought of without local extension <note>taking up space in a specific location</note>. And the substance in which these reside, we call **body**; nor can it be imagined that there is one substance which is the subject of shape, and another which is the subject of local motion, etc., because all those acts agree under the one common nature of **extension** <term>extension: the defining quality of physical matter, namely the property of occupying space</term>. <margin>15</margin> There are then other acts, which we call thought-based <note>original Latin: *cogitativos*</note>, such as understanding, willing, imagining, sensing, etc., which all agree under the common nature of thought, or perception, or consciousness. And the substance in which they reside, we say is a **thinking thing** <term>res cogitans: Descartes’s term for the mind or a conscious entity</term>, or a **mind**, or by <margin>20</margin> any other name, provided we do not confuse it with corporeal substance. This is because thought-based acts have no affinity with corporeal acts, and 
<margin>242</margin> | **thought**, which is their common nature, differs entirely in kind from **extension**, which is the common nature <margin>25</margin> of the others. Once we have formed two distinct concepts of these two substances, it is easy, from what was said in the Sixth Meditation, to determine whether they are one and the same, or different.

### THIRD OBJECTIONS.
<meta>200-201.</meta>

### OBJECTION III.

What is it then that is distinguished from my thought? What is it that can be said to be separate from myself?<sup>a</sup>
<margin>5</margin> Perhaps someone will answer this question: I myself who think am distinguished from my thought; and that my thought is not indeed separate from me, but different, in the same way that (*as was said before*) dancing is distinguished from the dancer. But if Mr. Descartes <note>original Latin: *D. C.*, for *Dominus Cartesius*</note> shows that the one who understands and the understanding itself are the same, we shall fall back into the Scholastic <term>Scholastic: a medieval method of philosophy and logic that Descartes and Hobbes often criticized for being overly complex or circular</term> way of speaking: *The intellect understands, the sight sees, the will wills, and by an excellent analogy, the walking—or at least the faculty of walking—will walk.* All of which are obscure, improper, <margin>243</margin> and most unworthy of Mr. Descartes' usual clarity.

### REPLY.

<margin>15</margin> I do not deny that I, who think, am distinguished from my thought, as a thing is distinguished from a mode <term>mode: a specific way of being or an activity, like how "sitting" is a mode of a "body"</term>; but when I ask, *what then is it that is distinguished from my thought?*, I understand this to refer to the various modes of thinking listed there, not to my substance <note>The "substance" is the underlying "thing" that exists; the "modes" are the various thoughts it has</note>; and when I add, *what is it that can be said to be separate from myself?*, I mean only that all those modes of thinking are within me; nor do I see what doubt or obscurity can be imagined here.

### OBJECTION IV.

It remains then for me to concede that I do not even imagine what this wax is, but conceive it by the mind alone<sup>b</sup>.

There is a great difference between *imagining*—that is, having a certain idea—and *conceiving* in the mind—that is, gathering through reasoning that a certain thing is, or that a certain thing exists. But 
<margin>244</margin> Mr. Descartes <note>original: *D. C.*, for *Dominus Cartesius*</note> has not explained to us in what way they differ. The 
<margin>5</margin> ancient Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy, known for walking while teaching</term> also taught clearly enough that substance <term>substance: the fundamental "thing" or "stuff" that exists, underlying its various qualities</term> is not perceived by the senses, but is gathered by the reasons of the mind.

What then shall we say if, perhaps, reasoning is nothing other than a coupling and concatenation <term>concatenation: a linking together in a chain-like sequence</term> of names or designations, by means of the word "is"? From this we 
<margin>10</margin> would gather through reason nothing at all regarding the nature of things, but only about their designations—namely, whether or not we couple the names of things according to the agreements (which we have made at our own discretion regarding their meanings). If this be the case, as it may well be, reasoning will depend 
<margin>15</margin> on names, names on the imagination, and imagination perhaps—as I believe—on the movement of the bodily organs; and thus the mind will be nothing other than movement in certain parts of the organic body.

The difference between imagination and the

<margin>25</margin> reasoning, there is a coupling not of names, but of the things signified by the names; and I marvel that the contrary could occur to anyone's mind. For who doubts that a Frenchman...

[that there] are some creatures serving God, invisible and immaterial, we assign the name "Angel" to this believed or supposed thing, even though the idea under which I imagine an Angel is composed of ideas of visible things.

In the same way, regarding the venerable name of God, we have no <margin>5</margin> image or idea of God; and for that reason, we are forbidden to worship God under an image, lest we seem to ourselves to conceive of Him who is inconceivable <term>inconceivable: in this context, "inconceptibilis" refers to something that cannot be captured by a mental image or a finite concept</term>.

It seems, therefore, that there is no idea of God within us. But just as someone born blind, who is frequently brought near a fire and feels <margin>10</margin> themselves grow warm, recognizes that there is something by which they are heated, and hearing it called "fire," concludes that fire exists—yet they do not know what shape or color the fire might have, nor do they have any idea or image of the fire at all present in their mind; so too, a human being, recognizing that there must be some <margin>15</margin> <margin>248</margin> cause for their images or ideas, and another prior cause for that cause, and so on continuously, is finally led to an end, or the supposition of some eternal cause which, because it never began to be, cannot have a prior cause; they necessarily conclude that something eternal exists. Yet they have no <margin>20</margin> idea that they can say is the idea of that eternal thing, but they name or call the thing believed or acknowledged "God."

Now, since Monsieur Descartes <note>original: "D. C." standing for *Domini Cartesii*, Latin for "of Mr. Descartes"</note> proceeds from this position—that we have an idea of God in our soul—to the proof of this theorem, <margin>25</margin> that God (that is, a supremely powerful, wise creator of the world) exists, it was necessary to better explain that idea of God, and not only to derive His existence from it, but also the creation of the world.

### REPLY.

Here, by the name "idea," he <note>Referring to Thomas Hobbes, the author of these objections.</note> wishes only for it to be understood as images of material things depicted in the corporeal imagination <term>corporeal imagination: the "phantasia corporea," which early modern philosophers often viewed as a physical faculty of the brain that processes sensory images</term>; which being granted, it is easy for him to prove that there can be no proper idea of an Angel or of God. However, I show everywhere, and <margin>5</margin> especially in this very place, that I take the name "idea" for <margin>249</margin>| everything that is immediately perceived by the mind, so much so that when I will and I fear—because I simultaneously perceive that I am willing and fearing—volition <margin>10</margin> and fear themselves are numbered among ideas by me. And I have used this name because it was already common <note>original: "tritum," meaning well-worn or commonplace</note> among Philosophers to signify the forms of the perceptions of the divine mind <note>This refers to the Platonic tradition of "Divine Ideas" or archetypes in the mind of God</note>, although we recognize no imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> in God; and I had no more suitable term. I believe, moreover, that I have sufficiently explained the <margin>15</margin> idea of God for those who wish to pay attention | to my meaning; but for those who prefer to understand my words differently than I do, I could never do enough. Finally, what is added here concerning the creation of the world is plainly irrelevant to the question.

### OBJECTION VI.

<margin>20</margin> But other (*thoughts*) <note>Descartes is quoting his own "Meditation III" here, which Hobbes then critiques.</note> have certain other forms besides; as when I will, when I fear, when I affirm, or when I deny, I always indeed apprehend some thing as the subject of my thought. But I also embrace something more in thought than the mere <margin>250</margin>| likeness <margin>25</margin> of that thing; and of these, some are called wills or affects <term>affects: "affectus," referring to emotions or stirrings of the mind</term>, while others are called judgments<sup>a</sup>.

<meta>This page continues the "Third Objections" to René Descartes's *Meditations on First Philosophy*, written by the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes. Hobbes is challenging Descartes’s claim that mental activities like "willing," "fearing," or "affirming" are distinct types of "ideas."</meta>

<meta>206-207.</meta>

When someone wills, or fears, they certainly have an image of the thing they fear, and of the action they will; but what more is encompassed by the thought of the one willing or fearing is not explained. Even if fear were a thought, I do not see how <margin>5</margin> it can be anything other than the thought of the thing one fears. For what else is the fear of a charging lion but the idea of the charging lion, plus the effect (which such an idea produces in the heart) by which the one who fears is driven to that animal motion we call flight? Now, this motion of flight is not a thought; therefore, there remains <margin>10</margin> no other thought in fear | besides that which consists in the likeness of the thing <note>original: "similitudine rei"</note>. The same could be said of the will.

Furthermore, affirmation and negation do not exist without speech and names, so much so that brute animals <term>brute animals: a common 17th-century term for non-human animals, who were often thought to lack the capacity for reason or complex language</term> cannot affirm or deny, even in thought, and therefore they cannot <margin>15</margin> judge; yet a similar thought can exist in both man <margin>251</margin>| and beast. For, when we affirm that a man is running, we have no other thought than that which a dog has seeing its master running; therefore, affirmation or negation adds nothing to simple thoughts, unless perhaps the thought that the names, which make up the affirmation, are <margin>20</margin> names of the same thing in the mind of the one affirming; which is not to encompass a thought more than the likeness of the thing, but rather the same likeness twice.

### RESPONSE.

<margin>25</margin> It is self-evident that it is one thing to see a lion and at the same time to fear it, and another thing entirely just to see it; likewise, it is one thing to see a man running, and another to affirm to oneself <note>In the first edition, the phrasing was slightly different, omitting "to oneself."</note> that he is running.

### | OBJECTION VII.

<margin>5</margin>It remains for me to examine in what way I received this idea from God; for I did not draw it from the senses; nor did it ever come to me unexpectedly, as the ideas of sensible things usually do when those things encounter the external sense organs <margin>252</margin> (or seem to encounter them); nor was it created by me, for I can clearly subtract nothing from it and <margin>10</margin>add nothing to it; and therefore it remains that it is innate to me, just as the idea of myself is innate to me <margin>a.</margin>. <note>Descartes argues that certain ideas, like those of God or geometry, are "hard-wired" into the mind from birth rather than learned from experience.</note>

*If there is no idea of God (and it is not proven that one exists), as it seems there is not, this whole investigation collapses. If there is an idea of God (as it is manifest that there is), this whole objection collapses. And when it is added that there is no idea of the soul, but that it is | inferred by reason, it is the same as saying that there is no image of it depicted in the imagination <term>imagination (phantasia): in 17th-century philosophy, the faculty of forming mental pictures of physical objects, distinct from pure intellectual understanding</term>, but <margin>25</margin>that what I have called an "idea" nevertheless exists.

...infinite, omniscient, omnipotent, and the creator of all things which exist apart from himself, truly contains more objective reality in itself than those ideas through which finite substances are represented <margin>a.</margin>. <note>original: "plus profecto realitatis objectivæ." <margin>5</margin> *I have noted several times before that no idea is given of either God or the soul; I now add that there is no idea of substance either. For substance (insofar as it is the matter underlying properties and changes) is established by reasoning alone; it is not, however, conceived, nor does it present any idea to us. ### RESPONSE.

I have noted several times that I apply the name "idea" to that very thing which is established by <margin>20</margin> reason, as well as to other things that are perceived in any way whatsoever. I have also sufficiently explained how reality admits of "more" and "less": namely, in the sense that a substance is more of a "thing" than a mode <note>A "mode" is a quality or state of being, such as "roundness" or "sitting," which cannot exist without a substance.</note>; and if real qualities or incomplete substances exist, they are more of a "thing" than modes, <margin>25</margin> but less than complete substances; and finally, if an infinite and independent substance exists, it is more of a "thing" than a finite and dependent one. All these matters are, by their very nature, perfectly well known.

### | OBJECTION X.

<margin>256</margin>Therefore, there remains only the idea of God, in which it must be considered whether there is anything that could not have originated from myself. By the name of God, I understand a certain <margin>5</margin> **infinite substance, independent, supremely intelligent, supremely powerful, and by which both I myself and everything else, if anything else exists, were created.** All of these characteristics are such that the more diligently I attend to them, the less they seem capable of having originated from me <margin>10</margin> alone; and therefore, from what has been said before, it must be concluded that God necessarily exists <note>original: "Deum necessario existere, est concludendum." This is a quote from Descartes’s Third Meditation where he argues that the cause of an idea must have as much reality as the idea represents.</note>.

*By considering the attributes of God—so that we might have an idea of God from them, and to see if there is anything in that idea which could not have originated from ourselves—I find, unless I am mistaken, that what we think of under the name of God does neither originate from <margin>15</margin> us, nor is it necessary that it originates from anywhere other than external objects. For by the name of God, I understand a "substance"; that is, I understand that God exists (not through an idea, but through reasoning). "Infinite" (that is, I cannot conceive <margin>257</margin> nor | imagine its boundaries or outermost parts, without <margin>20</margin> being able to imagine further parts still); from which it follows that the name "infinite" does not give rise to an idea of divine infinity, but rather to an idea of my own limits or boundaries. "Independent" (that is, I do not conceive of a cause from which God originates); from which it is clear that I have no other idea attached to the name "independent" <margin>25</margin> besides the memory of my own ideas beginning at different times, and therefore being dependent.* <note>Hobbes is using a "nominalist" approach here, suggesting that words like "infinite" and "independent" don't describe a positive mental image, but rather our own inability to find an end or a cause.</note>

*Therefore, to say that God is independent is nothing*

is nothing other than saying *that God is* among the number of those things whose origin I do not imagine. Just as saying *that God is* *infinite* is the same as if we were to say that he is among the number <margin>5</margin> of those things whose limits we do not conceive. ## REPLY.

None of those things which we attribute to God can have originated from external objects as if from a model, because there is nothing in God similar to those things found in external objects—that is, in corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> things. <margin>10</margin>

Moreover, I can easily explain what idea I have of it by saying that by **idea** I understand everything that is the form of some perception. For who is there who does not perceive that he understands something? And consequently, who does not have this <margin>15</margin> form, or idea of understanding <note>original: "intellectionis"</note>, which, by extending <margin>260</margin> it indefinitely, forms the idea<sup>a</sup> of divine understanding, and so for his other attributes?

<margin>20</margin>
Furthermore, since we have used the idea of God that is within us to demonstrate his existence, and since such immense power is contained in this idea that we understand it to be contradictory—if God exists—for anything else to exist besides him unless it were created by him, it follows clearly that from the fact that his existence has been demonstrated, it has also been demonstrated that the whole world—or all things distinct from God, whatever exists—were created by him.

### RESPONSE.

It is of no relevance to ask whether the phrase, *great light*, is argumentative or not, provided that it is explanatory, as it <margin>266</margin> truly is. For no one is unaware that by "light in the intellect," one understands the **clarity of knowledge** <note>original: "perspicuitatem cognitionis."</note>, which <margin>20</margin> perhaps not everyone possesses who thinks they possess it; but this does not prevent it from being very different from an obstinate opinion conceived without evident perception.

However, when it is said here that we assent to things clearly perceived "whether we want to or not," it is the same <margin>25</margin> as if it were said that we desire a clearly recognized good "whether we want to or not": for the word *unwillingly* <note>original: "nolentes."</note> has no place in such matters, because it implies that we both will and do not will the same thing at the same time.

### OBJECTION XIV.

<margin>ON THE FIFTH MEDITATION.
Concerning the essence of material things.</margin>
For example, when I imagine a triangle, even if perhaps such a figure exists nowhere in the world <note>original: "nullibi gentium," literally "nowhere among the nations."</note> outside my thought, and never has existed, there is nevertheless certainly a <margin>5</margin> determined nature, or essence, or immutable and eternal form of it, which was not <margin>267</margin> created by me, nor depends on my mind; this is clear from the fact that various properties can be demonstrated regarding this triangle <gloss>See page 64, lines 11-18.</gloss>.

<margin>10</margin> *If a triangle exists nowhere in the world, I do not understand how it has any nature; for what is nowhere, is nothing; and therefore it has no being, nor any nature. The triangle in the mind arises from a triangle seen, or from things seen and then fashioned together. Once we have called the thing (from which we think the <margin>15</margin> idea of a triangle arises) by the name "triangle," although the triangle itself perishes, the name remains. In the same way, if we have once conceived in our thought that all the angles of a triangle together equal two right angles, and we have given this other name to the triangle—"having three angles equal to two <margin>20</margin> right angles"—even if no angle existed in the world, the name would still remain, and the truth of this proposition would be eternal: **a triangle is that which has three angles equal to two right angles.** But the nature of the triangle will not be eternal, if by chance every triangle were to perish.*

<margin>25</margin> *Similarly, the proposition, **man is an animal**, will be true for eternity because <margin>268</margin> of the eternal names; but if the human race were to perish, there would no longer be a human nature.* <note>Hobbes is arguing for "nominalism"—the idea that universal truths are simply properties of language and names, rather than reflections of "eternal essences" existing in a divine mind or an abstract realm.</note>

...merely that it is extended, shaped, mobile, etc., and by denying of it all those things that pertain to the nature of the mind, it does little to help the matter. For whoever might contend that our mind is corporeal would not for that reason think that <margin>5</margin> every body is a mind. Body, therefore, would relate to mind as a <term>genus</term> <note>A general category in logic.</note> relates to a <term>species</term> <note>A specific sub-category within a genus.</note>. But a genus can be understood without its <margin>279</margin> species, even while denying whatever is proper and peculiar to that species; hence Logicians commonly say that if the species is denied, the genus is not denied. Thus, I can understand a "figure" without <margin>10</margin> understanding any of those properties that are unique to a circle. It remains to be proved, therefore, that the mind can be completely and adequately understood without the body.

I see no other argument in the whole work suitable for this proof, except that which was proposed at the beginning <margin>15</margin>: I can deny that there is any body, or any extended thing, and yet it is certain to me that I exist, as long as I deny this, or think; I am therefore a <term>thinking thing</term> <note>original Latin: *res cogitans*; Descartes' famous definition of the soul.</note>, not a body, and the body does not pertain to the knowledge of myself.

But I see that from this it only follows that some knowledge of myself <margin>20</margin> can be prepared without knowledge of the body; but that this knowledge is complete and adequate, <gloss>in such a way</gloss> that I am certain I am not deceived when I exclude the body from my essence, is not yet clearly apparent to me. I will explain the matter with an example.

Suppose someone knows for certain that an angle in a semicircle is a right angle <margin>280</margin> <margin>25</margin>, and consequently that the triangle formed by that angle and the diameter of the circle is right-angled; but he may doubt, or perhaps has not yet discovered for certain—indeed, he might even deny, misled by some fallacy—that the square of the base of the right-angled triangle is equal to the squares of the sides <note>This refers to the Pythagorean theorem ($a^2 + b^2 = c^2$).</note>. ### | CONCERNING GOD.

<margin>287</margin>
There are two parts to the first demonstration of the existence of God, which the author explains in the **Third Meditation**: the first is that God exists because His idea is in me; the second is that I, who possess such an idea, cannot exist except by God’s power.
<margin>5</margin>
Regarding the first part, there is one point that I do not find convincing: namely, while the Illustrious Man <note>original: "Vir C." (Vir Clarissimus), a respectful way of addressing Descartes.</note> asserted that falsity in the strict sense is found only in judgments, he nevertheless admits shortly after that ideas can be false—not **formally**, to be sure, but **materially** <gloss>a</gloss>; which seems to me inconsistent with his principles.
<margin>10</margin>
But I fear that I may not be able to explain the thoughts of my mind clearly enough in such an obscure matter; the thing will become clearer through an example. "If," he says, "cold is only a <term>privation</term> <note>In philosophy, a "privation" is the absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present (like blindness being the privation of sight).</note> of heat, the idea of cold, which represents it to me as a positive thing, will be **materially false** <gloss>b</gloss>."
<margin>15</margin>
On the contrary, if cold is only a privation, no idea of cold can be given that represents it to me as a positive thing, and here the author is confusing judgment with the idea.

For what is the "idea" of cold? It is cold itself, insofar as it exists **objectively in the intellect** <note>This refers to the "objective reality" of an idea—the reality the object has as it exists in the mind.</note>. But if cold is a privation, it cannot
<margin>20</margin>
exist objectively | in the intellect through an idea whose **objective being** is a **positive entity**. | Therefore, if cold is only a privation, there can never be a positive idea of it, and consequently none that is **materially false**.
<margin>288</margin>

*...it is possible for such a being not to exist, yet it cannot be imagined that its idea presents nothing real to me.*

*This can clearly be said of every positive idea. For, although it can be imagined that cold (which I think is represented by a positive idea) is not something positive, it still cannot be imagined that a positive idea presents nothing real and positive to me. This is because an idea is not called "positive" according to the being it has as a mode of thinking—for in that way, all ideas would be positive—but from the <term>objective being</term> <note>Objective being (esse objectivum) refers to the reality of the object as it exists in the mind as a representation, rather than its existence in the physical world.</note> it contains and presents to our mind. Therefore, that idea might not be the idea of cold, but it cannot be false.*

*But, you will say, it is false precisely because it is not the idea of cold. On the contrary, it is your judgment that is false, if you judge it to be the idea of cold; but the idea itself in you is very true. Just as the idea of God should not be called false even <term>materially</term> <note>Material falsity (materialiter falsa) refers to an idea that provides "material" for an error of judgment, such as representing a non-thing as a thing.</note>, although someone might transfer it to a thing that is not God, as idolaters have done.*

*Finally, that idea of cold, which you say is materially false, what does it present to your mind? A <term>privation</term> <note>In philosophy, a privation is the absence of a quality that should be present; for example, blindness is the "privation" of sight.</note>? Then it is true. A positive being? Then it is not the idea of cold. And furthermore, what is the cause of that positive objective being, from which you want it to happen that the idea is materially false? "I," you say, "insofar as I am from nothing." Therefore, the positive objective being of some idea can come from nothing—which tears down the primary foundations of the Illustrious Man <note>original: "Clarissimus Vir" (C. Viri), a formal way of referring to Descartes. Arnauld is pointing out a contradiction: Descartes argues that everything must have a cause, yet here he seems to suggest a "positive" idea could arise from "nothingness."</note>.*

*But let us proceed to the latter part of the demonstration, in which it is asked whether I, who possess the idea of an infinite being, can exist from anyone else but an infinite being, and especially...*

...could not give [being to itself], so too it is impossible for the same thing to receive its own being from itself?

Furthermore, every cause is the cause of an effect, and every effect is the effect of a cause; consequently, there is a mutual relationship <term>relationship<note>original: "habitudo". In Scholastic logic, this refers to a relation between two distinct entities.</note></term> between cause and effect. But a relationship can only exist between two distinct things.

<margin>5</margin>Secondly, it cannot be conceived without absurdity that a thing should receive being, and yet already possess that same being before we have conceived of it as having received it. Yet this would happen if we attributed the notions of cause and effect to the same thing in respect to itself. For what <margin>10</margin>is the notion of a cause? To give being <note>The 1st and 2nd editions read "giving" (dans) rather than "to give" (dare).</note>. What is the notion of an effect? To receive being. Now, the notion of a cause is, by its very nature, prior to the notion of an effect.

Indeed, we cannot conceive of a thing under the notion of a cause as giving being unless we conceive of it as already possessing being; for no one gives what they do not have. Therefore, we <margin>293</margin>would have to conceive of the thing as possessing being <margin>15</margin>before we could conceive of it as receiving it; and yet, in the one who receives, the act of receiving must come before the state of possessing.

This argument can be formulated another way: no one gives what they do not have; <margin>20</margin>therefore, no one can give being to themselves unless they already possess that being; but if they already possess it, why would they give it to themselves?

Finally, the Author asserts that it is known by the <term>natural light<note>The human capacity for reason and logic, which Descartes believes allows us to discern fundamental truths.</note></term> that creation is distinguished from conservation <note>The divine act of keeping a thing in existence from moment to moment.</note> only by a distinction of reason<gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "solâ ratione distingui". This means the two concepts are identical in reality but are distinguished by how our minds perceive them.</note>. But by that same natural light, it is known that nothing can create itself; therefore, nothing can conserve itself.

<margin>25</margin>However, if we descend from this general thesis to the specific hypothesis concerning God, the matter will be even more manifest in my judgment: that God cannot be from Himself in a positive sense <note>original: "positive"; i.e., as if God were the active cause of His own existence.</note>, but only in a negative sense <note>original: "negative"; i.e., simply meaning He does not depend on any other cause.</note>—that is, as not being from another.

And first of all, this is clear from the reason brought forward by the Illustrious Gentleman <note>original: "V. C." (Vir Clarissimus), a respectful Latin abbreviation used here to refer to Descartes.</note> to prove that, *if a body exists by itself, it must exist from itself positively. For, he says, the parts of time do not depend on one another; and therefore, from the fact that this body*
<margin>5</margin> *is supposed to have existed until this very time from itself—that is, without a cause—this is not enough for it to also exist in the future, unless there is some power in it that continuously, as it were, reproduces it* ᵃ.

But so far is this reason from being able to hold a place in a *supremely perfect*
<margin>10</margin> *or infinite being*, that on the contrary, the opposite can be evidently deduced for opposite reasons. For in the idea of an infinite being is contained the fact that its duration is also infinite—namely, enclosed by no limits—and therefore indivisible, permanent, all at once <note>original: "tota simul." This is a classic philosophical definition of eternity, where time does not pass, but all moments exist simultaneously.</note>, and in which *before*
<margin>15</margin> *and after* can only be conceived through error and the imperfection of our intellect.

From this it clearly follows that the infinite Being cannot be conceived to exist for even a moment without it being simultaneously conceived both that it has always existed and will possess existence for eternity (which
<margin>20</margin> the Author himself teaches elsewhere) ᵇ, so that it is therefore useless to ask why it persists in *being*.

Indeed, as Augustine frequently teaches (than whom no one has ever spoken more worthily or loftily about God after the sacred authors), in God there is no *either "to have been" or "to be in the future," but only always*
<margin>25</margin> *to "be"* <note>original: "vel fuisse vel futurum esse, sed semper esse." Augustine argues that God exists outside of time, in an eternal present.</note>; so that it appears more clearly from this that it is only with absurdity <margin>295</margin> that one can ask why God persists in *being*, since this question clearly involves *before and after, past and future*, which must be excluded from the notion of an infinite Being.

### FOURTH OBJECTIONS

<margin>300</margin>
...method of philosophizing, by which all things are called into doubt. And indeed, the Author <note>original: "Author" (referring to Descartes)</note> himself admits in the *Method*<sup>a</sup>, that for average minds this path is dangerous; I admit, however, that this hostility is softened in the *Synopsis*<sup>b</sup>.

<margin>5</margin>

Rather, it should show that—having set aside for a little while those things which leave even the smallest and **hyperbolic** <note>original: "hyperbolicam". In this context, "hyperbolic doubt" refers to an extreme or exaggerated form of skepticism used as a tool to find absolute certainty.</note>—as the Author himself calls it in another place<sup>c</sup>—occasion for doubt, something
<margin>10</margin>
so firm and stable might be found that it is not permitted even for the most stubborn to doubt it in the least. <margin>15</margin>
In the Fourth Meditation, *On Truth and Falsity*, for many reasons which would be long to list, I would greatly desire that he should indicate two things, either in the Meditation itself or in the *Synopsis*. The first is that, while he investigates the cause of error, he is concerned primarily with that error which is committed in the **distinguishing of truth and falsity**, 
<margin>20</margin>
and not with that error which occurs in the **pursuit of good and evil**.

<margin>301</margin>

<margin>25</margin>
 to the latter category, prudence (unless I am mistaken) demands—and the order of teaching, which our Author is most fond of, requires—that whatever does not pertain to the matter and provides an occasion for disputes...

...can be provided, should be omitted, lest the reader be pointlessly annoyed by superfluous details and delayed from grasping the essential points.

The second point I would like to suggest to our Author <note>original: "Authorem"; referring to René Descartes</note> is that, when he asserts we should not agree to anything except what we know clearly and distinctly, he is only speaking about things that concern academic disciplines and fall under the **intellect** <note>original: "intelligentiam"; here meaning human reason and scientific understanding</note>. He is not referring to matters of **faith** <note>original: "fidem"</note> or the conduct of daily life. Therefore, he condemns the recklessness of those who jump to conclusions, but not the conviction of those who believe with prudence.

For there are three things, as Saint Augustine wisely advises in *The Profit of Believing* <note>original: "de utilit. credendi", referring to the work *De Utilitate Credendi*</note>, chapter 15 <gloss>a</gloss>, which are like neighbors to one another and very much deserve to be distinguished in the human mind: **understanding**, **believing**, and **opining** <note>original: "intelligere, credere, opinari"</note>.

<margin>302</margin><margin>15</margin> One **understands** <note>original: "Intelligit"</note> who grasps something by certain reason. One **believes** <note>original: "Credit"</note> who, moved by some heavy authority, thinks something is true even though they do not grasp it by certain reason. One **opines** <note>original: "Opinatur"</note> who thinks they know what they actually do not know.

<margin>20</margin> To **opine** is most shameful for two reasons: first, because someone who has already convinced themselves they know a thing cannot truly learn it (if it is learnable); and second, because such rashness is a sign of a poorly disciplined mind.

Therefore, what we understand, we owe to **reason**; what we believe, we owe to **authority**; and what we opine, we owe to **error**. These things are said so that we might realize that, while holding onto our faith in things we do not yet fully grasp, we are protected from the recklessness of those who merely opine.

For those who say nothing should be believed unless we know it, they are simply trying to avoid the stigma of "opinion," which...

<meta>This page continues René Descartes’ response to Antoine Arnauld in the "Fourth Replies." Descartes is clarifying the conditions under which we can claim two things—specifically the mind and the body—are truly distinct. He introduces the crucial distinction between "complete" knowledge and "adequate" knowledge, arguing that while we cannot know everything about a thing (adequate knowledge), we can know enough to see it as a complete entity.</meta>

*I must also explain in what sense I understand that a "real distinction"* <term>real distinction: a metaphysical gap where two things, like mind and body, can exist independently of each other</term> *is not inferred simply because one thing is conceived without the other by an abstraction of the mind conceiving the thing inadequately. Instead, it is inferred only when each thing is understood without the other "completely," or as a "complete thing"* <note>original: "ut res completa intelligatur"</note><sup>a</sup>.

| *For I do not believe that "adequate knowledge"* <note>original: "adaequatam rei cognitionem"</note> *of a thing is required here, as the Distinguished Gentleman* <note>original: "Vir C." (Vir Clarissimus), referring to Antoine Arnauld</note> *assumes. The difference is this: for knowledge to be "adequate," it must contain absolutely every property that exists in the thing being known. Therefore, God alone knows that He possesses adequate knowledge of all things.*

<margin>308</margin>
| *A created intellect, however—even if it might actually possess such knowledge about many things—can never *know* that it has it, unless God reveals it specifically. For a mind to have adequate knowledge of some thing, it only requires that its capacity for knowing matches that thing; this can easily happen. But for the mind to *know* that it has this knowledge—or to know that God has placed nothing more in that thing than what the mind perceives—it would have to match the infinite power of God* <note>original: "infinitam Dei potestatem"</note><sup>b</sup> *with its own power of knowing. This is clearly impossible.*

*Now, to recognize a real distinction between two things, our knowledge of them does not need to be adequate, unless we were required to *know* that it is adequate. But as I just said, we can never know this; therefore, it is not required that the knowledge be adequate.*

*Therefore, when I said that it is not enough for one thing [to be conceived] without the other*...

<meta>This page continues Descartes’s Fourth Set of Replies, specifically responding to the theologian Antoine Arnauld. Descartes is clarifying his definition of a "complete thing" to support his argument that the mind and body are distinct substances. He is addressing the objection that we might not have "adequate knowledge" of the mind, arguing instead that we only need "sufficient" knowledge to identify something as a substance.</meta>

<page-num>222</page-num>
<header>### THE WORKS OF DESCARTES.</header>

Therefore, in response to the first point, I understand by a **complete thing** <term>res completa: a philosophical term for an entity that can exist on its own without needing to be attached to something else</term> nothing other than a **substance** <term>substantia: the underlying "stuff" or reality that possesses properties</term> endowed with those forms or **attributes** <term>attributa: the qualities or characteristics of a substance, like "thinking" for the mind or "extension" for the body</term> which are sufficient for me to recognize from them that it is itself a substance.

For we do not know substances immediately <note>original: "immediate cognoscimus"</note>, as has been noted elsewhere, but only from the fact that we perceive certain forms or attributes. Since these must reside in something in order to exist, we call that thing in which they reside a *Substance*.

If, however, we later wished to strip that same substance of those attributes through which we know it, we would destroy all our knowledge of it. Thus, we might indeed be able to utter some words about it, but they would not be words whose meaning we could perceive clearly and distinctly.

<margin>311</margin>
I am not unaware that certain substances are commonly called *incomplete*. But if they are called incomplete because they cannot exist alone on their own, I confess it seems contradictory to me that they should be substances—that is, things *subsisting on their own* <note>original: "per se subsistentes"</note>—and at the same time "incomplete"—that is, not able to subsist on their own. However, they can be called **incomplete substances** in another way: namely, that insofar as they are substances, they have nothing incomplete about them, but are only "incomplete" insofar as they are referred to some other substance, with which they form a single thing *through itself* <note>original: "unum per se," meaning a unified entity like a human being</note>.

Thus, a hand is an **incomplete substance** when it is referred to the whole body of which it is a part; but it is a **complete substance** when it is viewed alone. And in exactly the same way, the **mind** and the **body** are incomplete substances when they are referred to the human being whom they compose; but, viewed alone, they are complete.

For just as being extended, divisible, having a shape, and so on, are the forms or **attributes** <term>attributa: the fundamental characteristics that define what a thing is</term> through which I recognize that **substance** <term>substantia: a thing that can exist on its own</term> which is called *body*; so too being intelligent, willing, doubting, and so on, are the forms through which I recognize the substance called *mind*. I understand a thinking substance to be a **complete thing** <term>res completa: an entity that possesses everything necessary to be a substance in its own right</term> no less than I understand an extended substance to be one.

| Nor can it be said in any way what the illustrious gentleman <note>original: "Vir C." (Vir Clarissimus), referring here to the author of the objections, Arnauld</note> added: *perhaps the body is related to the mind as a genus is to a species* <sup>a</sup>; for although a **genus** <term>genus: a general category, like "animal"</term> can be understood without this or that **specific difference** <term>differentia specifica: the trait that identifies a sub-type, like "rationality" makes a human a specific type of animal</term>, a **species** <term>species: a specific type within a category</term> cannot be thought of in any way without its genus.

For example, we easily understand "shape" without thinking anything about a "circle" (though this understanding is not distinct unless it refers to some specific shape, nor does it concern a complete thing unless it includes the nature of a body); but we cannot understand any specific difference of a circle without simultaneously thinking of "shape."

The mind, however, can be perceived distinctly and completely—or at least enough to be considered a complete thing—without any of those forms or attributes by which we recognize that the body is a substance, as I believe I sufficiently demonstrated in the Second Meditation; and the body is understood distinctly and as a complete thing without those things that belong to the mind.

<margin>313</margin>
Here, however, the illustrious gentleman insists: *even if some knowledge of myself can be obtained without knowledge of the body, it does not follow from this that such knowledge is complete and adequate, such that I can be certain I am not mistaken when I exclude the body from my essence* <sup>b</sup>.

<margin>316</margin> For indeed, this is the very notion of a substance: | that it can exist by itself, that is, without the aid of any other substance. And therefore, had I not sought a certainty greater than the common sort, I would have been content to show, in the second | Meditation, that the *Mind* is understood as a subsisting thing <note>Original: "rem subsistentem," a thing that exists in its own right.</note>, even <margin>10</margin> though nothing at all is attributed to it that belongs to the body; and conversely also that the *Body* is understood as a subsisting thing, even if nothing is attributed to it that belongs to the mind. And I would have added nothing more to demonstrate that the mind is really distinct from the body: because we commonly judge that all things <margin>15</margin> relate to truth itself in the same way that they relate to our perception. But, because among those hyperbolic doubts <term>hyperbolicas dubitationes: the extreme, "over-the-top" skeptical arguments Descartes used to clear away false beliefs</term> which I proposed in the first Meditation, one proceeded so far that I could not be certain <margin>20</margin> of this very point (namely, that things are in truth such as we perceive them), as long as I supposed myself to be ignorant of the author of my origin <note>Descartes refers to the possibility that a "deceiving god" or "evil demon" created him with a flawed mind.</note>, | <margin>317</margin> for that reason, everything I wrote concerning God and truth in the third, fourth, and fifth Meditations contributes to the conclusion about the real distinction between mind and body <margin>25</margin>, which I finally completed in the sixth Meditation.

Yet, says the Distinguished Gentleman <note>Original: "Vir C." In contrast, regarding the mind, we not only understand it to exist without the body, but also that all those things belonging to the body can be denied of it; for this is the nature of <margin>10</margin> substances, that they mutually exclude one another.

In that same Sixth Meditation, in which I dealt with the distinction between the mind and the body, I also proved at the same time that the mind is <margin>5</margin> substantially united to the body; and I used arguments, stronger than any I remember having read elsewhere to prove the same thing. And, just as a person who learned that a human arm is a <term>substance|In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is something that can exist by itself without needing something else to sustain it</term> <margin>319</margin> really distinct from the rest of | that person's body would not therefore deny that it belongs to the nature of the whole human <margin>10</margin> being; nor does the person who says the same arm belongs to the nature of the whole human being give any reason to suspect that it cannot exist on its own: so too I do not think I have proved too much by showing that the mind can exist without the body, nor too little by saying it is <margin>15</margin> substantially united to the body, because that substantial union does not prevent us from having a clear and distinct concept of the mind alone as a <term>complete thing|Descartes uses the term "res completa" to describe an entity that has all the properties necessary to be a substance in its own right, rather than just a quality of something else</term> <note>original: "rei completæ"</note>. Therefore, it differs greatly from the concept of a surface or a line<sup>a</sup>, which cannot be understood as complete things unless depth is also attributed to them in addition to <margin>20</margin> length and width.

Finally, from the fact that the *power of thinking* <note>original: "vis cogitandi"</note> *is dormant in infants and, in those who have lost their minds, not indeed extinguished but* <margin>25</margin> *disturbed*<sup>b</sup>, we must not think that it is so attached to the bodily organs that it cannot exist without them. For from the fact that we often experience it being hindered by those organs, it in no way follows that it is produced by them; nor can this be proved by any reason, even the smallest.

<margin>320</margin> Nevertheless, I do not deny that close conjunction of the mind with the body, which we constantly experience through our senses...

This refers to the theological concern that if "cause" implies a priority in time or status, describing the Father as the cause of the Son might suggest the Son is inferior, a view associated with Arianism.</note> | But where no such danger of error can exist, and we are not dealing with God as Triune, but only as One, I do not see why the name "cause" should be so greatly avoided, especially when we have reached a point where it seems very useful and almost necessary to use it.

There can be no greater utility for this name than if it serves to demonstrate the existence of God; and no greater necessity, than if without it, existence cannot be clearly demonstrated.

Moreover, I think it is manifest to everyone that the consideration of the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The agent or force that brings something into existence; for example, a carpenter is the efficient cause of a table.</note> is the first and primary means—not to say the unique one—that we have for proving the existence of God. But we cannot pursue that means accurately unless we give our mind the freedom to inquire into the efficient causes of all things, even of God himself; for by what right would we exclude God from this inquiry, before it has been proved that he exists? Therefore, we must ask regarding each thing whether it is <term>of itself</term> <note>original: "a se" — existing by its own nature rather than being created by something else.</note> or from another; and indeed, through this means, the existence of God can be concluded, even if it is not expressly explained <margin>334</margin> | how it is to be understood that something is *of itself*. For whoever follows the guidance of the <term>natural light</term> <note>The human capacity for reason and innate knowledge, which Descartes believed was given by God to allow us to discern truth.</note> alone, spontaneously forms in this context a certain concept common to both efficient and formal causes; specifically, so that what is from another is from it as if from an efficient cause, but what is *of itself* <note>original: "a se"</note> is as if from a <term>formal cause</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, the "essence" or "definition" that makes a thing what it is.</note>—that is, because it has such an essence that it does not need an efficient cause.

<margin>5</margin> But since those who are accustomed to judging that nothing can be the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The active agent that brings something into being, like a builder building a house.</note> of itself, and to accurately distinguishing that from a <term>formal cause</term> <note>The essence or definition that makes a thing what it is; for example, the "formal cause" of a triangle is having three sides.</note>, see the question asked whether something can be <term>of itself</term> <note>original: "a seipso" — existing by its own power rather than being created by another.</note>, it easily happens that, thinking only of an efficient cause properly so called, they do not think that the phrase "of itself" should be understood as referring to a cause, but only negatively as meaning <margin>10</margin> **without a cause**, so that it is simply something about which we ought not to inquire why it exists. <margin>15</margin> However, to respond appropriately to this point, I think it is necessary to show that there is something intermediate between an efficient cause properly so called and no cause at all: namely, the **positive essence of a thing**. To this essence, the concept of an efficient cause can be extended in the same way that we are accustomed <margin>20</margin> in **Geometry** to extend the concept of a very large circular line to the concept of a straight line, or the concept of a <term>rectilinear polygon</term> <note>A shape with straight sides, like a square or hexagon.</note> whose number of sides is indefinite to the concept of a circle.
