In philosophy, an "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being. Descartes argues that since God's very nature ("essence") includes existing, He doesn't need an external maker.</note>. From these points, he <note>Arnauld</note> claims that what I had said collapses—namely, that if I believed no thing could stand in relation to itself in the same way an **efficient cause** stands to its **effect**, I would never reach a **first cause** of all things when investigating their origins.
<margin>342</margin> Yet this seems to me neither to collapse, nor to be shaken or weakened in any way; indeed, the primary force, not only of my own proofs but of all possible proofs used to demonstrate the existence of God from His **effects** <note>A proof "from effects" (a posteriori) moves from the observed world back to its creator.</note>, depends on this very principle. Almost all **theologians**, moreover, maintain that no proof of God can be offered except one based on effects.

Therefore, far from clarifying the demonstration of God’s existence, his refusal to allow the **analogy** of an efficient cause to be applied to God in relation to Himself actually distracts readers from understanding it. This is especially true at the end, where he concludes: *if he thought it necessary to search for an efficient cause (or a quasi-efficient cause) for every thing, he would look for a cause distinct from the thing itself.* For how would those who do not yet know God search for the efficient cause of other things, so as to reach the knowledge of God through that process, unless they believed that the efficient cause of **every** thing could be sought? And how, finally, [could we seek] in God as the cause

### WORKS OF DESCARTES

...tiny **channels** <term>channels: original "meatus," referring to the microscopic pores or passages within a solid body</term> which are found between the fine grains of flour from which **bread** is composed, and between the particles of **spirit** <note>original: "spiritûs." In 17th-century science, "spirits" referred to the most volatile, active parts of a liquid, such as alcohol in wine.</note>, water, vinegar, and dregs or **tartar** <note>original: "tartari," the potassium bitartrate crystals that precipitate out of wine.</note>, from the mixture of which **wine** consists, and likewise between the tiny bits of other bodies. For indeed those particles, since they have diverse shapes and motions, can never be joined so perfectly that many spaces are not left between them; these spaces are not empty, but are filled either with air or another matter. We see such spaces with our own eyes in bread—they are large enough that they can be filled not only with air, but also with water, or wine, or other liquids. And since the bread remains always the same, even though the air or other matter contained in its pores changes, it is clear that these materials do not belong to its **substance**. Therefore, the bread's **surface** is not merely that which surrounds the whole thing in the shortest circuit, but that which is immediately placed around each of its individual particles.

<margin>351</margin>
It must also be noted that this surface not only moves as a whole when the whole bread is moved from one place to another, but it also moves in part, when some particles of the bread are agitated by air or other bodies entering its pores. This is so much the case that, if any bodies are of such a nature that either some or all of their parts move constantly (which I believe to be true of most parts of bread and all parts of wine), it must also be understood that their surface is in a certain continuous motion.

Finally, it should be noted that by the "surface" of bread, or wine, or any other body, we do not mean here any part of the **substance** <term>substance: the underlying reality of a thing that remains constant even if its properties change</term> nor even of the **quantity** of that body, nor even a part of the surrounding bodies, but only—

...only that boundary which is conceived as being between its individual particles and the bodies surrounding them, and which has absolutely no entity except a **modal** <term>modal: in Scholastic philosophy, a "mode" is a quality or state of a substance (like its shape or position) that cannot exist independently of the substance itself</term> one.

Descartes is arguing that the Scholastic concept of "real accidents"—physical properties that exist independently of matter—is not only logically contradictory but also a stumbling block for the faith. He suggests that his own philosophy, which treats qualities like color and taste as results of surface structure, provides a more rational explanation for how the appearances of bread remain after transubstantiation.</meta>

# WORKS OF DESCARTES. 292-293.

<page-num>254</page-num>

...is called a **real accident**, to remain: which, if not in words, certainly in concept involves a contradiction.

   And this seems to be the principal reason why some have dissented from the Roman Church <note>original: "Ecclesia Romana"</note> on this point. <margin>5</margin>Who indeed would deny that where one is free, and no reason—neither theological nor even philosophical—compels us to embrace certain opinions, those should be preferred which can give others no occasion or pretext for turning away from the truth of the faith? That the <margin>10</margin>opinion which posits **real accidents** <term>real accidents: in Scholastic philosophy, these were physical qualities like color or smell that were thought to have their own "real" existence, potentially separable from the object itself</term> does not agree with theological reasons, I think has been shown clearly enough here; and that it is plainly opposed to philosophical reasons, I hope to demonstrate clearly in the summary of philosophy <note>Descartes refers here to his *Principles of Philosophy*, which he was preparing for publication</note> which I now <margin>15</margin>have in my hands; and there I will show how color, taste, weight, and everything else that moves the senses depend solely on the outermost surface of bodies.

   Finally, **real accidents** cannot be supposed without adding, for no reason, another new and indeed incomprehensible miracle to the miracle of **transubstantiation** <term>transubstantiation: the Catholic doctrine that the substance of bread and wine changes into the body and blood of Christ during the Mass, while the appearances remain</term>, <margin>20</margin>which alone can be concluded from the **words of consecration** <term>words of consecration: the specific ritual words spoken by a priest—"This is my body"—which are believed to effect the change of the bread</term>. By this added miracle, these real accidents would exist without the substance of bread in such a way that they do not, in the meantime, become substances themselves. This not only fights against human reason, but also <margin>25</margin>against the axiom of theologians, who say that those words of consecration effect nothing except their own literal meaning, and they do not wish to ascribe to a miracle what can be explained through natural reason <note>original: "ratio naturalis"</note>. All these difficulties are plainly removed by my explanation of this matter: for it is so far from being the case that...

### FOURTH REPLIES.
<meta>Descartes's replies to the Fourth Set of Objections, pages 293-294.</meta>

<page-num>255</page-num>

...according to [my view] <note>Descartes is referring to his own philosophical system</note> itself, some miracle might be necessary to preserve the accidents after the substance has been removed; on the contrary, they could not be removed without a new miracle (specifically one by which the dimensions are changed). 
<margin>5</margin> It has been recorded in memory that this has occasionally happened: when, in place of the consecrated bread, flesh or a child appeared in the hands of the priest; for it has never been believed that this happened through the ceasing of a miracle, but entirely through a new miracle.

Furthermore, there is nothing incomprehensible or difficult in the fact that God, the creator of all things, can change one substance into another, and that this later substance remains under exactly the same surface under which the prior one was contained. 
<margin>10</margin> Nor can anything be said to be more in agreement with reason, nor more widely accepted among **Philosophers**, than that not only every sense, but generally every action of body upon body, occurs through **contact**, and that this **contact** can only occur on the surface: from which it follows evidently that the same surface, however much the substance beneath it is changed, 
<margin>20</margin> must always act and be acted upon in the same way.

Therefore, if it is permitted here to write the truth without causing offense <note>original: "sine invidia," meaning without provoking ill-will or jealousy</note>, I would dare to hope for a time to come when that opinion which posits **real accidents** <term>real accidents: the Scholastic idea that physical qualities like color or shape could exist as "things" independent of the matter they belong to</term>—as being alien to reason, incomprehensible, and not entirely safe for the faith—will be exploded <note>original: "explodetur," in the sense of being hissed off stage or rejected</note> by **Theologians**, and mine will be received in its place as certain and 
<margin>25</margin> indubitable. I thought I should not hide this here, so that, as far as is in my power, I may counter the slanders of those who, because they wish to appear more learned than others, find nothing more difficult to bear than if something new in the sciences is proposed 
<margin>30</margin> which they cannot pretend they already knew.

...than a vessel containing it? Why should you not be considered to be bounded by the same surrounding environment as the body, or by the body’s skin? <note>Gassendi is asking Descartes why the soul shouldn't be viewed as a physical substance that fits inside the body like liquid in a jar.</note> Why would you not fill space, or those parts of space, which the solid body or its parts do not fill? # WORKS OF DESCARTES. 302-303.

...whether you are playing games with us, or you are deceiving yourself, we should not linger on it. But if you are speaking seriously, you must prove that you neither have any body which you give form to, nor are you the kind of thing that is able to be nourished and move along with it.

<margin>364</margin> <margin>5</margin> You go on to say that you do not even possess sensation. <note>original: "neque te sentire"</note> Yet it is surely you who sees colors, hears sounds, and so on. Nor is it true that you have never <margin>15</margin> used the eye, through which you have sensed and taken in the images that you are now able to use even without the eye.

You must also prove that this thick, physical body <margin>365</margin> contributes | absolutely nothing to your thought (since, after all, you have never been without it, nor have you ever, up to this point, been separated from it...).

Here I admit that I was mistaken. For I thought I was addressing the human soul, or that internal principle by which a human being lives, feels, moves, and understands; and yet I was addressing <margin>10</margin> only the mind <note>original: "mens"</note>, since it has not only stripped off the body, but has also stripped off the soul itself. Are you doing this, most distinguished sir, in the manner of those ancients who, although they thought the soul was diffused throughout the whole body, nonetheless believed that the sovereign part—the *governing part* <note>original Greek: τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν</note>—had its seat in a specific part <margin>15</margin> of the body, such as the brain or the heart? Not because they thought the soul was not also found in that part, but because they believed <margin>366</margin> that the mind was, as it were, added to the soul existing there, and united with it, and together with it gave form to that part. And I truly should have remembered this from the discussions in your *Discourse on the Method* <note>original: "Dissertatione de Methodo"</note>: <margin>20</margin> for in that work you seemed to want all these functions, which are attributed to both the vegetative and sensitive souls <note>Aristotelian terms for the biological functions of life (growth) and sensation</note>, to not depend on the rational soul <note>original: "rationali"</note>, and to be capable of being exercised even before it arrives—just as they are also exercised in brutes, in whom you contend there is no reason at all. But somehow I had <margin>25</margin> forgotten this, perhaps because I remained doubtful whether you would not want that principle by which both we and the brutes are nourished and feel to be called a "soul," but rather that our mind is properly our "soul": whereas that principle is properly said to "animate" <note>original: "animare"</note>, while the mind provides nothing other than <margin>30</margin> that we think—which you indeed assert happens. However that may be...

<margin>25</margin> *distinctly conceived? We do indeed conceive that besides the color, shape, liquidity, etc., there is something that serves as the subject for the accidents and the observed changes; but what that something is, or what it is like, we do not know. <meta>This page continues the "Fifth Set of Objections" by Pierre Gassendi, a contemporary of Descartes who championed a more sensory, experimental approach to philosophy. On the previous page, Gassendi began critiques of Descartes’ "wax argument" from the *Second Meditation*. Descartes had argued that even when wax melts and loses its color, smell, and shape, he still knows it is the same wax through his mind alone, not his senses or imagination. Gassendi is now challenging this, arguing that what Descartes calls "mind" is actually just a refined form of imagination based on physical properties.</meta>

In the previous section, Gassendi challenged Descartes’ "Rule of Truth" (that whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived is true). <meta>324-325.</meta>

...existing outside the mind itself, and falling under some sense. Specifically, the mind has the faculty (or rather is itself the faculty) not only of perceiving **adventitious Ideas** <note>original: "Ideas adventitias"; these are ideas that Descartes claims come to us from the external world via the senses</note>, or those which it receives from things transmitted through the senses—perceiving them, I say, bare and distinct, and exactly as it receives them into itself; <margin>5</margin> but also of variously composing, dividing, contracting, <margin>391</margin> enlarging, comparing, and other such similar actions<sup>a</sup>.

Hence, the third class of Ideas <term>Factitious ideas: ideas the mind constructs itself, like imaginary creatures</term> is at least not distinct from the second: for the Idea of a **chimera** is nothing other than the Idea of a lion's head, a goat's belly, and a serpent's tail, from which <margin>10</margin> the mind composes one whole, though these parts individually, or one by one, are **adventitious**. Thus the Idea of a **Giant**, or of a man conceived as being like a mountain or the entire world, is nothing other than an adventitious one: namely, the Idea of a man of ordinary size, which the mind enlarges <margin>15</margin> at its pleasure, although it conceives it more confusedly the more it enlarges it. So too the Idea of a **Pyramid**, a city, or any other thing never seen, is nothing other than the adventitious idea of a previously seen Pyramid, city, or other thing, slightly deformed, and consequently multiplied and compared in some confused manner.

As for the species which you call **innate** <note>original: "innatas"; ideas Descartes believes are born within the mind, such as the idea of God or geometric truths</note>, these indeed <margin>20</margin> seem to be non-existent, and whatever things are called such seem to have an **adventitious** origin as well. You are also not speaking <margin>25</margin> of the Idea of any particular Thing: for the **Sun**, this **stone**, and all singular objects are **Things**, yet you do not say that there are innate Ideas of these. <meta>This page continues Pierre Gassendi’s "Fifth Objections" to René Descartes' "Third Meditation." In the preceding section, Gassendi argued that even complex or "invented" ideas (like chimeras or giants) are actually constructed from simpler "adventitious" ideas—those we get from our senses. Here, he extends this critique to the very concepts Descartes claims are "innate" to the human mind: the ideas of a "Thing," "Truth," and "Thought."</meta>

### FIFTH OBJECTIONS.

### ->WORKS OF DESCARTES, VOLUME II.<-
<meta>Secondary page numbering: 325-326; catchword/edition mark: ŒUVRES. II.</meta>

...insofar as it is synonymous with **being**, and is as wide-ranging as that term. But I ask you, how can this **Idea** be in the mind unless there are simultaneously so many individual things and their genera, from which the mind abstracts and forms a concept that belongs to none <margin>5</margin> of the individuals, and yet fits them all? Truly, if the **Idea of a Thing** is innate, then the **Idea** of an animal, a plant, a stone, and all universals <term>Universals: general concepts that apply to many things, like "redness" or "humanity"</term> will also be innate. And there will be no need for us to labor to distinguish between many individuals so that, having cut away various differences, we retain only that which <margin>10</margin> appears common to all—or, what is the same thing, the **Idea of the genus**.

You say also that you possess by your nature the ability to understand what **truth** is—or, as I would interpret it, the **Idea of truth**. Furthermore, if truth is nothing other than the conformity of a judgment <margin>15</margin> with the thing about which the judgment is made, truth is a certain relation, <margin>393</margin> and therefore nothing distinct from the thing and the **Idea** themselves related to each other—or, what is the same thing, from the **Idea** of the thing itself: since it represents both itself and the thing as it is. Therefore, the **Idea of truth** is nothing other than the **Idea** of the thing, insofar as it conforms to the thing, or <margin>20</margin> insofar as it represents the thing as it is. Consequently, if the **Idea** of the thing is not innate, but **adventitious** <note>original: "adventitia"; ideas that Descartes claims come to us from the external world via the senses</note>, then the **Idea of truth** is also adventitious, not innate. And since this is understood regarding any individual truth, it can also be understood universally regarding truth, the notion or **Idea** of which (as has just been said <margin>25</margin> regarding the **idea of a thing**) is drawn out from the notions or **Ideas** of individual things.

You say again that you possess by your nature the ability to understand what **thought** is (I will always interpret this as the **Idea of thought**). But, just as the mind fashions the **Idea** of one city from the **Idea** of another, so from the **Idea** of one action, such as seeing or tasting, it can fashion the **Idea** of another—for instance, of **thought** itself. For indeed, a certain analogy is recognized between the faculties...

<sig>36</sig>
<vocab>Idea, truth, thought, innate, adventitious, universals, particulars, Pierre Gassendi, René Descartes</vocab>

<summary>Gassendi argues that "innate" ideas like "thing," "truth," and "thought" are actually derived from sensory experience through abstraction and analogy. He contends that if the general concept of a "thing" were innate, then every specific category of thing (like plants or stones) would also have to be innate, which he finds absurd.</summary>

...recognizing, and one easily leads to the knowledge of the other. <note>original: "cognofcenteis, unaque ad alterius notitiam facile deducit"</note> Although one should not labor over the **Idea of thought**, but rather over the <margin>394</margin> **Idea** of the **mind itself**, and even of the **soul** <term>Anima: While 'mens' refers to the intellectual mind, 'anima' refers to the soul or life-giving principle; Gassendi uses both to challenge Descartes' focus on pure intellect</term>; for if <margin>5</margin> we grant that this is innate, there will be no difficulty in also admitting that the **Idea of thought** is innate. Therefore, we must wait until the matter is proven regarding the mind itself, or the soul.

3. You seem afterwards to cast doubt not only on whether some **Ideas** proceed from external things, but also on whether there are any external things at all. <margin>10</margin> And you seem consequently to infer: although there are **Ideas** in you of things called external, these **Ideas** do not prove that things exist, since they do not necessarily proceed from them, but could come from you, or in some other unknown way. I think it is for this reason you said before: you did not previously perceive the <margin>15</margin> earth, the sky, the stars, but the **Ideas** of the earth, sky, and stars, through which there could be a delusion. Thus, if you do not yet believe that the earth, sky, and stars, and other things exist, why, I ask, do you walk upon the earth, or move your body to look back at the Sun? Why do you go to the fire to feel heat? Why to the table, or <margin>20</margin> food, to satisfy your hunger? Why do you move your tongue to speak, or your hand to write these things to us? Certainly, such things <margin>395</margin> can be said, or subtly thought out; but they do not advance the business at hand. And since you do not truly doubt that these things exist outside of you, let us act seriously and in good faith, and <margin>25</margin> let us speak as things are. But if, while assuming the existence of external things, you think it has not been sufficiently demonstrated that we cannot borrow the **Ideas** we have of them from those things, you must solve the reasons, not only those you object to yourself, but those which can be further objected <gloss>a</gloss>.

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS.
<page-num>283</page-num>
<meta>AT numbering: 328-329.</meta>

<margin>5</margin> That is to say, you take it as if ideas are admitted to come from things because we seem taught by nature to think so, and because we experience that these ideas do not depend on us or our will. <margin>10</margin> Truly, to say nothing of your reasons or your solutions, one should also have objected and solved, among other things, why a person born blind has no **idea** of color, or a person born deaf has no **idea** of sound, if not because those external things were unable to transmit any likeness <note>original: "speciem," a term referring to the mental image or "species" that Scholastic philosophers believed traveled from an object to the eye</note> of themselves into the mind of that unfortunate person. It is because the doors have been closed since birth, and obstacles to those things passing through have been permanently placed.

<margin>15</margin> You later urge the example of the **Sun**, of which you say there are two **ideas**: one drawn from the senses, by which it appears small; the other from astronomical reasoning, by which it is conceived as vast. You claim that the latter is more similar and true, as it is not drawn from the senses but elicited from **innate notions** <note>original: "notionibus innatis"</note>, or produced in some other way. <margin>20</margin> <margin>396</margin> But indeed, those twin **ideas** of the **Sun** are both similar and true, or conformable to the **Sun**; it is just that one is more so, and the other less. It is the same way that two **ideas** of the same man—one sent from ten paces away, the other from a hundred or a thousand—are both similar and true, or conformable. However, the one that comes from closer is "worn down" less, while the one from further away is worn down more <note>original: "deteritur minus... magis"; Gassendi is using a physical metaphor for how sensory information weakens over distance</note>, as could be explained in a few words if allowed, though even you might not fully grasp it.

<margin>25</margin> Furthermore, the fact that we perceive that vast **idea** of the **Sun** by the mind alone does not mean it is elicited from some **innate notion**. Rather, the **idea** that enters through the senses is simply expanded by the power of the mind itself, insofar as experience proves and reason (resting upon that experience) confirms that distant things appear smaller than they are when they are close.

<margin>5</margin> **omniscient**, **perfect**, **supremely blessed**, and so forth. <margin>25</margin> also: these few qualities that we discover within ourselves, how do we recognize them to be in God? And once we have recognized them,

Truly, God is beyond all grasp by infinite intervals; and when our mind applies itself to the contemplation of Him...

# WORKS OF DESCARTES.
<page-num>288</page-num>

...is constructed, it is not only dim, but is nothing at all. Therefore, there is no reason for us to say that there is any genuine <note>original: "germanam"; a true or authentic representation</note> idea that represents God. It is quite enough if, from the analogy of these things of ours, we can extract and
<margin>5</margin>form some kind of idea for our own use—one that does not exceed human capacity, and contains no reality that we do not perceive in other things, or by the occasion of other things.

5. You *assume* consequently that it is manifest by the **natural light** <term>natural light</term> <note>The human capacity for reason and intuition, supposedly independent of divine revelation.</note> that there must be at least as much in the
<margin>10</margin>**efficient** and total **cause** <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary agent or force that brings something into being, such as a carpenter building a chair.</note> as there is in the effect. You do this so that you can infer that there must be at least as much **formal reality** in the cause of an idea as there is **objective reality** in the idea itself. <note>Descartes argued that if you have an idea of a perfect God (objective reality), the cause of that idea must itself be actually perfect (formal reality).</note> *This is surely a great leap, and one on which we must dwell for a while.*

<margin>404</margin>First, that common saying—<margin>15</margin>*nothing is in the effect which was not in the cause*—seems like it should be understood as referring to the **matter** <note>The physical "stuff" something is made of.</note> rather than the **efficient cause**. For the efficient cause is external, and is usually of a different nature than the effect. And although an effect is said to have its reality from the efficient cause, it nevertheless has not what the
<margin>20</margin>efficient cause necessarily has in itself, but what it can borrow from elsewhere. This is clearly evident in the products of art. For, although a house has all its reality from the builder, the builder nevertheless does not bestow it from his own being, but from what he has received from elsewhere. The Sun does the
<margin>25</margin>same when it transforms lower matter in various ways and produces various animals. Indeed, even a parent—from whom the offspring may get some portion of matter—nonetheless provides it not as an efficient principle, but as a material one. As for your objection, that the [reality] of the effect must be either **formally** or **eminent[ly]**... <note>Gassendi is cutting off Descartes' argument that a cause must contain the perfections of its effect either exactly ("formally") or in a higher, more superior way ("eminently").</note>

***

<summary>Gassendi challenges Descartes' metaphysical principle of causality, arguing that the "cause" of an idea (like a builder or the sun) does not need to possess the same qualities as the "effect" it produces. He suggests our idea of God is a composite of earthly observations rather than a reflection of a perfect cause.</summary>

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS.
<sig>(WORKS. II. 37</sig>

...to be contained in the cause, proves nothing more than that an effect sometimes has a form similar to the form of its cause, and sometimes a dissimilar and indeed more imperfect one, so that the form of the cause surpasses that of the effect. But it does 
<margin>5</margin>not follow that on this account either an **eminent cause** <term>eminent cause</term> <note>A cause that contains all the perfections of its effect in a higher or more excellent way, rather than having the exact same qualities. For example, a person’s mind is the "eminent cause" of a poem.</note> gives anything from its own being, or that a cause which contains something **formally** <term>formal reality</term> <note>When a cause possesses a quality in the same way it appears in the effect—like a fire (formally hot) causing a stone to become hot.</note> shares its own <margin>405</margin> form with the effect; for although this may seem to happen in the generation of living things, which comes from seed, you would not say, 
<margin>10</margin>I imagine, that a father, when he begets a son, cuts away and gives to him a part of his own **rational soul** <note>original: "rationalis animæ"; the part of the soul responsible for reason, which Scholastics believed was unique to humans.</note>. In a word, an **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary agent that brings something into being.</note> does not contain its effect in any other way than insofar as it can sketch it out and perfect it from a certain material.

Next, regarding what you infer about **objective reality** <term>objective reality</term> <note>The reality of an object as it exists in the mind as an idea, rather than as a physical thing in the world.</note>, I will use the example of my own image, which can be seen either 
<margin>15</margin>in the mirror I stand before, or in a painting that a painter is preparing. For just as I myself am the cause of the image in the mirror, insofar as I project my own **likeness** <note>original: "speciem"; in the science of the time, "species" were thin films or emissions shed by objects that traveled to the eye to produce vision.</note> into the mirror, and the painter is the cause of the image presented on the canvas: so, when an idea 
<margin>20</margin>or image of me exists in your intellect or anyone else's, it can be asked whether I myself am the cause of it, insofar as I project my likeness into the eye, and through the eye into the intellect itself; or whether there is instead some other cause that outlines that image in the intellect with a kind of brush or stylus. It 
<margin>24</margin>seems, furthermore, that no other cause besides myself need be sought; for <margin>406</margin> even though the intellect can afterwards enlarge, diminish, 
<margin>26</margin>combine, or otherwise handle the idea of me, I am nonetheless the primary cause of all the reality it contains within itself.

Now, that reality of an idea is distinguished as twofold by you; <margin>5</margin> and the **formal reality** <term>formal reality</term> <note>The actual existence of something as a thing in the world. For an idea, its "formal reality" is simply its existence as a mental state or a mode of the mind.</note> can indeed be nothing other than that thin substance which has flowed out from me, been received in the intellect, and formed into an idea. (Unless you prefer to say that the "species" <note>In older philosophy, a "species" was an image or likeness that traveled from an object to the senses.</note> proceeding from the object is a substantial **efflux** <term>effluxion</term> <note>original: "effluxio"; a flowing out or emission. Gassendi is testing a more physicalist interpretation of how ideas are formed.</note>; do whatever you please, you will always diminish the reality.) The **objective reality** <term>objective reality</term> <note>the reality of an idea in terms of the object it represents. If I think of a sun, the "objective reality" of my idea is the "sun-ness" contained in my thought.</note>, however, can be <margin>10</margin> nothing besides the representation or likeness of me which the idea carries, or certainly nothing besides the **symmetry** <note>The proportional arrangement of parts.</note> by which the parts of the idea are so disposed that they represent me. In whatever way you take it, it seems indeed to be nothing real; since it is only a relation of parts among themselves and toward me, or a mode of formal reality, insofar as it is <margin>15</margin> formed in this way. But it matters not: let it be called, because it is pleasing to do so, objective reality.

This being established, you would seem to be obliged to compare the **formal reality** <margin>407</margin> of the idea with my formal reality (that is, with my substance), and the objective reality of the idea with the symmetry of my parts (that is, my external outline and form); <margin>20</margin> yet it pleases you instead to compare the objective reality of the idea with my formal reality.

Furthermore, whatever the case may be regarding the explanation of the aforementioned **axiom** <note>The principle Descartes uses: "There must be at least as much reality in the cause as in the effect."</note>, it is clear not only that there is as much formal reality in me as there is objective reality in my idea, but that the <margin>25</margin> formal reality of the idea is almost nothing in respect to my formal reality, or my entire substance. Wherefore you must also concede that there must be at least as much formal reality in the cause of an idea as there is objective reality in the idea.

<margin>409</margin>
*...capacity <note>original: "tate"; the end of the word "capacitate" from the previous page</note>; even though in reality you either have no idea of yourself at all, or one that is quite confused and imperfect, as we already observed regarding the previous Meditation <note>Referring to the Second Meditation, where Descartes famously concludes "I think, therefore I am."</note>. And you inferred in that Meditation that nothing could be more easily or evidently perceived by you than yourself. Yet, what if—since you neither have nor can have an idea of yourself—it were said that you could perceive anything else more easily and evidently than yourself?*

*In truth, as I reflect on why it might be that neither the eye sees itself nor the intellect understands itself, the thought occurs to me that nothing acts upon itself. Indeed, neither the hand (nor even the tip of its own finger) strikes itself, nor does the foot kick its own heel. Since, on the other hand, to draw out the knowledge of any thing, it is necessary for that thing to act upon the faculty of knowing—namely, by sending its **species** <term>species</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, "species" were the forms or images emitted by objects that traveled to the senses or the mind to make perception possible.</note> into it, or by informing that faculty with its own species—it seems clear that the faculty itself, since it is not outside of itself, cannot transmit its own species into itself, and consequently cannot draw out knowledge of itself; or, what amounts to the same thing, it cannot perceive | itself.*

<margin>410</margin>
*And why do you think it is that the eye, though it does not see itself within itself, nevertheless sees itself in a mirror? It is surely because there is a gap between the eye and the mirror, and the eye acts upon the mirror by sending its species into it, so that the mirror reacts upon the eye, sending the eye's own species back to it. Give me, then, a mirror in which you can act in the same way, and I promise that when it reflects your species back into you, you will then finally perceive yourself—not indeed by direct knowledge, but by **reflected knowledge** <term>reflected knowledge</term> <note>A indirect form of self-awareness where the mind "looks back" at its own actions or representations rather than perceiving its essence directly.</note>. Until you provide this, there is no hope of you knowing yourself.*

*I could also press you here: how can you be said to have an idea of God? Unless, perhaps, it is of the kind and in the manner we have already described. How can you have an idea of Angels? About whom, unless you had heard something, I do not know whether...*

Gassendi argues that our recognition of our own imperfections does not require an innate idea of God, but rather a simple comparison with the world around us or other more capable human beings.</meta>

*Since you doubt, if you desire anything, if you recognize that something is lacking in you,*
<margin>418</margin> *what is so surprising, since you do not know all things, since you are not all things, since you do not possess all things? Do you recognize that you are not, therefore, entirely perfect? And this is certainly true, and can be said without offense. Therefore, do you understand that there is something more perfect than you? Why not? Although whatever you desire might not always be, for whatever reason, more perfect than you. For instance, when you desire bread, the bread is not in every way more perfect than you or your body; it is only more perfect in relation to that emptiness* <note>Gassendi is using a humorous, down-to-earth analogy here to deflate Descartes' metaphysical heights: wanting bread doesn't mean the bread is "holier" than you, just that it fills a specific hole.</note> *which is in your stomach. How then do you conclude there is something more perfect than you? Surely insofar as you see the totality of things* <note>original: "universitatem rerum"</note>*, which includes you, and the bread, and everything else: so much so that, since individual parts of the universe possess some degree of perfection, and some serve others and can be added to them, it is easy to understand that there is more perfection in the whole than in the part; and therefore you, since you are only a part, must acknowledge something more perfect than yourself. In this way, then, there can be an idea of a more perfect being* <note>original: "entis perfectioris"</note> *within you, by comparison with which you recognize your defects. Not to mention that other parts can also be more perfect, and you might* <margin>419</margin> *desire what they have, and by comparing those parts with yourself, your own defects can be recognized. Indeed, you could have known a man who was healthier, stronger, more beautiful, more learned, more moderate, and therefore more perfect; it was not difficult for you to conceive an idea of him, and by comparison with him, to understand that there is not in you that degree of health, strength, and other perfections which were in him.*

*You later object to yourself: "But perhaps I am something greater than I myself understand, and all those perfections which I attribute to God are in me in some potential state, even if they are not yet reduced to action,"* <note>Descartes explores the idea that humans might eventually "grow" into divine perfection, a possibility Gassendi is preparing to dismantle.</note> *as might happen if my—*

Gassendi argues that having an idea of something (like an architect's floor plan) doesn't make the thing real.</meta>

...knowledge might increase more and more to infinity <note>original: "in infinitum"</note> <sup>a</sup>. *But you respond:* <note>Gassendi is now quoting or paraphrasing Descartes' anticipated defense.</note> *Even if it were true that my knowledge increases by degrees, and that many things are in me potentially which are not yet in actuality, none of these things, however, pertain to the idea of God, in which nothing is potential: for this very fact—to increase by degrees—is a most certain proof of imperfection* <sup>b</sup>. <term>potential vs. actual</term> <note>These are technical terms from Aristotelian philosophy: "potential" (what could be) vs. "actual" (what currently is). Descartes argues that God is "pure act," meaning He is already everything He can be, without needing to grow or change.</note> *Furthermore, it is indeed true that those things you perceive in the idea are actually in the idea itself; but they are not, therefore, actually in the thing itself of which it is the idea. <margin>420</margin>
*an idea of a house, which idea actually consists of designed walls, floors, roofs, windows, etc., and yet that house and its parts do not yet actually exist, but only potentially.* <note>Gassendi uses the architect as a counter-example: a mental blueprint can be detailed and "actual" as a thought without the physical building existing in reality.</note> *Thus, that idea of the Philosophers* <note>Likely referring to ancient atomists like Epicurus who hypothesized an infinite number of worlds.</note> *actually contains infinite worlds; but you would not say for that reason that those worlds are infinite in actuality. Therefore, whether something is in you or not by potential, it is enough that your idea or knowledge can be increased or expanded by degrees; nor should it be inferred from this that what is represented or known through it exists in actuality. Next, your acknowledgment that your knowledge will never be infinite* <sup>c</sup> *is readily accepted; but surely you must also acknowledge that there will never be in you a true and authentic idea of God, concerning whom there will always remain more (indeed, infinitely more) to be known than about a man of whom you have seen only a single hair.* <note>Gassendi's famous "hair" analogy: he argues that Descartes' "clear and distinct" idea of God is as incomplete as someone trying to describe a whole person after seeing just one hair on their head.</note> *Certainly, even if you have not seen that whole man, you have seen another, from the comparison of whom you might make some conjecture about him; but it has never been granted to know anything similar to God and His immensity.*

<margin>427</margin>...to act, until he appeared all the more to be held in awe, if nothing were lacking or could be added to his knowledge, power, duration, and the rest, and thus he would be omniscient, omnipotent, eternal, and all other things? And when you saw that such perfections could not fall to human nature, why could you not have judged that nature to be blessed if those qualities belonged to it? Why not think it worthy of investigation whether such a being existed or not? Why not be led by certain arguments to think it more likely that it exists than that it does not? Why not consequently remove from it corporeality, limitation, and all other things that imply a certain imperfection? Indeed, many people seem to have proceeded in this way; though, because there are various modes and degrees of reasoning <term>ratiocinatio; the mental process of using logic to reach a conclusion</term>, some have left God as a corporeal being, others as having human limbs, others not as one but as many, and other such too common notions. Regarding that point about the perfection of unity, nothing prevents us from conceiving all the perfections attributed to God as intimately joined and inseparable; even if the idea you have 
<margin>428</margin>of them was not placed in you by Him, but was drawn by you from things you have perceived and then enlarged, as has been said. In this way, certainly, they depict not only Pandora <note>original: "Pandoram"; in Greek mythology, the first woman, whose name means "all-gifted" because every god gave her a unique attribute or perfection.</note>, a goddess adorned with all gifts and perfections, but also a perfect Republic <note>A reference to Plato’s *Republic*, an idealized model of a state.</note>, a perfect Orator <note>A reference to Cicero’s *De Oratore*, describing the ideal, perfect public speaker.</note>, and so on. Finally, from the fact that you exist and have in you the idea of a most perfect being, you conclude that it is most evidently demonstrated that God exists. But while the conclusion may be true—namely, that God exists—it does not appear from what has been said that it has been most evidently demonstrated by you.

10. You continue: **And indeed it is not surprising that God, in creating me, should have placed this idea within me, so that it would be like the mark of the craftsman <note>original: "nota artificis"; a famous metaphor used by Descartes to describe the idea of God as a signature left by the creator on the mind of the creature</note> impressed <margin>20</margin> upon his work. What is the shape of that mark? In what way do you distinguish it? If the mark is nothing other than the work itself, or the thing itself, then are you yourself the idea? Are you nothing other than a **mode of thought**? Are you both the impressed mark and the subject of the impression? <margin>10</margin> You say it is believable that you were made in the **image and likeness of God.** <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis 1:26: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness."</note> Certainly, it is believable through religious faith; but by natural reason, how can this be understood unless you make God **human-shaped** <term>hominiformem: having a human form or appearance; Gassendi is accusing Descartes of accidental anthropomorphism</term>? And in what can this likeness consist? Since you are but dust and ashes, can you <margin>15</margin> presume yourself to be like that eternal, incorporeal, boundless, most perfect, <margin>431</margin> most glorious, and—most importantly—most invisible and most incomprehensible nature? Do you know that nature's face, so that by comparing yourself with it, you can assert a resemblance? You say it is believable because he created you. But <margin>20</margin> from that very fact, it is instead unbelievable. For a work is not like the one who made it, except when it is generated through a **communication of nature** <note>Gassendi distinguishes between "creation" (making something from nothing) and "generation" (biological reproduction or sharing the same essence). He argues that a builder is not "like" a house.</note>. But you were not generated by God in this way: for you are not his offspring, nor do you share in his nature; you are merely created—that is, made by him according to an idea. Thus, you can no more say you are <margin>25</margin> like him than a house is like the mason who built it. And this assumes your creation by God, which you have not yet proven. You say you perceive this likeness when you understand yourself to be an incomplete thing, dependent, and [tending] toward greater things...

...and aspiring to better things. But why should this not rather be an argument for **dissimilarity**, since God is, by contrast, **most complete**, **most independent**, and **most self-sufficient**, being indeed the greatest and the best? <note>original: "completissimus, independentissimus, sibi sufficientissimus"; Gassendi uses these superlative Latin terms to emphasize the infinite gap between a finite human and an infinite God.</note> To pass over the fact that, when you understand yourself as a dependent being, you do not therefore immediately understand that the one on whom you depend <margin>432</margin> is anything other than your parents; or if you do understand it as something else, there is no underlying reason why you should think yourself **like** him. To pass over also that it is strange why other humans, or other minds, do not understand the same thing as you; especially since there is no reason to believe that God would not have impressed the idea of himself upon them just as he did upon you. Indeed, even this one fact argues that the idea was not **impressed by God**; for if it were so, it would have been impressed on everyone, and would be one and the same idea. All humans would conceive of God with a similar form and appearance; they would attribute the same qualities to him, and they would clearly feel the same way about him; whereas the opposite is common knowledge. But enough of these matters, perhaps too much already.

<margin>433</margin> ## ON THE FOURTH MEDITATION.

### On the True and the False.

I. Regarding the fourth Meditation <note>Previously, page 52.</note>, you review at the start those things which you think were demonstrated in the previous sections, and by which you presume the way has been cleared for proceeding further. For my part, lest I cause a delay, I will not insist immediately that you ought to have demonstrated those points more firmly; it will be enough if you remember what has been granted and what has not, so that the matter is not turned into a **prejudice**. <term>præjudicium: here meaning a "pre-judgment" or a biased assumption that takes a premise for granted before it is fully proven.</term>

You reason consequently that God cannot deceive you <note>original: "non posse Deum fallere te"</note>, and in order to excuse the fallible or error-prone faculty that you hold from Him, you cast the blame upon **nothingness** <note>In the Fourth Meditation, Descartes argues that error arises because humans are a "middle ground" between God (perfect being) and nothingness (non-being). From this "nothingness," you claim to participate, assuming yourself to be a middle ground <margin>5</margin> between it and God. This is indeed a beautiful bit of reasoning; but to pass over the fact that it cannot be explained how one can have an "idea of nothing," or what kind of thing it is, or how we might "participate" in nothingness, and other such points, I observe only that this distinction does not prevent the fact that God could have given <margin>434</margin> <margin>10</margin> man a faculty of judgment immune to error <note>original: "erroris immunem"</note>. For, even if He had not given an infinite faculty, He could still have given one that would not assent to error; such that it would clearly perceive what it knew, and as for what it did not know, it would simply not pronounce it to be one way rather than another.

<margin>15</margin> Objecting to this yourself, you think it is not to be wondered at if some things are made by God whose purpose you do not understand. And that is indeed right; but it is still a wonder that there is in you a true idea which represents God as all-knowing, all-powerful, and entirely good, and yet you nevertheless see that some of His works are not <margin>20</margin> entirely perfect. It would seem to follow—since He could at least have created more perfect works, and yet did not—that He either did not know how, or was not able, or did not wish to do so. At the very least, He would seem imperfect in this: that if He were knowing and able but unwilling, He preferred imperfection to perfection.

<margin>25</margin> Furthermore, as for your rejection of the use of **final causes** <term>final causes: The Aristotelian idea that nature acts with a purpose or "end goal" (e.g., "rain falls so plants can grow"). Descartes argued that scientists should only look at mechanical causes, not God's hidden purposes.</term> from the study of Physics, you might have had a right to do so on another occasion...

## FIFTH OBJECTIONS.

to which there is no judgment, pursuit, or avoidance <note>original: "prosequutio, aut fuga." In classical philosophy, these are the basic reactions of the will: seeking the good and fleeing the bad</note>. And the faculty of judging is so often balanced that—when the reasons are of equal weight, or when none exist at all—no judgment follows, even though the understanding <term>understanding: "intellectus," the faculty of pure perception or apprehension</term> meanwhile apprehends those things that remain unjudged.

But, in short, tell us: to what can the will extend itself that escapes the understanding? It does not seem, therefore, that error arises from the fact—as you assert—that the will is wider than the understanding and extends itself to judge those things which the understanding does not perceive <gloss>c</gloss>, but rather from the fact that, while they both extend equally wide, the understanding perceives something poorly, and the will judges poorly.

Therefore, there is no reason why you should promote the will beyond the boundaries of the understanding, since the will neither judges things that the understanding does not perceive, and only judges wrongly what the understanding perceives wrongly.

<margin>b. Ibid., l. 28, etc.</margin>
Finally, the nature of error seems to consist not so much in the incorrect use of free will <gloss>b</gloss> <term>free will: "liberi arbitrii," the faculty of choice</term>, as you claim, but in the dissonance between the judgment and the thing judged; this arises from the fact that the intellect <term>intellect: "intellectus," the faculty of understanding or perceiving</term> perceives that thing differently than it actually is. Therefore, it seems to be not so much a fault of the will that it does not judge correctly, as a fault of the intellect that it does not demonstrate correctly. Indeed, the dependence of the will upon the intellect seems to be such that if the intellect perceives something clearly—or seems to perceive it—the will issues a firm and determined judgment, whether the thing is actually true or is merely thought to be true. However, if the perception is obscure, then the will issues a doubtful and fearful judgment, yet one held for the time being as truer than its opposite, whether truth or falsity lies in the thing itself. From this it follows that we cannot so much take care to avoid falling into error as we can take care not to *persevere* in error <margin>448</margin>; we should weigh our own judgments, not so much by forcing the will, as by applying the intellect toward a clearer knowledge, which the judgment will always follow.

<margin>c. Page 62, l. 21-25.</margin>
4. You conclude by exaggerating the benefit you can gain from this Meditation, and you prescribe what must be done to reach the truth: namely, you say you will reach it if you only pay enough attention to everything you perfectly understand, and separate those things from the rest, which you perceive more confusedly and obscurely <gloss>c</gloss> <note>original: "secernas." Gassendi is summarizing Descartes' rule that we must isolate clear and distinct ideas from fuzzy ones.</note>.

<margin>454</margin>
Hence, one should not think that the properties demonstrated of material triangles belong to them because they borrow them from an "ideal" triangle; rather, the material triangles possess these properties in themselves. The "ideal" triangle does not possess them either, except insofar as the intellect, after inspecting the material ones, attributes those same properties to the ideal, to be given back later during the process of a logical demonstration. In the same way, the properties of human nature are not in Plato and Socrates as if those men received them from a universal "Human Nature"; rather, it is the universal nature that possesses them because the intellect attributes the properties to it after noticing them in Plato, Socrates, and the others, only to return those properties to the individuals whenever a piece of reasoning is required.

For it is well known that the intellect, from seeing Plato, Socrates, and others—all of whom are rational beings—collected this universal proposition: *every human is rational* <note>original: "omnis homo est rationalis"</note>; and then, when it wants to prove that Plato is rational, it introduces that proposition as a principle in a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A syllogism is a formal logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion (e.g., All humans are rational; Plato is a human; therefore Plato is rational).</note>. # FIFTH OBJECTIONS.

<margin>377-379.</margin>
*...that one could better separate omnipotence, for example, from the essence of God than one could separate that equality of the sum of the angles from the essence of a triangle; or certainly, that one could no more separate God’s existence from His essence than one could separate a triangle's*
<margin>5</margin> *existence from its essence. For in that way, either comparison would have proceeded well. Not only would the first point have been granted, but even the second—although you would not have proven thereby that God necessarily exists. This is because a triangle also does not necessarily exist, even if its essence and existence cannot be separated in reality,*
<margin>10</margin> *no matter how much they are separated in the mind or thought of separately, just as the divine essence and existence can also be thought of separately.* <note>Gassendi is arguing that even if "essence" and "existence" are linked in our definition of a thing, that doesn't force the thing to actually exist in the real world.</note>

*Next, it must be noted that you place existence among the divine perfections, yet you do not place it among the perfections of a triangle or a mountain, even though it could just as well, and in its*
<margin>15</margin> *own way, be called a perfection for each. But surely, neither in God nor in any other thing is existence a perfection; rather, it is*
<margin>457</margin> | *that without which perfections do not exist.*

*Indeed, that which does not exist has neither perfection nor imperfection; and that which exists and has several perfections*
<margin>20</margin> *does not have existence as a single perfection or one among that number, but rather as that by which both the thing itself and its perfections exist, and without which the thing is not said to possess perfections, nor are the perfections said to be possessed. Hence,*
<margin>25</margin> *existence is not said to exist in a thing in the manner of a perfection; nor, if a thing lacks existence, is it said to be imperfect (or deprived of a perfection), so much as it is said to be nothing.*

*Therefore, just as in enumerating the perfections of a triangle you do not include existence, and consequently do not conclude that the triangle exists; so, in enumerating the perfections of God, you*
<margin>30</margin> *should not have included existence among them to conclude that God exists, unless you wished to beg the question.* <note>original: "principium petere." This is a logical fallacy where the conclusion one is trying to prove is already assumed in the premises.</note>

I pass over the other points, which you either do not explain, or do not prove, or which are resolved by what has already been put forward, such as: that nothing can be thought of to whose **essence** <note>The fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note> existence belongs, except God alone; that two or more such Gods cannot be understood; that such a God has existed from eternity and will remain for eternity; and that you perceive many other things in God from which nothing can be taken away or changed <gloss>b</gloss>. *These things ought to be inspected more closely and investigated more diligently <note>original: "Oportere iſta propiùs inſpici, ac diligentiùs inveſtigari"</note>, so that they may be uncovered and held as certain, etc.*

3. *Finally, you declare that the certainty and truth of all science depends so much on the knowledge of the one true God that, if this is not held, no certainty or true science can be had <gloss>c</gloss>. # FIFTH OBJECTIONS.
## 382-384.

...[I would doubt] whether it is true, as long as I am ignorant of God. For I could persuade myself that I was so made by nature that I might sometimes be deceived in those things which I think I perceive most evidently: especially since I remember that I have held many things as true and certain which I later, led by other reasons, judged to be false. But after I perceived that God exists, because I simultaneously understood that all other things depend on him, and that he is not a deceiver, and from this I concluded that all those things which I clearly and distinctly perceive are necessarily true: even if I no longer attend to the reasons for which I judged that to be true: provided that I remember that I have clearly and distinctly perceived it, no contrary reason can be brought forward that might push me to doubt; but I have true and certain knowledge of this. <meta>This page continues Pierre Gassendi’s critique in the "Fifth Objections." Having previously touched upon how our ideas of immaterial things are derived from corporeal ones, Gassendi now directly challenges Descartes’ skepticism regarding the reliability of the senses. He argues that while the senses can be deceived under certain conditions, they also provide us with certainty under others.</meta>

# FIFTH OBJECTIONS.

<meta>Refers to pages 390-391 of the standard edition.</meta>

Indeed, there is no need to go looking for obvious examples. I will only say, regarding what you put forward or rather suggest, that it seems entirely certain that when we look at a tower from up close and touch it, we are sure it is square; <margin>5</margin> even if, from further away, we had reason to judge it round, or at least to doubt whether it was square, round, or some other shape.

Thus that sensation of pain <note>original: "sensus ille doloris"</note> <sup>a</sup>, which seems to still be in a foot or a hand after those limbs have been cut off, can sometimes deceive—namely in those who have had them cut off—and this is because the **sensory spirits** <term>sensory spirits: "spiritus sensorios," thought to be thin, fluid-like substances that traveled through the nerves to convey sensations to the brain</term> <margin>10</margin> are accustomed to traveling there and expressing the sensation in those parts. However, those whose bodies are whole are so certain that they <margin>472</margin> feel pain in the foot or hand that they see being pricked, that they are unable to doubt it.

Thus, as we wake and dream in turns <margin>15</margin> throughout our lives, there is indeed a deception in dreams, in that things appear to be present before us which are not actually there; yet we do not dream all the time, nor, while we are truly awake, can we doubt whether we are awake or rather dreaming.

Thus, while we might consider that we are subject to <margin>20</margin> nature’s deceptions even in things that seem most true, we nonetheless also consider that we are by nature capable of truth. And just as we are sometimes deceived—as when a logical fallacy <note>original: "sophismate"</note> is not detected, or when a stick is half-submerged in water—so we also <margin>25</margin> sometimes understand the truth, as in a geometric demonstration or when a stick is pulled out of the water, so that we can clearly have no doubt about the truth of either. And even if it were permitted to doubt everything else, at least it is not permitted to doubt that such things *appear* to us; it cannot but be entirely true that they appear so.

...you say? Namely, this coarse body consisting of limbs, regarding which these words are no doubt spoken: *I have a body joined to me*, and, *it is certain that I am distinct from my body*, etc. Yet, O Mind, concerning this body there is no difficulty. There would be a difficulty, however, if I were to object, along with most Philosophers, that you are an *entelechy* <term>entelechy: an Aristotelian term for the "actuality" or "form" that gives life and function to a physical body</term> <note>original: ἐντελέχειαν</note>, <margin>5</margin> a perfection, an act, a form, a species, and to speak in the common way, a mode of the body. For they no <margin>476</margin> | more recognize you as being distinct and separable from that body than they do a shape or any other mode; and this holds whether you are the soul in its entirety, or whether you are additionally a *potential intellect* or a *passive intellect* <margin>10</margin> <note>original: νοῦς δυνάμει (nous dynamei), νοῦς παθητικός (nous pathētikos)</note>, as they say. But I prefer to deal more generously with you, considering you indeed as an *active intellect* <note>original: νοῦν ποιητικόν (noun poiētikon)</note>, and even as *separable* <note>original: χωριστόν (chōriston)</note>, though for a reason different than theirs.

For while they established that this [active intellect] was common to all men (<margin>15</margin> *if not rather to all things*) and superior to the *potential intellect* so that it might understand—in exactly the same way and by the same necessity as *light* acts upon the *eye* so that it might see (whence they were accustomed to compare it to solar light, and consequently to regard it as something coming from the outside)—I instead consider you (for you also <margin>20</margin> wish it so) as a *certain special intellect* that rules within the body.

I repeat, however, that the difficulty is not whether you are separable or not from this body (whence I also hinted a little earlier that it was not necessary to recur to the *power of God* by which those things are separable which <margin>25</margin> you understand separately), but about the body which you yourself might be: as if you yourself could be a thin body, <margin>477</margin> | diffused within this coarse one, or holding a seat in a part of it.

<margin>482</margin> Tell me, how do you understand this? Is it truly possible for one single thing to be entirely present in several places at once? Faith may teach us this regarding the sacred mystery <note>Gassendi is referring to the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist, where Christ is believed to be fully present in many places at the same time</note>; but here, we are discussing you as a natural entity, and we are doing so by the light of nature <note>original: "ex lumine naturali" — a philosophical term for human reason and logic as opposed to divine revelation</note>. Is it possible to conceive of there being many places without there being many things located within them? <margin>5</margin> And are not a hundred things more than one thing? And if a thing is present in its entirety in one place, can it be in others unless it is "outside of itself," just as one location is outside another? Say what you will: at the very least, it remains obscure and uncertain whether you are whole in every part, rather than existing in individual parts through individual parts of yourself. And since it is far more evident <margin>10</margin> that nothing can be entirely in several places at the same time, it becomes even more evident that you are not whole in every single part, but whole only in the whole; thus, you are diffused through the whole by means of your own parts, and in this way, you possess extension <term>extension: the physical property of taking up space or having dimensions</term>.

Suppose then that you are in the brain alone, or only in a small <margin>15</margin> part of it. You see that the exact same problem remains; for no matter how small that part may be, it is still extended, and you are co-extended with it. Therefore, you are extended, and you have parts of yourself that correspond to its parts. Or will you say that you consider this part of the brain to be a point? That is surely unbelievable; but let us pretend it is a point. <margin>20</margin> If it is a **physical point**, the same difficulty remains, because such a point is extended and is not entirely without parts.
<margin>483</margin> If it is a **mathematical point**, you know first of all that such a thing does not exist except in the imagination. But let it be granted, or rather let us imagine it is granted, that there is a mathematical point in the brain to which you are joined and in which you exist: <margin>25</margin> see how useless this fiction would be. For if we are to imagine it, it must be imagined that you are at the meeting point of the nerves, through which all the parts animated by the soul transmit to the brain the ideas or images <note>original: "species" — in the philosophy of the time, these were the mental representations or forms of objects perceived by the senses</note> of things perceived by the senses. But first of all, all the nerves do not meet at a single point; <margin>30</margin> since the brain continues into the spinal cord <note>original: "spinalem medullam"</note>, many nerves...

they branch off into the back; or because those that tend toward the middle of the head are found not to end in the same place in the brain. But let us grant that they all converge; nonetheless, their meeting point cannot be in a mathematical point <term>mathematical point: a theoretical location that has no length, width, or depth</term>, because they are clearly bodies, not mathematical lines, and thus they cannot meet in a mathematical point. *I say the same of those [spirits] which you must transmit for the purpose of feeling, reporting, or moving. Let me pass over the fact that it is impossible to understand how you could impress motion upon them if you yourself are in a point, unless you are a body yourself, or unless you have a body with which you might touch them and simultaneously propel them. For if you say they move of themselves and you only direct their motion, remember that you have denied elsewhere that a body moves itself <sup>a</sup>, so it follows that you must be the cause of that motion. And then explain to us how such direction can exist without some effort <term>effort: original "contentio," implying a physical tension or striving</term> and thus motion on your part? How can there be effort toward a thing, and its motion, without mutual contact between the mover and the moved? How can there be contact without a body, when (as is so clear by the light of nature <note>original: "lumine naturali" — the philosophical concept of human reason</note>) "Nothing can touch or be touched without a body" <sup>b</sup>?*

*How are you mixed, or as it were mixed, with the particles of this part?*
<margin>488</margin> *For there is no mixture without parts on both sides that can be mixed together. And, if you are completely distinct, how can you be blended and form a single unit with matter itself? And since composition, conjunction, or union occurs between specific parts, must there not be a proportion* <note>original: "proportio" — Gassendi uses this to mean a correspondence or commonality in nature between two things that allows them to interact.</note> *between such parts? But what proportion can be understood between the corporeal and the incorporeal? Can we grasp how stone and air are joined together—for example, in a pumice stone—so that a genuine composition results? And yet the proportion is greater between stone and air, which is itself a body, than between the body and the soul, or a mind that is entirely incorporeal. And must not a union happen through intimate contact? How can this happen, as I said before, without a body? How will that which is corporeal grasp that which is incorporeal, so as to hold it joined to itself? Or how will the incorporeal grasp the corporeal, so as to hold it bound in return, if there is absolutely nothing in it—neither anything to be grasped nor anything that can grasp?*

<margin>489</margin> *Hence, because you confess that you feel pain, I ask you: how do you think you can be capable of the sensation of pain if you are incorporeal and unextended* <note>original: "inextensa" — In Cartesian philosophy, "extension" is the primary attribute of matter (taking up space). To be "unextended" is to have no physical dimensions.</note>*? For the affliction of pain is understood only as a certain pulling apart of parts, when something is thrust between them that causes a breach of continuity.* <note>original: "continuitatis solutionem" — A classical medical and philosophical term for a physical wound or tear in the body's structure.</note> *Namely, the state of pain is a certain state contrary to nature; but how can something be contrary to nature, or be affected, if by nature it is uniform, simple, indivisible, and unchangeable? And since pain is either an alteration itself or does not happen without alteration, how can that be altered which—being more indivisible than a mathematical point—cannot become something else, or cease to be what it is, without being reduced to nothingness? <summary>Pierre Gassendi critiques Descartes' theory of mind-body dualism, arguing that a non-physical, "unextended" mind could not possibly interact, mix, or feel physical pain through a material body. These are the points, distinguished Sir, which occurred to me to be noted regarding your *Meditations*. I repeat that there is no reason why you should concern yourself with them, as my judgment is not of such weight that it should be considered of the slightest importance by you. For just as when some food is sweet to <margin>5</margin> my palate, though I see it displeases others, I do not defend my taste as being more perfect than another’s; so too, when an opinion pleases my mind but does not appeal to others, I am far from maintaining that I have happened upon a truer one. I rather think it is truly said that everyone is satisfied with their own sense <note>original: "suo quemque sensu abundare" — a common Latin phrasing of a biblical sentiment from Romans 14:5, suggesting that everyone is entitled to their own conviction.</note>; and I consider it nearly as unjust to <margin>10</margin> wish that everyone held the same opinion as to wish that everyone shared the same taste. I say this so that you may consider yourself free, as far as I am concerned, to value all these things I have criticized at a straw's worth <term>flocci-facere: a Latin idiom for considering something utterly worthless.</term>, and to hold them in no regard at all. It will be more than enough if you acknowledge my favorable affection toward you, and do not regard as nothing my veneration for your virtue <note>original: "virtutis" — here referring to Descartes' intellectual excellence and character.</note>. <margin>15</margin> Perhaps something might have been expressed too thoughtlessly, as <margin>492</margin> nothing is more likely to happen in the midst of <column-break/> disagreeing <column-break/>. If that should occur, I utterly disavow it; you should strike it out <note>original: "duc lituram" — literally to draw a line through the text to erase it.</note>, and be assured that nothing has been more important to me than to earn your favor and to preserve our friendship perfectly intact <term>sartam tectamque: literally "patched and roofed," a legal metaphor for keeping a property in good repair.</term>. Farewell. Written at Paris, the day after the Ides of <margin>20</margin> May <note>May 14th.</note>, in the year of salvation 1641.

## TO THE FIFTH OBJECTIONS <gloss>a</gloss>.

Most distinguished Sir,

<margin>5</margin>You have attacked my *Meditations* with such an elegant and accurate dissertation, and one which seems to me so likely to be of benefit in illustrating their truth, that I consider myself greatly indebted to you for writing it, and also greatly to the Reverend Father Mersenne for urging you to write. For that man, a most diligent investigator <margin>10</margin>of all things | and an untiring promoter especially of those matters <margin>494</page-num> | which concern the glory of God, knows very well that there is no better way to know whether my arguments should be held as true demonstrations <note>Descartes uses "demonstration" in the mathematical sense: a proof so certain it cannot be doubted.</note> than if some of those who surpass others in learning and genius were to <margin>15</margin>examine them and attack them with all their might, so that a trial might then be made as to whether I could respond adequately to everything they proposed <gloss>b</gloss>. Therefore, he challenged as many as possible to this task; he obtained it from several, and I am glad that he did so from you as well. For although <margin>20</margin>you have not used philosophical arguments to refute my opinions so much as certain rhetorical arts to evade them, nevertheless, this very thing is pleasing to me, because from it I conjecture that arguments different from those which [were previously...] could not easily be brought against me.

Nor would a philosopher have said that *I, by holding all doubtful things as false, am not so much shedding an old prejudice as adopting a new one* <sup>c</sup> <note>original: "me, habendo dubia omnia pro falſis, non tam vetus exuere quàm induere novum praejudicium"</note>; or rather, he would first have attempted to <margin>497</margin> prove that from such a supposition arises the danger <margin>20</margin> of some deception. Nor would a philosopher wonder at a supposition of this kind any more than he would wonder that sometimes, <margin>25</margin> in order to make a stick that is bent straight, we bend it back in the opposite direction. For he knows that false things are often usefully assumed as true in this way to illustrate the truth: as when...

For when the question concerns the conduct of life, it would certainly be foolish not to trust the senses. Those Sceptics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that argued for the suspension of judgment and the impossibility of certain knowledge.</note> were clearly ridiculous who so far neglected human affairs that they had to be <margin>5</margin> watched over by their friends to keep them from throwing themselves over cliffs. For that reason, I have noted elsewhere that no one <margin>499</margin> of sound mind seriously doubts such things <note>original: "neminem sanæ mentis de talibus seriò dubitare"</note>. However, when we are inquiring into what can be known most certainly by the human mind, it is entirely contrary to reason to refuse to seriously reject those same things as doubtful, or even as false, so as to <margin>10</margin> realize that certain other things—which cannot be rejected in this way—are by that very fact more certain and, to us, more truly known.

As for my saying that I do not yet sufficiently understand "who" it is that thinks, you do not act in good faith when you take that as a serious statement, since I later explained that very thing. Nor are you fair regarding my statement <margin>15</margin> that I did not doubt the nature of the body, and that I attributed no power of self-movement to it, and that I imagined the soul to be like a wind, or a fire, and similar things. I only reported those here according to the common opinion <note>original: "ex vulgi opinione"</note> so that I might show them to be false in their proper place.

<margin>20</margin> With what honesty do you claim that nutrition, walking, sensing, and so on, are referred by me to the soul, only to immediately add: *so be it, provided we are careful about your distinction between the soul and the body*? For a little later, in express words, I referred nutrition to the body alone, and movement and sensation I <margin>24</margin> also refer for the most part | to the body. I assign nothing to the soul <margin>500</margin> that pertains to these functions, except for that part alone which is **thought** <note>original: "cogitatio"</note>.
