Next, what reason do you have for saying *there was no need for such an elaborate apparatus to prove that I exist*?<sup>a</sup> <note>Gassendi had argued that Descartes’ "I think, therefore I am" was an over-complicated way of proving something obvious.</note> Indeed, from these very words of yours, I think I have the best reason to judge that I have not yet used a *sufficiently* elaborate apparatus there, since I have not yet been able to make you understand the matter correctly. For when you say *I could have gathered the same thing from any other of my actions*,<sup>b</sup> you wander far from the truth, because I am not entirely certain of any of my actions (namely, with that Metaphysical certainty <term>Metaphysical certainty: an absolute level of proof that remains true even if we imagine an all-powerful deceiver or a dream-state</term>, about which alone we are questioning here), except for thought alone. Nor is it permitted to infer, for example: "I walk, therefore I am," except insofar as the awareness of walking is a thought, about which alone this inference is certain, and not about the motion of the body. This is because the motion of the body is sometimes non-existent in sleep, when I nonetheless seem to myself to be walking; so much so that from the fact that I *think* I am walking, I can best infer the existence of the mind which thinks this, but not the existence of the body which walks. And the same applies to the rest.

When I realize that I am a **thinking substance** <term>thinking substance: "substantia cogitans," a fundamental term in Cartesian philosophy referring to the mind as a thing that exists solely to think, doubt, and understand</term>, and I form a clear and distinct concept of that thinking substance—in which nothing that belongs to the concept of a "corporeal" or physical substance is contained—
<margin>5</margin> this is plainly sufficient for me to affirm that, as far as I know myself, I am nothing other than a **thinking thing**. This is the only claim I made in the Second Meditation, which is the subject we are currently discussing. Nor was I required to admit that this thinking substance is some kind of agile, pure, or refined body, and so on,
<margin>10</margin> since I had no reason that would persuade me of such a thing. If you have any such reason, it is your responsibility to present it; it is not your place to demand that I prove | <margin>505</margin> something to be false which I refused to admit for no other reason than that it was unknown to me. For you act just as if,
<margin>15</margin> when I say I am currently in Holland, you were to deny that this should be believed unless I also proved that I am not in China, nor in any other part of the world—because perhaps it could happen that the same body might exist in two different places at once by divine power. <margin>20</margin> prove that the **souls of brutes** <note>animals</note> are incorporeal, and that the gross physical body contributes nothing to thoughts <gloss>a</gloss>, you demonstrate that you not only do not know who bears the "burden of proof," but you do not even know what must be proved by whom. <margin>25</margin> nor that the physical body contributes nothing to thought; I simply maintain that a consideration of these matters has no place in this stage of the argument.

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ response to Gassendi (referred to as "O Flesh") regarding the nature of the mind and how we perceive physical objects like wax. WORKS OF DESCARTES.
422-423.

<margin>512</margin>
...[those] who, since they conceive of nothing except quite confusedly, are ignorant of what should be sought in each thing; but as for me, I have never thought anything else was required to manifest a **substance** <term>substance: in 17th-century philosophy, the underlying reality that supports qualities like color or shape</term>, besides its various **attributes** <term>attributes: the essential characteristics or properties of a thing</term>, so that the more attributes of a substance we know, the more perfectly we understand its nature. And just as we can distinguish many different attributes in the wax—one that it is white, another that it is hard, another that it becomes liquid from being hard, etc.—so too there are just as many in the **mind**. One [attribute] is that it has the **power of knowing** <note>original: *vim cognoscendi*</note> the whiteness of the wax, another that it has the power of knowing its hardness, another the change of its hardness or its liquefaction, etc.; for someone can know hardness who does not therefore know whiteness—namely, someone born blind—and so with the rest. From this it is clearly concluded that we know as many attributes of no other thing as we do of our own mind; because, however many are known in any other thing, just as many can be counted in the mind by the fact that it knows them; and therefore its nature is the best known of all. Finally, you here incidentally rebuke me<gloss>a</gloss> <note>a. Referring to Gassendi’s objection on page 274.</note> because, although I admitted nothing to be in me except a mind, I nevertheless *speak of the wax which I see and touch, which cannot be done without eyes and hands.* But you should have noted that I carefully warned that this was not a matter of sight and touch, which occur by means of physical organs, but of the **sole thought** of seeing and touching, for which we experience daily in our dreams that those organs are not required. Nor indeed have you failed to note this, but you only wished to point out how absurd...

<margin>5</margin> 1. Bravo: here at last you bring forward some reason against me, which I have noticed you doing nowhere previously. For in order to prove that *it is not a certain rule that those things which we perceive very clearly and distinctly are true*<sup>b</sup>, <margin>10</margin> you say that very great geniuses—who it seems ought to have perceived many things clearly and distinctly—nevertheless judged that the truth of things was hidden either in God or in a well <note>This refers to a famous saying by the ancient philosopher Democritus, who claimed truth lies at the bottom of a deep well, unreachable by man.</note>. I contend that this was performed in its proper places, where I first removed all prejudices, and afterwards I enumerated all the principal ideas, and distinguished the clear from the obscure or confused.

2. I am truly amazed by the reasoning by which you wish to prove that all <margin>5</margin> our ideas are **adventitious** <term>adventitious: ideas that come from external sources through the senses, rather than being innate or created by the mind</term>, and that none are created by us, because, you say, the mind has the faculty not only of perceiving these adventitious ideas, but furthermore of variously composing, dividing, contracting, enlarging, comparing them, and the like: <margin>10</margin> from which you conclude that the ideas of **Chimeras** <note>In mythology, a Chimera is a hybrid creature (part lion, goat, and snake); here, it refers to any imaginary concept formed by combining existing ones.</note>, which the mind makes by composing, dividing, etc., are not | created by the mind itself, but are adventitious. Yet certainly, the form of a chimera consists neither in the parts of the goat nor the lion; nor does the form of your objections consist in the individual words you have used, but solely in their composition.

It is also marvelous that you maintain that the idea of a **Thing** <note>original: *Res*; a fundamental metaphysical category for Descartes used to denote anything that exists.</note> <margin>20</margin> cannot be in the mind, unless the ideas of animal, plant, stone, and all **universals** <term>universals: general concepts or categories that apply to many individual things (like "redness" or "humanity")</term> are there at the same time. You are no more dealing with the truth here. And <margin>25</margin> finally, since you attack only those things which I have never affirmed, you are merely **tilting at windmills** <note>original: *in ventos præliaris*; literally "battling against the winds."</note>.

3. At this point, in order to tear down the reasons for which I judged that one should doubt the existence of material things, you ask why then I walk upon the earth, and so on. In this, the **question is clearly begged** <term>begging the question (principium petitur): a logical fallacy where the proof of an argument assumes the truth of the very thing it is trying to prove.</term>: for you assume that which should have been proven—namely, that it is so certain that I walk upon the earth that it cannot be doubted.
<margin>516</margin> And when you wish to add one more to the reasons that I raised against myself and then refuted—*namely, why there is no idea of color in one born blind, or of sound in one who is deaf* <note>original: "quamobrem in cæco nato nulla ſit idea coloris, aut in ſurdo vocis"</note>—you clearly show that you have no reason of any importance. <meta>426-427.</meta>

...you restrict [ideas] to only images depicted in the imagination, contrary to what I expressly assumed.

<margin>517</margin>
4. You do the same thing here^a, when you deny that there is a true idea of substance, simply because substance is perceived not by the imagination, but by the intellect alone. But I have long since declared, **O Flesh** <note>original: "ô caro." Descartes uses this sarcastic nickname for Gassendi to mock his opponent's focus on the physical body and senses rather than the rational mind.</note>, that I have nothing to do with those who wish to use only their imagination and not their intellect.

But where you say that *the idea of substance has no reality except what it takes from the ideas of those accidents under which, or in the likeness of which, it is conceived*^b, you prove that you truly have no distinct idea of it. For substance can never be conceived in the likeness of accidents, nor can it borrow its reality from them. On the contrary, philosophers commonly conceive of accidents in the likeness of substances—that is, whenever they are called "real." For the idea of the infinite, in order to be true, must in no way be **comprehended** <note>In Descartes's vocabulary, to "comprehend" something is to fully embrace it with the mind, like holding an object in one's hand; to "understand" is merely to reach out and touch it with the mind.</note>, since incomprehensibility itself is contained within the <term>formal nature</term> <note>original: "ratione formali" — the essential definition or conceptual structure of a thing</note> of the infinite. This is by the same reasoning that we do not doubt that someone unskilled in **Geometry** has an idea of a whole **triangle** when they understand it to be a figure enclosed by three lines, even though Geometers can know many other things about that same triangle and notice things in its idea that remain unknown to the beginner. For just as it suffices to understand a figure contained by three lines to have an idea of the whole triangle; so too it suffices to understand a thing enclosed by no limits to have a true and entire idea of the whole infinite.<sup>a</sup>

<margin>25</margin> reason, but only with naked negations. And I shall perhaps deserve greater faith among others—because I affirm what I have experienced, and what anyone can experience within themselves—than you, who deny the same only because you have perhaps not experienced it.

# ADDITION

## TO THE 5TH OBJECTIONS AND REPLIES,

Gassendi’s *Objections* and Descartes’s *Replies* were published in the first edition of the *Meditations*, in Paris, by Soly (printing completed August 28, 1641). Gassendi replied in lengthy <term>Instances</term> <note>These were Gassendi's counter-rebuttals to Descartes's answers</note>, which were completed on March 15, 1642. However, he did not decide to print them immediately, contenting himself with circulating them within a small circle of friends. Descartes learned of this and complained about it in Holland: the complaint became public in a passage of his *Letter to Father Dinet*, printed in Amsterdam in 1642, with the second edition of the *Meditations*. On the other hand, a friend of Gassendi, Sorbière, finally obtained the manuscript of the *Instances* from him and had them printed in Amsterdam. At the same time, he reprinted Gassendi’s first *Objections* and Descartes’s *Replies*. However, instead of presenting all the *Objections* in a single sequence as one letter, and then the *Replies* in the same manner, he printed the different parts separately, following the indicated numbers. This allowed him to insert the *Instances* in their proper place, according to which specific *Objection* and *Reply* they addressed. Thus, each *Objection* is detached from the others and followed immediately by the *Reply*; after this comes the *Instance*, or the *Instances*. Hence the new title of the work: <term>Pierre Gassendi’s METAPHYSICAL DISQUISITION. Or DOUBTS AND COUNTER-OBJECTIONS: against RENÉ DESCARTES’S Metaphysics, and Replies.</term> (Amsterdam, published by Johannes Blaeu, 1644.) The <term>Dubitationes</term> <note>Latin for "Doubts"</note> refer to the *Objections* of 1641. Furthermore, this work contains a very complete *Index*, which provides a summary not only of each *Instance*, but also of each *Reply* and each *Objection*.

We reproduce here, as documentary evidence, first two pieces that appear at the beginning of that work—namely, a letter of transmission from Gassendi to Sorbière, and a Printer’s Notice to the Reader—then the full *Index* which follows immediately after, and finally several passages from the first *Instance*, because of the interest they hold for the publication history of this work.

# I

-> TO SAMUEL SORBIÈRE <-
-> FROM PIERRE GASSENDI <-
-> GREETINGS <-

"I am finally satisfying your request, Sorbière: I am sending the manuscript of my *Counter-Rebuttals* <term>Instances</term> <note>original: *Inantiarum*. These were Gassendi's detailed responses to Descartes's replies to his initial objections.</note> against Descartes’s *Metaphysics*, which you have been demanding for a long time. If I did not do so sooner, that excellent young man and your dear friend Thomas Martel wrote to you of the cause; he is aware that the manuscript had left me, went into exile far from me, and has only now returned to my hands through various detours. Indeed, friends held it in turn and shared it even far outside the city; and this did not escape you, as you indicated that Descartes told you—when he publicly complained about books written against him that were not published but read privately <gloss>a</gloss>—that he especially wanted to mark mine. As for the fact that you demand permission not only to read it but also to publish it, it shall be as it seems best to you, who love me so and demand it so, even though the matter does not seem of such great importance to me. 

For I wrote the work to gratify friends, when they could not bear that the man <note>referring to Descartes</note> wanted to have private criticisms from me and others for the sole purpose of being able to boast publicly that he did not lack adversaries, when in truth he had none (at least he had not had me). But although I seemed to have satisfied those friends, I did not satisfy myself. For while they judged that, just as I had previously followed the sequence of the text and Descartes had adapted his *Replies* to the individual articles of my letter, I should likewise press upon each of his *Replies* in the same order; yet to me it seemed the work would be far more harmonious if, once the state of the case was proposed, everything I had to say were woven together in a special and coherent arrangement. 

And they indeed objected that this should only be done if perhaps Descartes were to provide something later that required a new hand; but meanwhile, there is a reason why I fear that, given the structure the matter has, if you decide to publish it, it will not be pleasant enough to read. You, however, once the matter is clearer through reading, shall see to that; except that I advise that, if you still wish to proceed, however many distinct articles there were in my letter, let them now be distinguished and titled as so many *Doubts* <term>Dubitationes</term>, and let there be headings to relieve boredom and show, by the arguments placed there, what is contained in each. For even though the letter (written for a different purpose than to lay the foundation for a formal dispute) was not arranged so that every article would become a specific objection or *Doubt* (otherwise I would have completed each with its own conclusion and proofs like musical movements), nonetheless, because things have turned out this way, and Descartes has turned my private warning into a public quarrel, we must strive, as much as possible, that the matter does not proceed indecorously...

## II

### THE PRINTER

->TO THE CANDID AND LEARNED READER.<-

> « There has come into our hands, dear reader, the *Metaphysical Disquisition* 
> » of that great man Pierre Gassendi <note>original: *Petri Gassendi*</note>, 
> » whose publication I know has been greatly desired, both because of the 
> » subject matter and the fame of the Author as well as of Descartes 
> » <note>original: *Cartesii*</note>, against whom it was written. Yet for almost 
> » two entire years, the modesty of that excellent man stood in the way; 
> » who, destined to be famous among posterity for other reasons, 
> » considered it unimportant to pull the rope of contention. He shared his 
> » manuscript only with friends of the inner circle, showing them how 
> » easily he could dissolve his adversary's reasonings and laugh at his 
> » sharper words. 
> » But at last, overcome by the persistent pleading of the friend to whom 
> » he sent his manuscript—who indeed placed no end to his prayers—he 
> » gave permission to publish it. I hope, and it is no empty faith, that 
> » this work will be received with great applause by all the learned, as 
> » nothing could have been written more accurately in this genre of writing. 
> » How diligently that most learned man examines every word of his adversary! 
> » With what skill he uncovers the hidden traps! <note>original: *cuniculos*, literally "underground tunnels" or "mines" used in siege warfare to collapse walls.</note> 
> » With what sharpness he solves the intricacies! How powerfully he 
> » hurls the darts back at his adversary! How firm are the steps he 
> » places on slippery and steep ground! With what judgment he handles 
> » a difficult matter! How learnedly he discourses! How modestly he 
> » speaks of himself! How gentle he is toward his adversary—a man 
> » who is more troubled than others, and whom he ought to look up to 
> » and revere above all! What brilliance, what elegance of speech! It 
> » was truly in the interest of students of a good mind that a book 
> » so perfect in all its parts should no longer be suppressed, and 
> » that something born for the public good should not serve only the 
> » private use of a few. "For this strife is good for mortals." 
> » <note>original Greek: *Ἀγαθὴ γὰρ ἔρις ἥδε βροτοῖσι*. A quote from the poet Hesiod, meaning that healthy competition or intellectual struggle is beneficial for humanity.</note> 
> » The question is grave, undoubtedly worthy of having noble and lofty 
> » minds exercise their strength upon it. The men who contend are 
> » beyond all reproach. I regret only one thing, that Gassendi was not 
> » sufficiently...

1. That a philosopher is not a boaster, but a lover of wisdom...................... 13
2. That it is falsely supposed that all prejudices can be cast off, and thereafter most certain and evident principles held.................................................................... 14

6. That God is undeservedly held as if he were a deceiver, making us doubt whether we might not be deceived in those things which seem most evident and certain to us. ......................................................................................................... 21

### <term>COUNTER-REBUTTAL</term> <note>original: "Instantia." A formal objection raised by Pierre Gassendi in response to Descartes' previous answers.</note>

1. That the difficulty concerning the reasoning of animals was avoided without merit .................................................. 73

## DOUBT VII.

Concerning the example of the Wax: that, even when the mind strips away all its <term>accidental qualities</term> <note>original: "accidentibus." 1. That the principal difficulties were ignored .................. 89
2. That whatever we know about things is not their innermost nature; which God willed to be hidden from us, as the knowledge of it is not as necessary for us as that of its accidental qualities ............................... 90
3. That it is a witty evasion to claim that as many properties of the mind are recognized as there are individual things that can be known by it; in order to argue from this that *a fuller knowledge of it is held than of any other thing* ................. 92

## ON MEDITATION III, which is
->*Concerning God, that He exists.*<-

### DOUBT I.

Regarding the need for a <term>Rule</term> <note>original: "Regulâ." Descartes sought a universal rule of truth: that whatever is perceived clearly and distinctly must be true.</note>—not one that establishes *that what we perceive clearly and distinctly is true*; but one by which we may know that we are perceiving so clearly and distinctly that we are not deceived (p. 277, l. 11) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 95
REPLY (p. 361, l. 7) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 97

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. On the connection of the Meditations, and the contradictions that follow from the Rule assumed here—and not yet established—concerning the knowledge of God, which is assumed to be forthcoming . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 98
2. That the principal difficulty, which was objected against the Rule or its application, was avoided and concealed . . . . . . . . . 100
3. That there is still a lack of a Rule, or Method, by which we—thinking that we perceive something clearly and distinctly—may be certain that all things have been examined, so that nothing can arise from which we are found to have erred . . . . . 102

### DOUBT II.

On the <term>adventitious</term> <note>original: "adventitiâ." Ideas that Descartes claims come from outside the mind through the senses, rather than being innate.</note> origin of all Ideas, even of <term>Chimeras</term> <note>original: "Chimærarum." In 17th-century philosophy, these are "fictitious" ideas constructed by the mind, like a mountain of gold or a centaur.</note>, and even of Thing, Truth, and thought (p. 279, l. 18) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 103
REPLY (p. 362, l. 5) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 105

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That the principal difficulties were avoided, by which it is established that there are no ideas except adventitious ones; and by what artifice some ideas were taken as examples while others were omitted . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 105
2. That what had been objected specifically regarding the Idea of a "Thing"—which is not formed except from observed particulars and previously held ideas of them—was avoided: and that he who, after pretending to cast off all <term>prejudices</term> <note>original: "præjudicia." Preconceived notions or sensory beliefs Descartes seeks to doubt.</note>, discovers some ideas in himself, cannot say that they are <term>innate</term> <note>original: "innatas." Ideas Descartes believes are born within the mind, placed there by God, such as the idea of infinity or God himself.</note> . . . . 107

### DOUBT III.

On the adventitious origin of Ideas, proven from those things lacking in the blind and the deaf; and on the single Idea of the Sun, which, having been received through sense, is expanded by reason (p. 282, l. 7) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 109
REPLY (p. 363, l. 1) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 110

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That the objection made concerning the blind and the deaf is unresolved. Nor can what is intended be legitimately concluded from only certain propositions . . . 111

2. That the main difficulty regarding the <term>Idea of the Sun</term> <note>original: "Idea Solis." Descartes used the sun as an example: we have a small sensory idea of it and a large astronomical idea. Gassendi argues both are ultimately derived from the senses.</note> has been concealed. That an Idea is properly an image. That some things are perceived through a true idea, and others by way of consequence . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 113

## DOUBT IV.

On the improper Idea of <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantiæ." In 17th-century philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that can exist on its own (like a mind or a body), as opposed to "accidents" (like color or thought) which must exist in something else.</note>, perceived through its accidents and in their likeness. And on the idea of God derived from things or their perfections (p. 284, l. 25) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 115
REPLY (p. 364, l. 3) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 118

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That <term>intellection</term> <note>original: "intellectionem." Pure understanding by the mind, which Descartes argued could happen without any mental pictures.</note> seems unable to be separated from imagination; and that the same image is present or contemplated in both . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 119
2. That it seems false that substance is perceived not by imagination, but by the intellect alone; and that the idea we have of it does not depend on those ideas we have of its accidents . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 121
3. By what reasoning it seems the first humans could have had the Idea of God, if they did not have it as <term>innate</term> <note>original: "ingenitam." Ideas that Descartes claimed are born within the mind rather than learned through experience.</note>; and how a person reasons who thinks they possess an innate idea . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 123
4. That of God, since He is infinite, no true idea is held. That the infinite is known by negation alone. From where the expansion of the idea arises. It is wrongfully denied that God would be a tiny God if He were not greater than what we can understand . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 126

## DOUBT V.

On that axiom, *nothing is in the effect that was not first in the cause*, understanding this to refer to the material cause. And to what extent it can be true that *there must be at least as much <term>formal reality</term> in the cause of an idea as there is <term>objective reality</term> in the idea itself* (p. 288, l. 8) <note>Descartes argued that the "objective reality" (the content/complexity) of our idea of God is so great that its "cause" must have an equal amount of "formal reality" (actual existence), meaning only God could have caused our idea of Him.</note> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 128
REPLY (p. 366, l. 1) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 130

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That the "royal road"—by which God's existence is proven from the manifest effects in the universe—should not be abandoned in favor of proving it through the so-called <term>objective reality</term> of an idea. That the word "reality" is used improperly here . . . . . . . . . . . 130
2. That an Idea with its objective reality seems to relate to its cause as a shape impressed on wax relates to the representation of the seal; so that, just as the representative shape is the representable seal, thus the idea has objective reality (representation of the cause), and the cause itself has formal reality (representability) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 132
3. That certain difficulties were concealed: and to what extent it is true or not true that the effect pre-exists in the cause, so that a conclusion may be drawn regarding the objective reality of the idea . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 134

### DOUBT VI.

On the mind not having an idea of itself from itself (as it does not seem able to understand itself any more than the eye can see itself), and neither of God, nor of Angels, nor especially of <term>corporeal things</term> <note>original: "corporearum rerum." Physical, material things that have "body" or extension in space, as opposed to the purely mental.</note> (p. 291, l. 3). . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 137
REPLY (p. 366, l. 10). . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 139

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. No room for trifling. That difficulties were evaded. Every idea is an image: therefore an image exists in the intellect no less than in the <term>imaginative faculty</term> <note>original: "imaginatrice." The part of the mind that deals with mental pictures or sensory representations.</note>. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 140
2. That it was not proven that the same thing does not act upon itself; that the point is wrongly mocked, and the fault is turned back upon the teacher. In the <term>rotation of a spinning top</term> <note>original: "circumductione turbinis." Gassendi uses the physical movement of a top to question Descartes’ claim about how the mind perceives its own actions.</note>, the same thing does not act upon itself. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 141
3. That nothing was fabricated when it was objected that the mind was said to be able to derive ideas of corporeal things from itself; nor was there a reply to the difficulty that had been proposed concerning that matter. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 142

### DOUBT VII.

On the <term>Principal Demonstration</term> <note>original: "Capitali Demonstratione." Refers to Descartes' primary argument for God's existence in the Third Meditation.</note> for the existence of God from the preceding preparation; in imitation of which it may be concluded that there actually exist infinite Worlds, an idea which was held by ancient Philosophers (p. 294, l. 2) . . . . . . . 144
REPLY (p. 367, l. 19). . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 147

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That Principal Demonstration is proposed in <term>syllogistic form</term> <note>original: "formâ Syllogisticâ." A formal logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (major and minor).</note>; and its weakness is first shown generally and in various ways. . . . . . . . . . . . 147
2. It is then shown specifically and in various ways in the <term>Major</term> <note>original: "Majore." The first, broader premise of a syllogism.</note> proposition of the prosyllogism . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 149
3. And similarly in the <term>Minor</term> <note>original: "Minore." The second, more specific premise of a syllogism.</note> or Assumption. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 151
4. And again in the <term>sub-assumption</term> <note>original: "Sub-assumptione." A secondary premise or supporting argument within a larger logical structure.</note>; where also concerning the inference for the existence of infinite Worlds . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 153
5. It is false that the idea we have of an <term>infinite Being</term> <note>original: "Entis infiniti." Referring to the concept of God as a being without bounds.</note> represents in truth not a part, but the whole infinite. And how the idea God has of himself differs from the one man has of God. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 156

### DOUBT VIII.

On the subsidiary Demonstration, based on the fact that one who feels he lacks something must infer the existence of a Being that is infinitely more perfect (p. 297, l. 25). . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 158
REPLY (p. 368, l. 21). . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 160

#### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That a difficulty was concealed regarding that inference: *If one thing is more perfect than another, then it is infinite* .................... 161
2. That <term>paralogisms</term> <note>original: "Paralogiſmos." A paralogism is a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning, often one that the person making it believes to be true.</note> are always committed, by which the actual existence of a thing is inferred from the actual existence of an idea; the infinity of the thing known from the finiteness of knowledge (which might still grow); and the existence of a thing as a cause from the fact that it exists within an idea ........................................ 162

### DOUBT IX.

Regarding another subsidiary demonstration, based on the fact that something could not be made or exist if an <term>infinite Being</term> <note>original: "Ens infinitum." For Descartes, this refers specifically to God as the only truly boundless substance.</note> did not exist; and that the parts of time are independent of one another (p. 300, l. 11) ................ 165
REPLY (p. 369, l. 14) ........................................ 168

#### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That it was not demonstrated in the preceding arguments that God is the creator; just as it was not demonstrated that God is the cause of things in the same way that the Sun is the cause of light ....................................................... 169
2. That the paralogism remains, because a condition or nature of Time was assumed to be other than what it is .......................................... 170
3. That the demonstration derived from the independence of the parts of time from one another fails in various ways ..................................... 173
4. That the issue here is not the truth of the Reality itself, but the force of the Reasoning, against which the primary objections were either left unresolved or untouched ... 176
5. That what had been objected regarding <term>infinite progress</term> <note>original: "progreſſu infinito." The logical problem of a chain of causes that goes back forever without a starting point.</note> in causes essentially and accidentally subordinate was perversely distorted ................. 177
6. That it does not follow that because a certain perfection is enlarged by the mind, that enlarged perfection exists in reality .............................................. 178

### DOUBT X.

Regarding the manner in which the idea of God is impressed upon the mind, like a mark impressed by a Craftsman, whose likeness the mind bears (p. 304, l. 28) ............ 179
REPLY (p. 371, l. 8) ........................................ 181

#### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. Those things concluded at the end of the Third Meditation are presented in <term>syllogistic form</term> <note>original: "Syllogiſticâ formâ." A formal logical structure (Major Premise, Minor Premise, Conclusion) used to test the validity of an argument.</note>, so that the extent of their force may be apparent at a single glance ......... 182
2. That it is false that nothing can be added to or taken away from the ideas we have of things .......................................................... 185
3. That it is false that nothing can be added to the idea we once have of God. In what sense the essences of things are indivisible, including the divine essence: and concerning the divine attributes .............................................. 187

# ON THE FOURTH MEDITATION, which is, *Of Truth and Error.* <note>original: "De vero & falso." This Meditation addresses the "problem of error"—how a perfect God could create a being capable of being deceived.</note>

## DOUBT I.

Regarding the faculty of judgment created by God, which is not immune to error; and regarding the rejection of the consideration of <term>final causes</term> <note>original: "caussarum finalium." In philosophy, a "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which something exists (e.g., the "end" of an eye is to see). Descartes famously argued that scientists should stop looking for God's purposes in nature and focus on how things work mechanically.</note> from <term>Physics</term> <note>original: "Physicâ." In this era, "Physics" referred broadly to the study of the natural world and physical substances.</note> (p. 307, l. 20). 198
### REPLY (p. 374, l. 10)....... 200

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL. <note>original: "INSTANTIA." In these debates, this term marks a point-by-point rebuttal to Descartes' previous reply.</note>

1. A difficulty, as is customary, concealed concerning the creation of a faculty liable to error. That which should be proven later is established as a principle; and that which was not demonstrated is assumed to be demonstrated....... 201
2. That the consideration of <term>ends</term> <note>original: "finium." Another term for final causes or purposes.</note> is most necessary in Physics, so that God may be recognized as both the Governor and the Author of the Universe....... 203
3. That not all of God's purposes are unknown to men; and that this is evident even from the purposes of the various parts of the human body....... 205
4. That the proposed difficulties regarding the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>original: "caussâ efficiente." The agent or mechanism that brings something about—in this case, the physical force that moves the valves of the heart.</note> of the heart’s valves are inexplicable, even though their purpose or use seems most clear. 206
5. It is false that if someone remained from the womb without any use of the senses, they would have the same (and even purer) ideas of things as someone who has use of their senses....... 208

## DOUBT II.

Concerning the faculty of judgment liable to error granted to man by God, who nonetheless could have granted him one immune to it (p. 310, l. 29)....... 209
### REPLY (p. 376, l. 1)....... 211

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. That the difficulty was avoided. The comparison of the World to a Republic, in which it is better that no citizen be evil, was appropriate; but not so the comparison with a man, of whom no part is not an eye <note>Gassendi is critiquing Descartes' argument that a variety of parts (some less "perfect" than others) makes for a more perfect whole, just as a body needs more than just eyes to function.</note>....... 212

2. A difficulty once again ignored regarding the weakness of the reasoning by which the faculty of judgment in man is concluded to be perfect................................................... 213

## DOUBT III.

Regarding the cause of error or falsity: whether it arises because the will or the faculty of judgment extends more widely than the intellect (p. 314, l. 13)..... 215
REPLY (p. 376, l. 20)....................................... 217

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL. <note>original: "INSTANTIA." A point-by-point rebuttal where Gassendi challenges Descartes' previous answers.</note>

1. For the sake of avoiding confusion, the intellect and the will ought to be distinguished such that whatever pertains to knowledge and judgment belongs to the Intellect, while whatever pertains to desire and choice belongs to the Will.......... 218
2. The progress of the Intellect from the first operation to the second, and from the second to the third (which is manifold), occurs without any interference from the actions of the will.......... 219 <note>In traditional logic, the "three operations of the mind" are: 1. Simple apprehension (forming a concept), 2. Judgment (forming a sentence), and 3. Reasoning (linking sentences into an argument).</note>
3. Every action of the will presupposes a judgment by the intellect regarding whether a thing is to be sought or avoided; even when the will commands the intellect itself to decide on something.......... 220
4. The will does not extend more widely than the intellect (indeed, not even as widely), and whether the love of one's own opinion was rightly made the object of the previous sentence.......... 222
5. Errors do not arise from the fact that the will, or even judgment, extends more widely than the intellect or <term>simple apprehension</term>.......... 224 <note>original: "simplex apprehensio." The basic mental act of grasping a concept without yet making a claim about its truth or falsity.</note>
6. The <term>indifference</term> of the intellect appears to be the root of the indifference of the will, in which freedom resides, and the latter is determined by the former; and it is not so much freedom as <term>willingness</term> when the will adheres to the highest good once it is clearly perceived.......... 226 <note>original: "indifferentiam" and "libentiam." "Indifference" here refers to a state where the mind is not yet pulled in one direction; Gassendi is arguing that we only have free choice because our intellect hasn't yet shown us a definitive reason to act.</note>
7. In order for the will to be corrected, the judgment of the intellect must first be corrected through a refined apprehension of things; the will does not command the intellect unless the intellect itself provides the light.......... 228
8. To what extent falsity exists in things, since properly speaking it exists only in the intellect.......... 230

## DOUBT IV.

Regarding the still-desired Method by which we might recognize that we perceive something so clearly and distinctly that the danger of error is not present (p. 317, l. 24)................................................... 231
REPLY (p. 378, l. 26)....................................... 232

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL.

1. So that it could be recognized whether the promised Method had been delivered, the principal parts of the *Meditations* had to be weighed individually.......................................... 232

2. A circular argument <note>original: "Circulum commissum." This refers to the famous "Cartesian Circle" critique: Descartes argues that we can trust our clear and distinct perceptions because God exists and is not a deceiver, but he also uses clear and distinct perceptions to prove that God exists.</note> committed by proving that God exists and is truthful because there is a clear and distinct knowledge of Him; and that the knowledge of God is clear and distinct because God exists and is truthful. Finally, the desired Method is still found wanting........................... 233

### ON MEDITATION V, which is,
### *On the essence of Material things; and again concerning God, that He exists.*

#### DOUBT I.

Regarding the essence of material things known solely from quantity, figure, etc.; and regarding the eternal and immutable nature attributed to ideas and Universals (p. 318, l. 16)................................. 236
REPLY (p. 379, l. 14)................................. 238

#### COUNTER-REBUTTAL. <note>original: "INSTANTIA." Gassendi’s follow-up challenge to Descartes' reply.</note>

1. That the treatment of the essence of material things was seen, and not without reason, as quite thin........................... 240
2. That there are no eternal and real natures of things, and those which we have as ideas in the mind are created by the mind itself from the inspection of singular <note>Meaning individual, specific objects.</note> things. 242
3. It is false that the ideas of Geometric figures are not drawn from the senses, and that such things could exist in the world as are considered by Geometers—that is, as indivisibles <note>original: "indivisibileis." Referring to points, lines, or surfaces that have no thickness or width, which Gassendi argues cannot exist in physical reality.</note>.............................. 244
4. It is false that a boy experiences having the idea of a triangle before he has seen a triangle or another figure from whose analogy he might reason. 245
5. That there is no idea in the mind of an animal, or any other thing that has not been perceived by the sense, is proved by experience itself............... 246

#### DOUBT II.

### DOUBT III.

Concerning the primary demonstration for the existence of the mind separately from the body, based on the fact that the mind itself is a thinking thing and the body is an extended thing (p. 334, l. 7) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 273
REPLY (p. 386, l. 11) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 275

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL. <note>original: "INSTANTIA." A follow-up objection or challenge to a previous reply.</note>

1. That a concealed fallacy <note>original: "Paralogismus." A piece of false or illogical reasoning.</note> regarding the separation of things based on the separation of concepts is revealed of its own accord. That it is falsely assumed as demonstrated that God can perform whatever is clearly and distinctly understood by anyone . . . . . 275
2. That the words of the demonstration were truly intended to be understood as referring to the dense body consisting of limbs, not to a subtle body or any body whatsoever . . 277
3. Although it may be gathered from the Second Meditation that the Mind is conceived as a substance <term>Substance: in 17th-century philosophy, this refers to something that can exist independently on its own.</term>, or a thing existing by itself, it is not therefore gathered that it *is* in fact a substance, or a thing existing by itself . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 279
4. A demonstration proposed in a confused manner is reduced to a syllogistic <note>A logical form of argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note> form . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 281
5. A faulty method of demonstrating, based on someone saying they experience it within themselves. That the fallacy which was emphasized in the Second Meditation—concerning the separability of things based on the separability of concepts—is repeated here . . . . . 282
6. From the Replies to others, one can gather what could have been answered to the objection regarding the two properties of a triangle, which can indeed be conceived separately, but cannot actually exist separately . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 284
7. That the question was poorly framed. The question is not whether two complete *substances are separable; but whether two certain things understood separately are indeed two complete substances* . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 286
8. That it is in vain to resort to the distinction between adequate and inadequate knowledge, since no knowledge is adequate, nor can it be known to be adequate . . . . . 287
9. That the question concerns specific thought and extension; and that it has not yet been proven that it is incompatible for an extended or corporeal thing to think . . . . . 289
10. Although there can be extension without thought, and thought without extension, it has not yet been proven that both cannot exist together in the same subtle body—such as the soul <note>original: "anima."</note> might be—and this is also shown by turning the examples back against the argument . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 291
11. From the proposed precision of concepts, it is just as much inferred that the mind <note>original: "mens."</note> is corporeal; indeed, it is concluded to be inseparable rather than separable . . . 293

### COUNTER-REBUTTAL. <note>original: "INSTANTIA." A follow-up objection or challenge to a previous reply.</note>

1. A clever evasion. That an image or representation <note>original: "speciem seu imaginem."</note> is also required for understanding; and that an image of an extended thing cannot exist without extension . . . . . 299
2. That the comparison is not weakened between someone who says *they clearly know the nature of the mind* because they can say, *It is a thinking thing*, and a blind person who says *they clearly know the nature of the Sun* because they can say, *It is a warming thing* . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 301
3. From the fact that one cannot say what else the mind is other than a thinking thing, it cannot be concluded that it is therefore nothing more than that . . . . . . 303
4. The difficulty remains that to say the Mind is a non-extended thing is to say not what it is, but what it is not; as if one were to say of Bucephalus <note>Bucephalus was the famous horse of Alexander the Great; the author is using him as a classic example of a physical entity.</note> that he is not a fly. That the point is being assumed <term>Begging the question (petitio principii): A logical fallacy where the conclusion one is trying to prove is assumed in the premise.</term>. That one's own authority is taken as a demonstration. That the main difficulties are being concealed . . . . . 305

## ->IV<-

After this *Index*, the ***Investigation*** <note>Referring to Gassendi's *Disquisitio Metaphysica* (1644), where he expanded on his disagreements with Descartes.</note> begins with the heading that Gassendi gave to his *Objections*, and which one could very well call the *Reason for writing* <note>original: "Scribendi occasio"</note>: "Our friend Mersenne has blessed me..." (Previously, p. 256, l. 12.) Then follows the *Reply* of Descartes to this preliminary: "By such an elegant and accurate..." (Page 347, l. 3.) To this, Gassendi retorts with a ***Counter-rebuttal***, divided into several parts; the first bears this title in the margin: *The necessity of rebuttal* <note>original: "Instandi necessitas"</note>. It gives interesting details on the circumstances of this polemic. We reproduce it therefore below:

> "Your *Meditations*, a manuscript copy of which Mersenne had shared with me, came off the press last autumn<note>a</note>. Joined to them was a collection of Objections and Replies which you wrongly assume I had read when I wrote to you: for I had absolutely refused to see those offered by Mersenne, so that I might approach the examination of the *Meditations* without being prejudiced. Among the other things Objected to you, I also saw my own rather lengthy Letter published. After I read through your Reply, I could not sufficiently wonder what spirit you were moved by toward me. For while you judged that what I had written should be held of no account, that was even according to my wishes, as I value nothing of my own so much as to think it worth any price. Yet I could not help desiring a certain greater candor, by which, if nothing seemed to you to be of any importance, you ought to have rather wrapped it in silence and darkness than to insult me thus by making it public. I certainly wrote to you, not of my own accord, but because I was asked—"

a. The 1st edition of the *Meditations*, in Paris, at Michel Soly’s, bears this date: “*Finished printing, August 28, 1641.*” — Gassendi’s *Disquisitio Metaphysica*, though published only in 1644, ends thus: “*Paris, Ides of March 1642.*”

<summary>This page concludes the index for the Fifth Set of Replies and introduces Pierre Gassendi's "Disquisitio Metaphysica," including a personal letter where Gassendi expresses his frustration over how Descartes published and responded to his private objections.</summary>
<keywords>Descartes, Gassendi, Mersenne, Meditations, Counter-rebuttal, Disquisitio Metaphysica, philosophical dispute, publishing history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Counter-rebuttal" from Pierre Gassendi to René Descartes. On the previous page, Gassendi began explaining that he originally shared his criticisms privately through their mutual friend Mersenne, intending to be helpful rather than confrontational.</meta>

<page-num>410</page-num>
<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES.</header>

» ...tumn. <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page.</note> I would have endured it; and by disagreeing with you, I had signaled my difficulties not publicly, but privately. That was certainly my intention: to propose to you candidly and as a friend the doubts that I observed arising in me during my reading. This was so that, if the matter seemed important enough, you could make the text somewhat clearer; if it did not seem so, it would then be up to you to suppress the matter entirely. I thought that you wanted that copy to be read by me and others so that, having tested various judgments, you could foresee whether the original manuscript should be amended in some way before you arranged for its publication.

But in truth, you received that counsel—which was full of goodwill—as if I had challenged you like an enemy. Writing nothing back to me privately, you instead launched a public battle, declaring by your actions that the copy had been shown by you not because you held any doubt about what you had once written, but because you wanted some people to be stirred up against whom you could test your strength. Did you not therefore force me into a necessary defense? You seemed to want nothing else than to turn a friend into an adversary and to drive me into the arena when I was thinking of no such thing.

As for the fact that you prefixed and subjoined certain kind words, I accept those with the gratitude they deserve—even though you treated me like a child whose cup is touched with honey <note>original: "poculum circùm contingitur melle" — a reference to Lucretius’s famous metaphor of a doctor sweetening the rim of a cup of bitter medicine (wormwood) to trick a child into drinking it.</note> around the rim so that he may drink down the foul liquid of wormwood. For the rest, however, you conducted yourself in such a way that you seem to have been testing whether I would prove myself a coward, or one who would hand over the herb <note>original: "herbam porrigere" — a Roman idiom meaning to admit defeat or surrender.</note> to you. I accept the conditions, then; being in retirement, I will not be envious if, just as you have begun to give yourself applause, you hunt for an ovation and a triumph.

I will be careful of this one thing: since I know you were offended that I addressed you by the name of "Mind" throughout your *Meditations* (where you speak in the persona of the Mind), and since you took as irony what was done with complete sincerity—as must be remembered later—I say, I will take care not to call you "Mind" any further. Instead, even though you speak only as a part of a human being, I shall address you as a whole man. You may address me as you wish; for, as far as I am concerned, you are free to address me not only as "Flesh"—the word which occurred to your cleverness so that it might be an <term>antithesis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίθετος (antitheton) — a contrasting opposite.</note> to the mind—but even as a rock, as lead, or as anything else you think is more obtuse. 

Indeed, because you say here that you respond: *“Not as if to me, a most sharp-witted Philosopher, but as if to one of the men of flesh,”* I first give you the thanks I owe, and return to you, as more deserving, the <term>epithet</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπίθετον (epitheton) — a descriptive label.</note> of "most sharp-witted"; and then I, who wrote to you, do not deny being that person to whom you yourself respond. Truly, I act far more simply than to know this distinction of yours; and as I do not know how to dissemble, I do not assume a double persona. I candidly reject that "philosopher" persona which you set aside, and I take up the other one which you leave remaining. 

*“And if it were indeed a matter concerning the truth of the thing—such as the existence of God and the immortal nature of souls—in that case I would certainly deny [the persona of the flesh]; for it could seem from the sense of Holy Scripture that the flesh is opposed to the spirit;”* but because this is no longer a matter of anything more than the force of your Reasoning, and thus your cause is private, and you alone must be resisted, it is not clear why I should avoid this persona any more than Aristotle himself did when he opposed Anaxagoras, who was commonly called "Mind." <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Greek philosopher known for introducing the concept of *Nous* (Mind) as the ordering force of the universe.</note> For although you call me "fleshly," you do not thereby make me soulless; just as, although you act as "Mind," you do not thereby make yourself fleshless.

He mockingly accepts Descartes's dismissal of him as "Flesh" vs. Descartes as "Mind," arguing that his philosophical objections remain valid regardless of these labels.</summary>

> » Therefore, it must also be allowed for you to speak according to your own nature; and it is enough that, God willing, neither I am purely flesh without mind, nor you purely mind without flesh; and that neither you are above, nor I below the human condition; although you refuse what is human, I do not think it alien to me... » <note>original: "Quare & permittendum tibi, ut pro genio loquaris tuo..." The following passage from the same *Counter-rebuttal* <note>original French: *Instance* — a legal and philosophical term for a formal rejoinder or counter-argument</note> offers a certain historical interest:

> *Moreover, when I realized that I felt none of the force of your boasted demonstrations, I asked several men of great name and exceedingly learned, who had read your* Meditations <note>Descartes's 1641 work *Meditations on First Philosophy*</note>, *what they thought; <margin>5</margin> I discovered that they, just like me, did not sense the force of the demonstration. How much, do you think, did we grieve when, expecting so much from you—such a great man, and on such a great matter—we fell short of our hope? This was indeed the common voice: "Is it possible that that man, raised on mathematical studies <margin>10</margin> and knowing so well what a demonstration is, should hold and publish those reasons as genuine demonstrations, which yet fail to elicit assent from us, though we are so attentive and so well-disposed? Or perhaps, elated by the applause with which he devised and demonstrated some new things in geometry, <margin>15</margin> was he led to believe that he could be equally successful in other matters, and especially in metaphysics? Or did he, like others, make nothing of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer and mathematician</note>, who, having pursued mathematics, <margin>20</margin> said that he left theology and physics untouched—the latter because of the unstable condition of matter, the former because of the incomprehensible nature of divine things? Or, after having promised such a great harvest in his* Synopsis, *did he think the readers would be content with hope, and would not studiously inquire whether the ears of corn were full or empty?" (Page 6.)*

### SIXTH OBJECTIONS

<margin>552</margin>

The first [objection] is that it does not seem so certain that we exist simply because we think<sup>a</sup>. For, in order to be certain that you are thinking, you must know what "thinking" or "thought" is, and what your "existence" is; and since you do not yet know what those things are, how can you know that you are <margin>5</margin> thinking or existing? Therefore, when you say **I think** <note>original: *cogito*</note>, since you do not know what you are saying, and when you add **therefore I am** <note>original: *sum igitur*</note>, since you likewise do not know what you are saying, <margin>553</margin> | indeed, since you do not even know that you are saying or thinking anything at all—for this would seem to require that you know that you know what you are saying, and again that you know that you know that you know what you are saying, and so on <margin>10</margin> to infinity—it is established that you cannot know whether you are, or even whether you are thinking.

But, to raise a second doubt, when you say that you think and exist<sup>b</sup>, someone might contend that you are deceived, and that you do not think, but are only moved, and that you are nothing other than physical <margin>15</margin> motion, since no one has yet been able to grasp in their mind your demonstration by which you believe you have proved that no physical motion can be what you call "thought." Have you, therefore, by that "Analysis" <note>the method of breaking down complex problems into simple parts</note> which you use, so examined all the motions of your <term>subtle matter: the extremely fine, fluid particles that Descartes believed filled all space and functioned as the medium for light and physical force</term> <margin>20</margin> that you are certain, and can show to us—who are most attentive and, as we believe, sufficiently perceptive—that it is a contradiction for our thoughts to be reduced to those physical motions?

A third doubt is very similar: for since several of the Church Fathers, along with the Platonists, believed that Angels were physical beings—whence the <term>Lateran Council: likely the Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517), which defined the soul as the form of the body and immortal</term> concluded that they <margin>25</margin> could be depicted in art—and they thought exactly the same regarding the rational soul, <margin>554</margin> | since some of them believed it was produced <term>from the lineage: referring to "traducianism," the theory that the soul is transmitted from parents to children through biological generation rather than created directly by God</term>, they nevertheless said that both Angels and the soul think; they would therefore seem to have judged that this could happen through physical motions, or even that thoughts themselves are physical motions, from which...

...they have not at all distinguished thought <note>original: *cogitationem*</note>. This can also be confirmed by the thoughts of monkeys, <margin>5</margin> dogs, and other animals. For dogs bark while sleeping, as if they were chasing hares or thieves; they know that they are running when awake, and indeed that they are barking while dreaming, even though, like you, we recognize nothing in them that is distinct from their bodies. But if you deny that a dog knows it is running or thinking—besides the fact that you assert this without proof—the dog itself perhaps forms a similar judgment about us: <margin>10</margin> namely, that we do not know whether we run or think while we are running or thinking. For you do not see the animal's internal way of operating, just as it does not inspect yours; nor is there a lack of great men who grant reason to beasts, and have attributed it to them in the past. We are so far from believing that all <margin>555</margin> their operations can be sufficiently explained by the help of <margin>15</margin> **Mechanics**, without sensation, life, and a soul, that we would be willing to wager any amount that such a thing is both impossible <note>original: *ἀδύνατον* (adynaton)</note> and worthy of laughter. And finally, there are many who would say that man himself—even without sensation and intellect—could do everything by means of **mechanical springs**, and without any mind, <margin>20</margin> if a monkey, a dog, and an elephant were able to perform all their operations in this way. For if the mediocre reason of beasts differs from the reason of man, they differ only according to "more or less," and such degrees do not change the essence<sup>a</sup>.

The fourth scruple <note>or "doubt"</note> concerns the knowledge of the **Atheist**<sup>b</sup>, which he <margin>25</margin> contends is most certain, and even, according to your rule, most evident, when he asserts: "if equals are taken from equals, the remainders will be equal"; "the three angles of a rectilinear triangle are equal to two right angles," and a thousand similar things; since he cannot think of them without [believing] them [to be] cer[tain]...

The crux of the matter <note>original: "Nodus est"; literally "the knot"</note> is that we perceive perfectly well that 3 and 2 make 5, and that if you take equals from equals, the remainders will still be equal. These are either our arguments—or, if you prefer, our prejudices. If you can provide a remedy for them, Immortal God, how much thanks we shall all give you together, most Illustrious Sir, for freeing us from these...

### REPLY
### TO THE SIXTH OBJECTIONS.

1. It is indeed true that no one can be certain that he thinks, or that he exists, unless he knows what thought is and what existence is<gloss>a</gloss>. Not that this requires reflexive knowledge <note>original: "scientia reflexa"; this refers to "thinking about thinking," or a secondary level of awareness where the mind examines its own processes.</note>, or knowledge acquired through demonstration, and much less a knowledge of reflexive knowledge, by which one knows that one knows, and again knows that one knows that one knows, and so on to infinity; for such knowledge can never be had of <margin>567</margin> anything. But | it is entirely sufficient that he knows it by that internal cognition which always precedes reflexive knowledge, and which is so innate in all men concerning thought and existence that—even if we are perhaps overwhelmed by prejudices and more attentive to words than to the meanings of words—we might be able to pretend that we do not have it, yet we cannot in reality not have it. Thus, when someone notices that he is thinking, and that it follows from this that he exists, even if he has perhaps never before asked what thought is or what existence is, he still cannot fail to know both well enough to satisfy himself in this regard.

| 2. Nor can it happen, when someone notices that he is thinking and understands what it is to be moved, that he thinks he is being deceived and that he is not thinking, but only being moved<gloss>b</gloss>. For since he has a plainly different idea or notion of thought...

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ defense of the distinction between the human mind and the animal body. He responds to the objection that if animals (like monkeys or dogs) can act without a mind, perhaps humans do as well. Descartes argues that our internal experience of thinking is undeniable, regardless of how animals function.</meta>

<meta>473-474</meta>

<margin>10</margin> therefore, from the fact that it is shown that <term>brute animals</term> <note>original: "bruta animantia"; non-human animals which Descartes viewed as complex biological machines without consciousness.</note> [in] all-

And this is proven by the words immediately preceding: *Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up* <note>original Latin: "Scientia inflat, charitas verò ædificat"</note>, and from those immediately following: *But if anyone loves God, this person (namely, God) is known by him* <note>original: "Si quis autem diligit Deum, hic (nempe Deus) cognitus est ab eo"</note>. Rather, he says only that those who do not have love, and therefore do not know God sufficiently (even if they perhaps think they know something in other matters), do not yet know in the manner that one ought to know; for, clearly, one must begin from the knowledge of God.

...are together <note>original Latin: "sunt simul"</note>. For indeed, when two bodies touch each other, there is one and the same extremity <term>extremity: in this context, the outermost boundary or edge where one thing ends and another begins</term> for both, which is a part of neither, but rather the same mode <term>mode: a Cartesian term for a quality or state of a substance—like its shape or position—that cannot exist without the substance itself</term> of both. This mode can even <margin>584</margin> remain, although those bodies are removed, provided only that other bodies of exactly the same size and shape succeed them in their places. Furthermore, that place, which is said by the Aristotelians <term>Aristotelians: followers of Aristotle's traditional philosophy, which Descartes was seeking to replace with his own system</term> to be the surface of the surrounding body, cannot be understood to be any other surface than this one, which is not a substance but a mode. For the place of a tower is not changed, even if the air surrounding it is changed, or if another body is substituted into the place of that tower; therefore, the surface, which is taken here for "place," is not any part of the surrounding air or of the tower.

Now, to explode <note>meaning to forcefully refute or drive out of common belief</note> the reality of accidents <term>real accidents: a Scholastic concept suggesting that qualities like color, heat, or heaviness are "real things" that could, in theory, exist independently of the objects they belong to</term>, I do not think there is a need to wait for other reasons than those I have already treated. For first, since every sense occurs through touch, nothing can be felt except the surface of bodies; and yet, if there are any "real accidents," they must be something different from that surface, which is nothing other than a mode; therefore, if any such things exist, they cannot be felt. But who has ever believed they exist, except because he thought they were being felt? And finally, it is completely contradictory for "real accidents" to be given, because whatever is real can exist <margin>585</margin> separately from any other subject; but whatever can exist so separately is a substance, not an accident. Nor does it matter if it is said that real accidents [can exist separately] not naturally, but only through divine power...

And yet, since on the other hand I clearly understand that nothing in any category of being can exist which does not depend on God, and that it was easy for Him to establish certain things in such a way that we humans cannot understand them being otherwise than they are, it would be contrary to reason to doubt what we do understand simply because we cannot understand or perceive everything. Therefore, we should not think that **eternal truths** depend on the human intellect, or on other existing things, but on God alone, who, as the **supreme legislator**, established them from eternity.

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ Sixth Replies, specifically addressing how we perceive the world through our senses. # SIXTH REPLIES.

...of the organ, and the change of shape and position resulting from 그 movement. The **second grade** contains everything that immediately results in the mind from the fact that it is united to the bodily organ affected in this way. Such are the perceptions of pain, 
<margin>5</margin>tickling, thirst, hunger, colors, sound, taste, smell, heat, cold, and the like. As I stated in the **Sixth Meditation**, these arise from the union and, as it were, the intermingling of the mind with the body. Finally, the **third grade** comprises all those 
<margin>10</margin>judgments which, on the occasion of movements in the bodily organ, we have been accustomed to make about things outside ourselves from our earliest years.

For example, when I see a stick, we should not think that some *intentional species* <note>original Latin: *species intentionales*. In older Scholastic philosophy, these were thought to be "likenesses" or "images" that physically traveled through the air from an object to the eye. Descartes rejects this idea.</note> fly from the object to the eye. Rather, we should understand that only rays of light reflected from that stick excite 
<margin>15</margin>certain movements in the optic nerve and, by means of that 
<margin>589</margin>nerve, also in the brain, as I have explained at quite some length in the *Dioptrics* <note>original: *Dioptricâ*; Descartes' 1637 scientific treatise on light and vision</note>. The **first grade of sensing** consists in this brain movement, which we share in common with unthinking animals. From this follows the 
<margin>20</margin>**second grade**, which extends only to the perception of the color or light reflected from the stick. This arises because the mind is so intimately joined to the brain that it is affected by the movements occurring within it. If we wished to distinguish "sense" accurately from "intellect," nothing else should be

When I first concluded, from the reasons set forth in these Meditations, that the human mind is really distinguished from the body and is better known than the body, and so on, I was indeed compelled to assent, because I perceived <margin>5</margin> nothing in these arguments that was not coherent and concluded from evident principles according to the rules of logic. But I confess that I was not, for that reason, entirely persuaded. The same thing happened to me as to astronomers who, after they have proved by reasoning that the Sun is many times larger <margin>10</margin> than the Earth, still cannot prevent themselves, when they turn their eyes toward it, from judging it to be smaller. <note>Descartes uses this analogy to show that intellectual certainty often struggles against the powerful, habitual "evidence" of our eyes.</note> However, after I proceeded further and, relying on these same foundations, passed on to the consideration of physical things <margin>593</margin>—first by attending to the ideas or notions of each thing that I found within myself, and by diligently distinguishing <margin>15</margin> one from the others so that all my judgments would agree with them—I noticed that absolutely nothing belongs to the nature of a body except that it is a thing that is long, wide, and deep, <note>original: "longa, lata & profunda". This is Descartes' definition of matter as "extension" in three dimensions.</note> capable of various shapes and various motions. I also noticed that its shapes and motions are merely **modes** <term>modes: the specific states or configurations of a substance, which cannot exist independently of that substance (e.g., "roundness" cannot exist without a round object)</term>, <margin>20</margin> which by no power can exist without the body itself. On the other hand, I saw that colors, smells, tastes, and such things are only certain sensations existing in my thought, and are no less different from bodies than pain differs from the shape and motion <margin>25</margin> of the weapon that inflicts the pain. <note>This is a crucial move in modern philosophy: distinguishing "primary qualities" (like shape/motion) which are in the object, from "secondary qualities" (like color/pain) which exist only in the mind of the observer.</note> And finally, I saw that gravity, hardness, the power of heating, of attracting, of purging, <note>original: "purgandi". In the 17th century, this refers to the medicinal properties of substances, such as their ability to cleanse the body.</note> and all other qualities that we experience in bodies, consist solely in motion or the lack of motion, and in the configuration and situation of the parts.

Once I had accurately distinguished the idea of the mind from the ideas of the body and of physical movement, and realized that all other ideas of <term>real qualities</term> <note>In older philosophy, "real qualities" were thought to be things that existed independently within an object, like "redness" or "heat."</note> or <term>substantial forms</term> <note>A term from Aristotelian philosophy referring to the essence that makes a thing what it is; Descartes rejected these in favor of purely mechanical explanations.</note> which I had previously held were actually fabricated or invented by me, I very <margin>597</margin> easily freed myself from all the doubts that have been proposed here. For first, I did not doubt that I had a **clear idea of my own mind** ᵃ, <margin>5</margin> as I was intimately conscious of it; nor did I doubt that **this idea was entirely different from the ideas of other things** ᵇ, and that it **contained nothing of a physical nature** ᶜ. This was because, when I sought the true ideas of other things as well and seemed to recognize them all in a general way, I found absolutely <margin>10</margin> nothing in them that was not entirely different from the idea of the mind. And I saw that there is a far greater distinction between those things that appear distinct even when we think about both of them attentively—such as the mind and the body—than between those things where we can understand one <margin>15</margin> without thinking of the other, but nevertheless cannot see how one could exist without the other when we think of both together. For instance, the **immensity of God** <note>God's quality of being present everywhere and infinite.</note> can be understood ᵈ even if one does not pay attention to His <margin>20</margin> justice; but it is completely contradictory that, when we attend to both, we should think of Him as being immense and yet not also just. Similarly, the existence of God can be correctly known ᵉ, even if the persons of the <margin>598</margin> Holy Trinity are not known—since these can only be <margin>25</margin> perceived by a mind enlightened by faith; yet, once they have been perceived, I deny that there is a <term>real distinction</term> <note>A "real distinction" in Descartes' logic is a difference between two "substances" that can exist independently of each other, like a mind and a body.</note> between them...
