### EXCERPT OF THE KING'S PRIVILEGE

---

By the grace and Privilege of the most Christian King, it is permitted to the Author of the Book entitled, *Metaphysical Meditations on First Philosophy* <note>original: *Meditationes Metaphysicæ, de prima Philosophia*. This is the Latin title of Descartes' most famous work.</note>, to have his Works printed by such Printer and Bookseller, and in such place as shall seem good to him, within and outside the Kingdom of France, and this for the term of ten consecutive years, counting from the day that the printing is completed. During this time, no one other than the Bookseller he has chosen may print it, or cause it to be printed, in whole or in part, under any pretext or disguise whatsoever, nor sell or distribute any edition other than that which has been made with his permission, under penalty of a thousand <term>livres</term> <note>The *livre* was the currency of France until 1795.</note> fine, confiscation of all copies, and as is more fully declared by the Letters issued at Paris on the 4th day of May 1637. By the King, in his Council, CEBERET. And sealed with the great Seal of yellow wax, on a <term>simple tail</term> <note>original: *simple queuë*. This refers to a method of sealing a document where the wax seal is attached to a strip of the parchment or paper itself, rather than a separate cord.</note>.

Monsieur René Descartes has permitted Michel Soly, merchant Bookseller at Paris, to print the present Book, entitled, *Metaphysical Meditations on First Philosophy*, and to enjoy the Privilege for the time and under the conditions agreed upon between them. At Paris, August 2, 1641.

<margin>5</margin>You ask many things of me, <term>Most Distinguished Sir<note>original: "V(ir) C(lariſſime)", a traditional formal address used between scholars in the 17th century.</note></term>, concerning a new <margin>A</margin> method for investigating the truth, and you not only request but insistently urge that I respond to them. # SEVENTH OBJECTIONS.

### § 1. WHAT IS THE MINIMUM OF DOUBT?

As for doubt, what is this "Minimum"? You say you will not delay me with many words. That thing possesses some doubt about which I can wonder whether it exists or whether it is as it seems, <margin>5</margin> not rashly, but for powerful reasons. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, something possesses some doubt if, even though it appears clear to me, I can be deceived by some malicious Spirit <note>original: *Genio*. While often translated as "Evil Genius," it refers to a powerful, supernatural being capable of manipulating one's perceptions.</note> who wishes to mock me and, by his arts and tricks, ensure that what is actually false appears clear and certain. The <margin>10</margin> <margin>8</margin> first | kind has no small amount of doubt; the second has a little indeed—that very *minimum*—yet it is enough for it to be called and to be doubtful. Do you want an example? That there is an earth, a sky, colors; that you have a head, eyes, a body and a mind—these are doubts of the first kind <note>The "first kind" refers to sensory experiences which can be doubted through simple skepticism (e.g., dreaming or optical illusions).</note>. But of the second kind are these: 2 and 3 make 5; <margin>15</margin> *the whole is greater than its part; and the like.*

Excellent indeed. But if that is the case, what, I ask, will be that which has only a little doubt? What is immune from that fear which the crafty *Spirit* <margin>D</margin> holds over us? Nothing, you say, absolutely nothing, until <margin>20</margin> we have established that God exists and cannot deceive, based on the most certain and firm principles of *Metaphysics* <note>Metaphysics is the study of the fundamental nature of reality, existence, and knowledge.</note>, so that this becomes the *sole law* <note>original: *lex unica*</note>: while remaining ignorant of whether God exists, and if He exists, whether He can be a deceiver, it seems I can never be fully certain of anything else. And indeed, so that you may fully recognize my thought here: unless I know <margin>25</margin> that God exists, and is a truthful God who restrains that evil spirit, I will always be able and obliged to fear lest I be mocked, and that the false be thrust upon me under the guise of truth as if it were clear and certain. But once I have thoroughly understood that God exists, and that He can neither be deceived nor deceive, and therefore must necessarily prevent that *Spirit*...

<summary>Descartes distinguishes between ordinary doubts (like the existence of the physical world) and "minimum" doubts (like mathematical truths), arguing that nothing is certain until God's existence and truthfulness are established to counteract the possibility of a deceiving spirit.</summary>

### § 2. WHAT IS TO BE CONSIDERED FALSE?

*For the sake of argument, since it is doubtful whether you have eyes, a head,* <margin>10</margin> *a body, and you therefore ought to hold that as false, I would like to know from you what it is to "hold it as false." Is it to believe and say: "it is false that I have eyes, a head, a body"? Or is it to believe, and with the will turned entirely to the contrary, to say: "I do not have eyes, a head, a body"; or, to put it in a word,* <margin>E</margin> *to believe, say, and posit the opposite of that which is doubtful? This is the very thing, you say. Fine. But I would still like you to respond. It is not* <margin>15</margin> *certain that 2 and 3 make 5. Should I therefore believe and posit: 2 and 3 do not make 5? Believe it, you say, and posit it. I continue. It is not certain that I, while I speak these things, am awake and not dreaming. Should I therefore believe and say: thus while I speak, I am not awake, but I dream? Believe it, you say, and say it. I will also add this last thing, so that I am not* <margin>20</margin> *troublesome. It is not certain that what appears clear and certain to one doubting whether he is awake or asleep, is [truly] certain and clear. Should I therefore believe and say: that which appears clear and certain to one doubting whether he is awake or asleep, that is not clear and certain, but obscure and false? Why do you hesitate? More than is just,* <margin>25</margin> <margin>10</margin> *you cannot indulge your distrust. Has it never happened to you, as it has to so many, that things seemed certain and clear to a dreamer, which you later found to be doubtful or false? Surely it is a matter of prudence never to fully trust those who [have deceived you...]* <note>The sentence cuts off, but refers to the skeptical principle that if the senses or the mind have deceived us once, they are not to be fully trusted again.</note>

### § 3. TO WHAT EXTENT SHOULD IT BE HELD AS FALSE?

I ask you: since it does not seem certain that 2 and 3 make 5, and since according to the previous rule I ought to believe and say: "2 and 3 do not make 5," should I immediately believe it in such a way that I persuade myself it cannot be otherwise, <margin>5</margin> and that this is certain? You wonder at this question of mine. Nor is it a wonder to me, since I wonder at it myself. Nevertheless, it is necessary for you to respond if you expect a response from me. Do you want me to hold this as certain: *2 and 3 do not make 5*? Indeed, do you want this to be and to appear <margin>12</margin> certain to everyone, and | so certain that it is safe even from the tricks of an evil <margin>10</margin> Genius? <note>original: *mali Genii*. This refers to Descartes's famous "Evil Demon" thought experiment, a being capable of deceiving us about even the most basic mathematical truths.</note>

You laugh, and say: *How could such a thing enter the mind of a sane man?*

What then? Will it be doubtful and uncertain, just as this is: *2 and 3 make 5*? If this is so—if it is doubtful that "2 and 3 do not make 5"—I will believe, and according to your law I will say, that <margin>15</margin> it is false; and thus I will propose the contrary, and I will establish it thus: *2 and 3 make 5.* And I will conduct myself in the same way in other matters; and because it does not seem certain that there is any body <note>term: *corpus* (body). In 17th-century philosophy, this refers to physical, material matter.</note>, I will say: *There is no body*; and because it is not certain that "There is no body," I will say—with my will turned completely to the contrary— <margin>20</margin> *There is some body*; and at the same time it will both be a body, and not be a body.

That is how it is, you say; and that is what it means to doubt: to be carried in a circle, to come and go, to affirm and deny this and that, to drive a nail and then pull it out again. <note>original: *clavum figere & refigere*. A metaphor for making a decision and then immediately undoing it.</note>

Quite excellent. But, in order to use those things which will be <margin>25</margin> doubtful, what shall I do? What about this: *2 and 3 make 5*? And about that: *some body exists*? Shall I assume it? Or shall I deny it?

You will neither assume it, you say, nor will you deny it. You will use neither; you will hold both as if they were false, nor from those things which thus waver, will you [take] anything...

<summary>Father Bourdin satirizes Descartes’s method of radical doubt by showing how it leads to a logical circle: if we treat everything uncertain as false, we are forced to deny basic math and the existence of the physical world, only to potentially affirm them again when the denial itself becomes uncertain.</summary>

1. We can doubt all things, and especially material things, 
<margin>5</margin> as long as we have no other foundations for the sciences than those we have had until now.
2. To hold something as false is to withhold one's assent from it as if it were openly false, and, with the will turned completely in the opposite direction, to imagine one's opinion of it as false and imaginary.
3. To such an extent must that which is doubtful <insert>is</insert> be held as 
false, that its opposite is also doubtful and should be held as false <note>See the continuation, p. 462, l. 16, below.</note>.

But I only ask readers to recall to memory what I wrote in the 1st Meditation, and at the beginning of the 2nd and 3rd, as well as in their synopsis; <margin>20</margin> for they will recognize that almost everything here is indeed taken from there, but is presented in such a confused, distorted, and wrongly interpreted way that, although they contain nothing there that is not highly consistent with reason, here they appear for the most part utterly absurd.

It is as if the reasons we sometimes have for doubting a certain thing were not <margin>15</margin> legitimate and valid unless they proved that we must *always* doubt that same thing.

### REPLY.

*Reply 1. If that law—that in searching for the truth, whatever has even the slightest doubt must be considered false—is understood in this way: that when we investigate what is certain, we must not rely in any way on those things which are not certain, or which have something of doubt in them, it is a legitimate law, accepted by use, and most common among all philosophers.*

*Reply 2. If the said law is understood thus: that when we investigate what is certain, we must reject everything that is not certain, or is in some way doubtful, so that we do not use them in any manner, and thus we regard them as if they did not exist, or rather we do not look at them at all, but withdraw the mind entirely from them, it is also legitimate, safe, and even well-worn...*

**Reply 3.** If the aforementioned law <note>The "law" refers to the rule Bourdin claims Descartes is following: treating anything doubtful as if it were definitively false.</note> is understood in this way: that when we are searching for what is certain, we must reject all doubtful things so thoroughly that we assume they <margin>5</margin> do not exist in fact, or that their opposite is the actual truth, and then use that assumption as if it were a certain foundation, or rely on their non-existence—then such a law is illegitimate, fallacious, and at odds with sound Philosophy. It would be using something doubtful and uncertain as a means to discover what is true <margin>10</margin> and certain; it would be assuming as certain something that could be either one way or the other—for instance, assuming that doubtful things do not exist, when it is entirely possible that they do.

**Reply 4.** If anyone, interpreting that law in the manner just described, wished <margin>15</margin> to use it to discover the truth and what is certain, he would "lose both oil and labor" <note>original: "oleum & operam perderet"; a Latin idiom meaning to waste one's time and effort on a fruitless task.</note>; | he would be "turning the millstone without any grain to show for it," <margin>18</margin> as he would be no more likely to establish his goal than its exact opposite. Do you want an example? Someone is investigating whether he can be a body, or something corporeal, and among other things he employs this rule: "It is not certain <margin>20</margin> that any body exists; therefore, according to the law laid down, I will assume and say: *no body exists*." Then he will continue: "*No body exists; but I am and I exist, as I have well established from other sources; therefore, I cannot be a body.*" That seems excellent! But look at how he can derive the opposite from the very same starting point. "It is not certain," he says, <margin>25</margin> "that any body exists; therefore, according to the law, I will assume and say: *no body exists*." But what kind of statement is that: "*no body exists*"? It is surely doubtful and uncertain. Who can guarantee it? From where does it come? The matter is settled: that statement is doubtful—"*no body exists*"; therefore, according to the law, I shall say: "*some body exists*." <margin>30</margin> But I am and I exist; therefore, I can be a body, provided nothing else prevents it. Behold, I can be a body, and I cannot be a body. Have I...

<margin>20</margin> nent; but, because you expect an accurate answer, and since I cannot give it until I have first tested that method of yours with some use and practice, let us enter upon the worn and safe path, and let us explore for ourselves what is actually in it. And because 
<margin>23</margin> you know its twists, its paths, and its shortcuts, and 
<margin>25</margin> have exercised yourself in it for a long time, offer yourself as a guide to me. Come, speak: you have a ready companion or disciple. What do you command? I approach that journey willingly, even if it is new and formidable to me, unaccustomed as I am to the darkness, so powerfully does the appearance of truth allure me. I hear you: you command me to do what I see you doing; 
<margin>30</margin> I will fix my foot where you have fixed yours. Truly a fine way of commanding and leading. How you please me! I am listening.

### § 1. THE ENTRANCE TO THE METHOD IS OPENED.

In the beginning, *you say*, as I revolved old thoughts in my mind, I am at last compelled to confess that there is nothing of those things I once thought were true about which it is not permitted to doubt; and this is not through thoughtlessness or levity, but on account of valid and considered reasons. <margin>5</margin> Therefore, assent must be withheld from these same things, no less than from those things which are clearly false, if I wish to find anything certain <note>original: "si quid certi velim invenire"</note>.$^a$ Wherefore I shall not act badly if, by turning my will in the opposite direction, I deceive myself and, for a time, feign that those old opinions are entirely false and imaginary <margin>10</margin> until at last—as if the weights of my prejudices were equalized—no longer may any crooked habit twist my judgment away from the correct perception of things.$^b$ 
<margin>24</margin> I shall suppose, therefore, some Evil Spirit <note>original: "Genium aliquem malignum"; also translated as "Evil Genius" or "Evil Demon," this is Descartes's famous thought experiment about a powerful deceiver.</note>, who is at once supremely powerful and cunning, <margin>15</margin> who has put all his effort into deceiving me. I shall think that the heavens, the air, the earth, colors, shapes, sounds, and all external things are nothing but the illusions of dreams, by which he has laid traps for my credulity.$^c$ *I shall persuade myself that there is absolutely nothing in the world: no sky, <margin>20</margin> <margin>K</margin> no earth, no minds, no bodies—I say no minds, no bodies, etc.; let this be the goal <note>original: "meta"; literally the turning post in a race, signifying the limit or target.</note>, and the principal goal. I shall consider myself as having no hands, no eyes, no flesh, no blood, nor any sense, but falsely opining that I have all these things.* <margin>25</margin> *I shall remain stubbornly fixed in this meditation.*$^d$

I took it to mean "to know." For there is a contradiction between the words *I knew* and *they are doubtful*, which he undoubtedly failed to notice. Nor should this be attributed to malice: for otherwise he would not have touched upon it so lightly, but, pretending the error came from me, <margin>5</margin> he would have attacked it with many words.

<margin>K</margin>
*“I say there are no minds, no bodies.”* <note>original: "Aio nullas mentes, nulla corpora." Bourdin is quoting Descartes's initial stage of universal doubt to make him look absurd.</note> He says this so that, later on, he may quibble at great length because at the beginning—when I supposed that the nature of the mind was not yet sufficiently clear to me—I listed it among doubtful things. But later, <margin>30</margin> noticing that a thing which thinks cannot fail to exist, <margin>10</margin> and calling that thinking thing by the name of "mind," I said that the mind exists. It is as if I had forgotten that I previously denied the same thing when I took "mind" to be something unknown to me; and it is as if I had judged that those things which I then denied—because they were doubtful to me—must be denied forever, <margin>15</margin> as if it were impossible for them to be rendered evident and certain to me later. It should be noted that he everywhere considers doubt and certainty not as relations of our knowledge to objects, but as properties of the objects themselves which perpetually inhere in them, <margin>20</margin> to such an extent that those things which we once knew to be doubtful can never be made certain. This should be attributed only to his good nature, not to his malice. <note>Descartes uses "goodness" (bonitati) here with heavy irony, suggesting Bourdin is simple-minded rather than intentionally deceptive.</note>

<margin>L</margin>
*“All things?”* <note>original: "Omniane?" Bourdin is questioning whether Descartes's doubt really extends to every single piece of knowledge.</note> Here he quibbles over the word *all*, just as he did above <margin>24</margin> with the word *nothing*, quite pointlessly.

And because hardly anyone else ever perceives anything clearly before this renunciation <margin>34</margin> <note>the act of setting aside all previous opinions</note>, at least <margin>5</margin> not with that clarity required for <term>metaphysical certainty</term> <note>a level of certainty so absolute that no ground for doubt remains, even a far-fetched or "metaphysical" one</note>, this renunciation is therefore very useful for those who are capable of such clear knowledge and do not yet possess it; but as for our author <note>Father Bourdin</note>, as the matter reveals, I believe he should studiously avoid it.

<margin>V</margin>
*Is it true that "Thinking, being nourished, and sensing do not belong to the body at all, but to the mind <gloss>a</gloss>"?* He reports these words as if they were mine, and simultaneously as if they were so certain that they could be called into doubt by no one. Yet, nothing is more notable <margin>15</margin> in my *Meditations* than the fact that I attribute nutrition solely to the body, and not to the mind or that part of a human being which thinks. Thus, by this one point, it is clearly proved, first: that he does not understand them <note>the Meditations</note> in the least, even though he has undertaken to refute them; and that he is wrong in <margin>20</margin> claiming that in the second Meditation, speaking according to common opinion, I attributed nutrition to the soul; and second: that he himself takes many things as beyond doubt which should not be admitted without examination. But finally, here at the end, he concludes most truly that in all these things he has merely proven "the slenderness of his own wit" <gloss>b</gloss>. <note>Descartes is sarcastically agreeing with Bourdin's own self-deprecating closing remark.</note>

...that "patchwork" <note>original: "centonem." A "cento" was a poem made up of verses from other authors; here, it refers to Bourdin's mocking description of Descartes's philosophy as a jumble of borrowed or incoherent parts.</note> and so on? I will use a very familiar example here to explain the reasoning behind my actions to him, so that he might not misunderstand it in the future—or, at least, so he will no longer dare to pretend he does not understand it. If he happened to have a basket full of apples, <margin>5</margin> and he feared that some of those apples were rotten and wanted to remove them so they would not corrupt the rest, how would he go about it? Would he not, first of all, throw absolutely everything out of the basket? And then, examining each one in order, take back and <margin>10</margin> put back into the basket only those he recognized as not being spoiled, leaving the others behind? By this same reasoning, those who have never philosophized correctly have various opinions in their minds; since they began collecting these from childhood, they rightly fear that many of them <margin>15</margin> are not true. They try to separate these from the others, lest the mixture of the two makes all of them uncertain. They can do this by no better way than if <margin>39</margin> they reject them all, at once and together, as if they were uncertain or false. Then, examining each one in order, they take back only those they recognize to be true and indubitable. <margin>20</margin> And so, I was not wrong to reject everything at the beginning. Next, noticing that nothing was known by me more certainly or more evidently than that I, as a thinking thing, existed, I was not wrong to assert this first. And finally, I was not wrong to ask later who I had <margin>25</margin> once believed myself to be—not so that I might still believe all those same things about myself, but so that if I perceived any of them to be true, I might take them back; if any were false, I might reject them; and if any were uncertain, I might set them aside to be examined at another time. From this it is clear that our Author [Bourdin] ineptly calls this the *art of drawing* <note>original: "artem eliciendi certa ex incertis."</note> *certainties from uncertainties*, or, as he says below, the *method of dreaming*; <gloss>b</gloss>

<margin>Bb</margin>*So it is, you say*. Here, and in almost all other places, he <note>Descartes is referring to Father Bourdin</note> portrays me as

### | § 5. AN ATTEMPTED ENTRANCE INTO THE METHOD.

It is well, you say; the foundations have been successfully laid. I am, as long as I think. This is certain, this is unshakable. Next, I must build, and proceed cautiously, lest an evil Genius <note>A reference to Descartes's "Malin Génie," a hypothetical powerful deceiver who could manipulate one's senses and logic</note> 
<margin>Dd</margin> deceive me. I am. But what am I? No doubt something of those things I formerly believed myself to be. In truth, I used to believe I was a man: that a man has a body and a soul. Am I therefore a body? Or a mind? A body is extended <note>taking up physical space</note>, contained in a place, impenetrable, and visible. Is any of these things in me? Extension? How could it be in me, since there is none? I renounced this at the beginning. Can I be touched, or be seen? Even if I indeed think now that I am seen, and that I am touched by myself, nevertheless I am not seen, I am not touched.
<margin>Ee</margin> This is certain to me, ever since I renounced [the senses]. What then? I pay attention, I think, I turn it over and over; nothing occurs to me. I am tired of repeating the same things. I find nothing in me of those things which pertain to the body. I am not a body. Yet I am, and I know that I am; and while I know that I am, I know nothing that belongs to the body.
<margin>Ff</margin> Am I then a mind? What did I formerly believe belonged to the mind? Is any of those things in me? I used to think it was the mind's nature to think. But wait, I am thinking! I have found it, I have found it! <note>original: "Εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα"</note>
<margin>48</margin> I am, I think. I am, as long as I think; I am a | <term>thinking thing</term> <note>original: *res cogitans*</note>, I am a mind, an intellect, a reason. Behold that Method of mine, by which I have successfully moved forward. You, follow along, if you please.

O happy you, who from such great darkness have escaped into the light in nearly a single leap! But, I beg you, do not refuse a hand, so that you may steady one who wavers while I follow in your footsteps. I repeat those same things, but, according to my own small measure, a little more slowly. I am, I think. But what am I? Something of those things I formerly believed myself to be? But did I believe well? That is uncertain. *But what am I? No doubt something of those things I once thought I was.*<sup>a</sup> He attributes this to me, as he does countless other things, in his usual manner—without any appearance of truth.

<margin>5</margin>
<margin>Ee</margin>
*This is certain to me, ever since I renounced [those things].*<sup>b</sup> Here again he falsely attributes a claim to me. For I never concluded anything based on the fact that I had renounced them; rather, I explicitly gave a warning in these words: "But perhaps it happens that these very things which I suppose to be nothing, because they are unknown to me, do not in truth differ from that 'me' whom I know, etc."<sup>c</sup>

<margin>Ff</margin>
*Am I then a mind?*<sup>d</sup> It is also false that I asked whether I was a <term>mind</term> <note>original: "mens." Descartes uses "mind" specifically to mean the faculty of consciousness, rather than the "soul" (anima) which was often linked to physical life.</note>: for I had not yet explained what I understood by the name of "mind." Instead, I asked whether there was anything in me from those things that I previously attributed to the <term>soul</term> <note>original: "anima"</note> as I had described it. When I did not find in myself all the things I had referred to the soul, but only <term>thought</term> <note>original: "cogitatio"</note>, I did not say for that reason that I was a soul, but only a <margin>15</margin> **thinking thing**. To this thinking thing I gave the name of "mind," or "intellect," or "reason"—not so that I might signify something more by the name of "mind" than by the name of "thinking thing," and thereby cry out **"I have found it! I have found it!"** <note>original: "εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα" (heureka, heureka). This refers to Archimedes' famous exclamation upon making a discovery.</note>, as he most foolishly <margin>20</margin> mocks me here. On the contrary, I explicitly added: "those words were previously of unknown meaning to me"<sup>e</sup>; so that it cannot be <margin>52</margin> doubted that I understood precisely the same thing by them as by the name **thinking thing**. <margin>25</margin>

### § 6. THE ENTRY IS ATTEMPTED AGAIN.

"It pleases me," you say, "as long as I tread closely in my footsteps."
<margin>5</margin> I obey, nor do I depart from you by even a fingernail's breadth. Resume.
"I think," <note>original: "Cogito"</note> you say.
I also.
"I am," you add, "while I think."
<margin>10</margin> I am equally myself, while I think.
"But what am I?" you set down.
O wisely! For this I ask, and with you I say willingly: but what am I?
You continue: "Who did I formerly <note>original: "olim"</note> believe myself to be? What sense of myself
<margin>15</margin> did I formerly have?"
Do not, I pray, repeat the words; I hear them enough. But ah, I pray, help. Where I may set my foot in such darkness, I do not see.
"Say," you say, "with me; track with me. What indeed did I formerly
<margin>20</margin> believe myself to be?"
Formerly? Was there a "formerly"? Did I "formerly" believe?
"You err," you add.
Nay, you yourself err, if you allow it, while you bring in that "formerly." I have
<margin>25</margin> renounced all old things; even that "formerly" was nothing, is nothing.
But you, kind leader! How you grasp my hand, how you <margin>54</margin> pull me!
"I think," you say, "I am." <note>original: "Cogito, ais, sum." This is a parody of the famous Cogito, ergo sum.</note>
It is so. I think, I am. This I have, and I have but one; and besides that one, there is nothing, there was nothing.

"Well done," you add; "what did you formerly believe about yourself?" <note>original: "Euge, addis ; quid de te olim credidiſti?"</note>
You wish, I suppose, to test me, to see whether I have spent fifteen days or an entire month in that apprenticeship of renunciation <note>original: "tyrocinio illo abdicationis"; referring to the period of time Descartes suggests one should spend doubting everything</note>; indeed, I have spent only an hour here with you, but certainly with such a great straining
<margin>5</margin> of the mind that the intensity of the operation compensates for the extension of time: I have spent a month, and, if you wish, a year. Look, I think, I am. <note>original: "En cogito, ſum."</note>
Nothing else exists. I have renounced everything.
But "remember," you say, "recall."
What is this "remember"? I am thinking now,
<margin>10</margin> that I formerly thought; but did I formerly think continuously, just because I might now think that I formerly thought?
"You are fearful," you say. "You fear a shadow. Resume." I think.
O unhappy me! The darkness intensifies, and that "I think,"
<margin>Kk 15</margin> which appeared clear to me before, I no longer notice. I dream that I think, I do not think.
On the contrary, you say, he who dreams, thinks.
Light dawns. To dream is to think, and to think is to dream.
<margin>55 Kk</margin> Nowhere, you say, does "to think" extend more widely than "to dream." <note>Bourdin is questioning the boundaries of Descartes's definition of thought.</note>
He who dreams, thinks; but he who thinks does not continuously
<margin>20</margin> dream, but thinks while waking.
Is it really so? But are you dreaming that? Or are you truly thinking it?

There is nothing; you do not exist, you do not think, you are not conscious of yourself. Behold the obstacle <note>original: "remora"; literally a sucking-fish once believed to be able to stop a ship's progress, here used to describe a logical hindrance.</note> which I place before your eyes, so that you may know it well and avoid it. If this proposition—"There is nothing"—is true, then this one is also true and necessary: "You do not exist, you do not think."*
*But the statement "There is nothing" is true, just as you wish it to be. Therefore, that other statement is also true: "You do not exist, you do not think."*
*"This rigor is too much," you say. "It must be softened a little."*
<margin>15</margin> *Because you ask, I shall do so, and willingly. You exist: I permit it. You think: I grant it. You are a <term>thinking thing</term> <note>Latin: "res cogitans"; Descartes' famous definition of the soul or mind as something whose essence is thought.</note>; add "thinking substance," since you delight so much in such magnificent words. I rejoice for you, I congratulate you; but let us go no further. Yet you insist, and thus you gather your final breaths:*
*"I am," you say, "a <term>thinking substance</term> <note>Latin: "substantia cogitans"; a philosophical term for an independent entity that performs the act of thinking.</note>, and I know that I exist as a thinking substance, and I know that a thinking substance exists, and I have a clear and distinct concept of that thinking substance; and yet I do not know that a body <note>Latin: "corpus"</note> exists, I know nothing of those things that belong to the concept of a <term>bodily substance</term> <note>Latin: "substantia corporea"; the physical matter that occupies space, which Descartes distinguishes from the mind.</note>; indeed, body does not exist, nor any bodily thing, for I have renounced everything. Therefore, the knowledge of the existence of a thinking thing (or the thing itself) does not depend on the knowledge of the existence of a body (or the body itself). Therefore, since I exist, and I exist as a thinking substance, and the body does not exist, I am not a body. Therefore, I am a <term>mind</term> <note>Latin: "mens"</note>. These are the points—these!—which compel me to assent, since there is nothing in them that is not coherent, and they are concluded from evident principles according to the rules of Logic."*

*Heavens! <note>original: "Papæ!" an exclamation of surprise or ironic wonder.</note> How subtle and sharp you are! How in a moment you penetrate and pervade all things—those that are and those that are not, and those that can be and those that cannot! *distinct concept of a mountain without a valley? But because I do not know your art, I marvel at this new development. Open up, I pray, and*
<margin>10</margin> *show me what that clear and distinct concept is.*

*It is ready at hand, you say. I clearly and distinctly conceive that a thinking substance exists, and I conceive of nothing corporeal, nothing spiritual, <note>Bourdin is likely distinguishing between "spiritual" as a general category and the specific "thinking substance."</note> nothing else besides, but only a thinking substance.*
<margin>15</margin> *Therefore, that concept of mine of a thinking substance is clear and distinct.*

*I hear you at last, and, unless I am mistaken, I understand. That concept of yours is clear because you know it with certainty; it is distinct because you know nothing else. Have I hit the mark? <note>original: "An rem digito attigi?"—literally, "Have I touched the thing with a finger?"</note> I think so. For*
<margin>20</margin> *you add:*

*Quite abundantly; and if I have clearly grasped your mind, the clear and distinct concept of a thinking substance which you form consists in this: that it represents to you that a thinking substance exists,*
<margin>25</margin> *while paying no attention to the body, to the soul, <note>original: "animum"</note> to the mind, <note>original: "mentem"</note> or to anything else, but only to the fact that it exists. And so you say that you, in so far as you know yourself, are nothing other than a thinking substance, not indeed a body, not a soul, not a mind,*
<margin>30</margin> *not anything else: so much so that, if you existed exactly <note>original: "accurate"</note> as you know yourself, you would be only a thinking substance, and nothing more. I think you both smile and applaud yourself, and you think that me by a long...*

I shall proceed. *I am a thinking thing <note>original: "Sum res cogitans." Wherefore to your question, "*Whether it is a good Method of philosophizing by way of the renunciation of all doubts*" <note>original Latin: "An sit bona Methodus philosophandi per abdicationem dubiorum omnium"</note>, I respond, as you expect, frankly, freely, and without a cloak of words.

### NOTES.

<margin>5</margin> Up to this point, the Reverend Father <note>The Latin "R. P." stands for *Reverendus Pater*, referring to the Jesuit Pierre Bourdin.</note> has been jesting; and because in what follows he seems to wish to act seriously and take on quite another persona, I will briefly set down here what I have observed in these jests.

<margin>10</margin> These words of his: *Once upon a time? Was there an "once upon a time"?* and, *I dream that I think, I do not think*, and the like, are jokes entirely worthy of the persona he has assumed. So too is his grave question: <margin>76</margin> *Whether thinking extends more widely than dreaming?* <note>Bourdin is mockingly asking if there is any real difference between Descartes' "clear and distinct" thoughts and a dream.</note> and that clever saying, *Regarding the Method of dreaming*, and, *So that one may reason well, let him dream.* But I do not think I have given the <margin>15</margin> slightest occasion for these, because I expressly indicated that when I spoke of things renounced <note>Descartes refers to the "renunciation" or setting aside of beliefs during his process of radical doubt.</note>, I was not asserting that they *were* so, but only that they *seemed* so; to the extent that, by asking what I once thought myself to be, I was only asking what it then seemed to me that I had once thought. And <margin>20</margin> while I said that I was thinking, I did not inquire whether I was thinking while awake or while dreaming. And I am surprised that he calls this a "Method of dreaming," since he seems to have been not a little awakened by it.

# WORKS OF DESCARTES
## Pp

He fashioned [this battle] out of **Nothing** <note>original: *Nihilo*</note>. But in all seriousness, he fights against it, argues, breaks a sweat, calls Logic to his aid, renews the battle, examines every detail, weighs, and balances them <gloss>a</gloss>. And because he does not dare to meet the blows of so powerful an opponent with his shield, he dodges them with his body, making distinctions, and <margin>5</margin> <margin>79</margin> finally escapes by fleeing through the detours of *determinately* and *indeterminately* <gloss>b</gloss>. Truly, the spectacle of this affair is most entertaining; especially if one understands the cause of such a great disagreement.

Namely, it seems he happened to read in my writings that if we hold any true opinions before we begin to philosophize seriously, <margin>10</margin> they are so mixed with many others—either false or at least doubtful—that, in order to separate the true from the false, it is best to reject them all at the beginning; or rather, to renounce every single one of them <note>original: *nihil plane ex iis non abdicare*; literally "to renounce nothing not from them," a double negative meaning to discard everything</note>, so that later those that were true may be more conveniently <margin>15</margin> recognized, or new ones found, and only the true ones admitted.

This is exactly the same as if I had said that, to prevent any rotten apples from being kept in a basket or crate full of fruit, <margin>20</margin> one must first pour everything out and leave absolutely nothing in it, and then either take back only those in which no flaw is found, or take up others from elsewhere. But he, not grasping a matter of such high speculation—or certainly, as is his way, pretending not to grasp it—wondered especially at the statement that "Nothing is not to be renounced"; and by thinking long and hard about that *Nothing*, he fixed it so firmly in his brain that <margin>25</margin> although he now frequently does battle with it, he cannot easily free himself from it.

After such a successful battle, elated by the prospect of victory, he challenges a new enemy, whom he again thinks...

<page-num>514</page-num>
# WORKS OF DESCARTES.

The method of seeking truth <note>original: *Methodum quærendæ veritatis*</note>, which commands us to begin from the knowledge of our own existence after rejecting all uncertainties, and then to proceed to the examination of our nature (or of that thing which we already know to exist), he attempts to prove allows no access to further knowledge. He uses this reasoning: *Since you only know that you are, but not who you are <note>original: *tantùm te esse, non autem quis sis*</note>, you cannot learn this from what you formerly knew, since you have renounced everything; therefore, you must learn it from what you do not yet know.* 

<margin>10</margin> To this, even a three-year-old child could respond that nothing prevents one from learning from what they formerly knew. For even if those things had been renounced while they were doubtful, they could nevertheless be taken up again later, once it was established that they were true. Furthermore, even if it were granted that nothing could be learned from things previously known, at least the other path—through those things which one did not yet know but was going to discover through study and observation <note>original: *animadversione*</note>—remains entirely open. 

<margin>15</margin> But our friend here <note>Referring to Bourdin</note> invents an opponent for himself who not only concedes that the first path is closed, but who also closes the second path himself with this little phrase: *I do not know that those things exist.* 

<margin>20</margin> It is as if no new knowledge of existence could ever be acquired, and as if ignorance of a thing's existence would prevent all knowledge of its essence <note>In philosophy, "essence" refers to what a thing is, while "existence" refers to the fact that it is</note>. This is truly as absurd as can be <note>original: *insulsum*, literally "unsalted" or "witless"</note>. 

<margin>82</margin> But clearly, he is alluding to my own words; for I wrote that it is impossible for the knowledge I already have of a thing I know to exist to depend on the knowledge of that which I do not yet know to exist^a. 

<margin>25</margin> And this, which I only said concerning the present, he ridiculously transfers to the future. It is the same as if—because we cannot now see those who are not yet born, but will be born this year—he were to conclude that we can *never* see them. For surely...

It is clear that the knowledge one already possesses of a thing known to exist <note>original: *rei, quæ cognoscitur ut existens*</note> does not depend on the knowledge of that which is not yet known to exist. This is because by the very fact that something is perceived as belonging to an existing 
<margin>5</margin> thing, it is necessarily also perceived to exist. But it is quite a different matter regarding the future, because nothing prevents the knowledge of a thing which I know to exist from being increased by other things which I do not yet know to exist, but which I will eventually learn when I 
<margin>10</margin> perceive that they pertain to that thing. Indeed, he <note>Bourdin</note> continues, saying: *Hope for the best; you will know eventually* <sup>a</sup>; and then: *I will not let you remain in doubt for long.* By these words, he bids us expect from him either a demonstration that no further knowledge can be reached through the proposed path, or certainly, if he 
<margin>15</margin> supposes that path to be closed by his adversary (which would, however, be foolish), that he might open some other path. But he only adds: 
<margin>83</margin> *You know who you are indeterminately and confusedly, but not determinately and clearly.* From these words, nothing is more obvious 
<margin>20</margin> than for us to conclude that the way is therefore open to further knowledge, because by meditating and paying attention <note>original: *meditando & advertendo*</note>, we can bring it about that what we previously knew only indeterminately and confusedly, we may afterwards perceive clearly and determinately. But he nonetheless concludes that the words 
<margin>25</margin> *Determinate* and *indeterminate* are a "sea urchin" <note>original: *echinum*; here used metaphorically to mean a prickly or thorny obstacle intended to stall progress</note> that could *delay us for an age*, and therefore another path must be sought. In all of this, it seems to me that nothing more fitting could have been devised by him to simulate the utter absurdity and weakness of his own intellect.

First of all, I deny that he complains with justice, as if I had said that I possess a clear and distinct concept of myself before I had sufficiently explained how it is obtained—and when, as he says, I had hardly *a hundred paces before asked who I was* <note>original: "paſſus centum quæſiviſſem quis eſſem"</note><sup>a</sup>. For, between those two points, I reviewed all the properties of a **thinking thing** <note>original: "rei cogitantis"; in Descartes' system, this refers to the mind or soul as a substance whose essence is thought</note>, namely that it understands, wills, imagines, remembers, feels, etc.; and likewise all other properties commonly known that do <margin>86</margin> not | pertain to its concept, so that I might distinguish the one <margin>10</margin> from the other—which was the only thing that could be hoped for once prejudices were removed. But I confess that those who do not strip off their prejudices cannot easily ever have a clear and distinct concept of anything: for it is manifest that those concepts which we had in childhood were not clear and distinct; and <margin>15</margin> consequently, unless they are set aside, any other concepts we later acquire are rendered obscure and confused by them. Therefore, when he wants that clear and distinct concept to be shown to him so that he may be *refreshed by the sight of it*<sup>b</sup>, he is talking nonsense; just as he does when he introduces me showing it to him in <margin>20</margin> these words: *I know for certain that I am, etc.*<sup>c</sup>. When, however, he wishes to refute that very nonsense with this example: *You also know for certain that no mountain exists without a valley; therefore you have a clear and distinct concept of a mountain without a valley*<sup>d</sup>, he deceives himself with a **sophism** <note>A clever but false argument, often used to deceive</note>. For from the premises it only follows: *Therefore <margin>25</margin> you clearly and distinctly perceive that no mountain exists without a valley*, but not: *You have a concept of a mountain without a valley*, because, since there is no such thing, it ought not to be had in order for one to perceive that no mountain is without a valley. But indeed he is so...

<margin>25</margin> smallest word from which such **trifles** <term>affaniae; nonsense or idle talk</term> could be deduced.

<sig>66</sig>

...to persuade others that, although he has nothing good to say, he is nevertheless thinking of something good.

Another of his sayings: *What concludes too much, <margin>89</margin> concludes nothing*<sup>a</sup>, should not be accepted without a distinction. <margin>5</margin> For if by the word "too much" he understands only something more than what was being sought—as when below<sup>b</sup> he criticizes the arguments by which I demonstrated the existence of God <term>the philosophical proof for the being of God</term>, because he thinks that more is concluded by them than the laws of prudence <term>practical wisdom or logic</term> require, or than any mortal demands—<margin>10</margin> this is plainly false and foolish. This is because the more that is concluded, provided it is concluded correctly, the better it is; nor can any laws of prudence ever be opposed to this. If, however, he understands by the word "too much" not simply something more than was sought, but something <margin>15</margin> that is beyond controversy false, then indeed it is true; but the Reverend Father <note>original: "R. P."; abbreviation for *Reverendus Pater*, referring to Father Bourdin</note> is plainly mistaken when he tries to attribute such a thing to me. For when I wrote as follows: 

> "The knowledge of those things
> which I know to exist does not depend on the knowledge of those things which
> I do not yet know to exist; but I know that a thinking thing <term>Latin: "rem cogitantem"; the mind or soul as a conscious entity</term>
<margin>20</margin> > exists, and I do not yet know that a body <term>Latin: "corpus"; physical matter</term> exists; therefore, the

<margin>97</margin> | Response 2. *The <term>Method</term> <note>Referring to the method of doubt established in Descartes' Meditations.</note> errs regarding the means. Namely, it has none, while it removes the old ones and does not apply new ones. <margin>5</margin> The other disciplines have logical forms, syllogisms, and certain modes of argument, by whose guidance, like <term>Ariadne’s thread</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth; here, it refers to logical rules that prevent a thinker from getting lost.</note>, they free themselves from labyrinths and extricate involved matters easily and safely. Propose a <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal).</note>. "What if I am dreaming? How often have things seemed certain and clear to a <margin>15</margin> dreamer, which after the dream were found to be false?" What, finally, will it do regarding the conclusion? It will flee everything entirely as if they were snares and traps. Do not the raving, children, and the insane believe themselves to be reasoning excellently, when they are lacking in all mind and judgment? ...<term>paralogisms</term> <note>original: *paralogismos*; these are fallacious or illogical arguments, specifically those where the speaker is unaware of the error.</note>. <margin>5</margin> Response 3. The <term>Method</term> <note>Descartes' systematic process of doubt and discovery.</note> sins against its own goal, for it achieves nothing certain. Indeed, it cannot achieve anything, since it closes off all paths to the truth against itself. You yourself have seen and experienced this in your "Ulyssean" errors <note>original: *erroribus Ulysseis*; a reference to the long, wandering journey of Ulysses (Odysseus) in the *Odyssey*, implying Descartes' reasoning is a long, winding path of mistakes.</note>, with which you have exhausted both yourself and me as your companion. You contended that you were a mind, or had a mind: <margin>10</margin> but you could by no means prove this; instead, you got stuck in the ruts and briars, and indeed so often that I can hardly remember them all. Although it will be helpful to recall them now, simply so that this response of ours may have its proper strength. Here, then, are the main points by which the Method itself cuts its own hamstrings <margin>99</margin> <margin>14</margin> and completely shuts off any hope of reaching the light of truth:

1. You do not know whether you are dreaming or awake; therefore, you ought to place no more weight on your thoughts and reasonings (if indeed you have any, and do not merely dream that you have them) than a dreamer does on his own. Hence all things are doubtful and wavering, and the <margin>20</margin> conclusions themselves are uncertain. I will not bring forward examples; go yourself and run through the storerooms of your memory, and if you find anything that is not infected by that flaw, bring it forth: I will congratulate you.

2. Before I know that God exists, who may bind the <term>Evil Spirit</term> <note>original: *Genium malum*; Descartes' hypothetical "Malicious Demon" who might deceive us about everything we perceive.</note>, I must doubt everything, and hold every single proposition to be <margin>25</margin> suspect; or surely—as is common philosophy and the old method of reasoning—one must define before all else whether there are any such immune propositions, and what they are, and the <term>apprentices</term> <note>original: *tyrones*; beginners or students of philosophy.</note> must be warned about retaining them. Hence, just as with the preceding point, all things remain doubtful and are completely <margin>30</margin> useless for tracking down the truth.

3. If there is anything that has even the least bit of doubt, that—with the will turned completely to the contrary—is [regarded as] false...

<margin>100</margin> *...believe [that it is], and believe the opposite, and use that as a principle. From here, all approaches to truth are closed off. For what can you hope from a person [who says]: "I have no head; there is no body, <margin>5</margin> no mind," and six hundred statements of that sort? And do not say that this rejection [of certainty] is not perpetual, but rather like a legal stay of proceedings* <note>original: *justitii*; a Roman legal term for a temporary suspension of public business, here used to mean a temporary suspension of belief.</note>, *for a time—for a month, or for fifteen days—depending on how much effort one applies to the task. Why should I not imitate them?* <note>Descartes often used the analogy of scaffolding to explain why he temporarily doubted everything: it was a tool to build something permanent.</note> *Imitate them, by all means; but see to it that neither the pedestal nor the column rely on that temporary machine in such a way that if it were removed, they would collapse. And that is what I think is worthy of blame in the Method. It lays down false foundations and leans on them so much that, once <margin>20</margin> they are removed, the structure itself must also be taken away.*

*Response 4. The Method sins by excess. That is, it attempts more than the laws of prudence require of it, and more than any mortal asks of it. Some do indeed ask that the existence of God and the immortality of the human soul be demonstrated to them; <margin>101 25</margin> but certainly, no one has been found until now who did not consider it sufficient to know that God exists, that the world is governed by Him, and that human souls are spiritual and immortal, just as surely as knowing that 2 and 3 make 5, or that "I have a head" and "I have a body"—to the point that any <margin>30</margin> concern for seeking some greater certainty would be superfluous. Furthermore,*

->### SEVENTH OBJECTIONS.<-

Just as in practical or active affairs there are certain limits of certainty which are abundantly sufficient for any person to conduct themselves prudently and safely; so too, in matters of meditation and speculation, there are defined limits. He who reaches them is certain—and so certain that, quite rightly, <margin>5</margin> while others are either despaired of or condemned for wanting to attempt anything further, he may rest there prudently and securely: *No further* <note>original: "Ne plus ultra"</note>, *Nothing in excess* <note>original: "Ne quid nimis"; a famous ancient Greek maxim often attributed to Solon.</note>. But, you say, this is no ordinary praise: to push back the boundaries, and to cross a ford untried by all past centuries. Indeed, that would be distinguished praise, provided the ford can be waded <margin>10</margin> without a shipwreck. Therefore:

**Response 5.** This method sins by deficiency. That is, while it tightens the requirements more than is fair, it gathers nothing. I want you to be the witness, you to be the judge. What have you provided with that magnificent apparatus of yours? What did you gain by that renunciation—so solemn, so general, and so generous that you <margin>15</margin> did not even spare yourself—except for this well-worn phrase: *I think, I am, I am a thinking thing*? This, I say, is so familiar even to the common people <margin>102</margin> that | since the world was founded, no one has been found who has even slightly doubted it, let alone someone who seriously demanded it be proven to them: that they are, that they exist, that they think, that they are a thinking thing. Quite rightly, <margin>20</margin> no one is going to give you any thanks for this, unless perhaps—as I do out of my friendship and singular goodwill toward you—they might approve of your extensive goodwill toward the human race and praise the effort.

**Response 6.** This method commits a common sin, which it rebukes in others. Specifically, it wonders why all mortals say and <margin>25</margin> posit these things so confidently: "I have a head, I have eyes," etc. And yet, the method does not wonder at itself when, with equal confidence, it says: "I do not have a head," etc.

**Response 7.** This method commits a sin peculiar to itself. Specifically, while other men hold some things to be certain, and <margin>30</margin> sufficiently so—"I have a head, there is a body, there is a mind"—this method, through a singular <term>certitude</term> <note>Bourdin is using "certitude" ironically here to describe Descartes' extreme standard of proof.</note>

<summary>Father Bourdin mocks Descartes' "I think, therefore I am" conclusion, arguing that such a discovery is trivial and that Descartes' method of doubting the existence of his own body is just as groundless as the common belief in it.</summary>

...to himself as a goal, the very opposite: "I have no head, there is no body, no mind." He posits this not only as certain, but so certain that an accurate *Metaphysics* <term>Metaphysics: The branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, and cause.</term> can be founded upon it; and he leans upon it to such an extent that, if you were to remove this prop, he would fall flat on his face. <margin>5</margin>

**Response 8. He sins unwittingly.** <note>original: "Peccat imprudens"</note> That is, by not noticing that doubt is a double-edged sword: while he flees one edge, he is wounded by the other. It is a matter of doubt for him "whether any body <margin>103</margin> | exists"; because it is doubtful, he removes it and posits the opposite: <margin>10</margin> "no body exists." And while he unwittingly leans on this doubt as if it were certain, he is wounded.

**Response 9. He sins knowingly** <note>original: "Peccat prudens"</note>, when, despite being warned, he consciously blinds himself. By a voluntary abandonment of those things necessary for tracking down the truth, he allows himself to be deluded by his own *Analysis*. He ends up achieving not only what he did <insert>not</insert> <note>The word "not" was added by later editors to make sense of the passage; see p. 552, l. 23.</note> intend, but even <margin>15</margin> that which he most dreads.

**Response 10. He sins by commission**, when he returns to his old ways despite his own solemn decree. Contrary to his laws of renunciation, he repeats what was renounced. You remember this well enough.

**Response 11. He sins by omission**, when he oversteps—not just once—the rule he prescribed <margin>20</margin> as a foundation: **We must take the greatest care not to admit anything as true that we cannot prove to be true.** He assumes, without proof, that the following are most certain and true: **the senses sometimes deceive us; we all dream; some <margin>25</margin> people are delirious**, and other such things.

**Response 12. The Method** <note>original: "Methodus"</note> has either nothing good in it, or nothing new, and indeed a great deal that is superfluous.

# SEVENTH OBJECTIONS.

<sig>69</sig>
**WORKS. II.**

...here, then, are the main points by which that art <note>Bourdin is referring to Descartes's "Method."</note> cuts its own hamstrings <note>original: *nervos succidit* — a Latin idiom meaning to weaken or disable something fundamentally</note>, and completely closes off every hope of moving the work forward.

1. You do not know whether there is sand or rock beneath the surface of the earth, and so you should trust the rock no more (if you ever actually stand upon any
<margin>5</margin> rock) than the sand. From this, everything is doubtful and wavering, and the structures themselves are weak. I will not bring forward examples; go yourself and run through the storerooms of your memory, and if you find anything that is not infected by this blemish, bring it forth: I will congratulate you. 

2. Before I find firm ground, beneath which I know there is no shifting 
<margin>10</margin> sand and no spirits <note>original: *Lemures* — in Roman mythology, these were restless or malevolent ghosts of the dead; Bourdin uses the term to mock Descartes's concern about deceptive demons or unknown forces</note> moving it about, I must reject everything and hold all material whatsoever as suspect; or surely, in what is the common and old Architecture, it must be defined above all whether there are, and which they are, those materials that are ultimately not to be rejected, and the ditch-diggers must be warned about retaining them in the 
<margin>15</margin> trench. From this, just as from the preceding, everything is weak and entirely useless for the construction of buildings. 

3. If there is anything that can be shaken in the slightest, believe it—with your will turned completely to the contrary—to have already collapsed; believe it must be dug out, and use the empty trench as a 
<margin>20</margin> foundation. From this, all approaches to building are
<margin>120</margin> blocked. For what could you hope from someone who says: | "There is no earth here now, no sand, no stones," and six hundred <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: *sexcentis* — in Latin, "six hundred" was often used to mean an indefinitely large number, similar to "a million" or "countless" today</note> such things? Nor indeed should you say that this digging is not perpetual, but, like a legal stay of proceedings <note>original: *justitii* — a period when public business or legal actions were suspended</note>, lasts for a time and reaches 
<margin>25</margin> a certain depth, just as the sand is deeper in some places. For let it be for a time; yet it is at that time when you think you are building, when you are using the emptiness of the trench—and abusing it, as if the whole building depends on it and consists in it, as if necessarily in a solid foundation <term>stereomate</term> <note>From the Greek *stereoma*, meaning a solid body or firmament; here used for a structural base.</note>. 
<margin>30</margin> But, you say, I use it as a pedestal <term>stylobatam</term> <note>The top step of the masonry platform upon which columns are placed in classical architecture.</note> and a stable column, as is customary for other Architects. Do those men not...

<margin>124</margin> chiefly those who demand that the **existence of God** and the **immortality of the human soul**
<margin>5</margin> be demonstrated to them. So much so that the things said here by our Author <note>Father Pierre Bourdin, the Jesuit critic whose objections Descartes is answering.</note> are of a very bad example, especially since he is known as a learned man: for they show that he himself does not think the errors of Atheists and Skeptics can be refuted; and thus, as much as he is able, he
<margin>10</margin> supports and confirms them. For indeed, all modern Skeptics do not doubt in practice whether they have a head, or whether 2 and 3 make 5, and such things; but they say they only use them as if they were true, because they appear so, but they do not certainly believe them, because they are driven to it by no **certain reasons**.
<margin>15</margin> And because it does not appear to them in the same way that God exists, and that the human mind is immortal, they think they should not use these as true even in practice, unless they have first been proven to them by reasons more certain than any of those for which they embrace all appearances.
<margin>20</margin> Since these things have been so proven by me, and by no one before me (at least that I know of), it seems to me that no greater or more unworthy slander could be imagined than that of our Author, when in this entire **Dissertation** of his, he continuously attributes to me and repeats six hundred times that one error in which the
<margin>25</margin> sect of Skeptics consists—namely, **excessive doubting**. And he is indeed generous in listing my "sins"; for although he says here that it is no ordinary praise to <term>advance the boundaries</term> <note>original: *metas promovere*; to extend the limits of human knowledge.</note> and to <term>cross a ford</term> <note>original: *vadum... pervadere*; a metaphor for successfully navigating a difficult intellectual passage where others have previously been stuck.</note> unattempted by all ages pastᵃ,
<margin>30 125</margin> and he has no reason to suspect that this [is being done] by me...

<header>Seventh Objections.</header>

-># Seventh Objections <-

"The rock, which is found beneath all the sand, is solid and firm"? <note>original: "Saxum, quod invenitur infra omnem arenam, est solidum & firmum"</note> This, I say, is so familiar even to the common people, etc., as stated above.<sup>a</sup>

<margin>5</margin>
And here I was expecting, both from the Mason <note>Descartes refers to Bourdin’s metaphorical character who represents the traditional, uncritical thinker.</note> and from our Author, that something would be proved. But, just as that Mason asked only what the Architect <note>Representing Descartes himself.</note> had accomplished by his digging, except that he had uncovered the rock—while pretending that he had built his own chapel upon that very rock—so our Author asks only what I have achieved by the rejection of doubts, except for this hackneyed phrase: ***I think, I am*** <note>original: "Cogito, sum." This is the core of Descartes's philosophy: that the act of doubting or thinking proves one's own existence.</note>. He clearly considers it of no value that from these foundations I have demonstrated both the existence of **God** and many other things. 
<margin>10</margin>
Moreover, he wants me to be the sole witness to his remarkable audacity; as he says elsewhere regarding other things that are also untrue: *Every single person believes this. Every pulpit rings with it. He received it from his teachers, and they from others, all the way back to Adam*<sup>b</sup>, and such things. 
<margin>15</margin>
No more faith is due to these claims than to the oaths of certain men, who are accustomed to use them more frequently the more they believe that what they wish to persuade others of is incredible and false. 

<margin>20</margin>
The other person <note>The "Mason" in Bourdin's dialogue.</note> responded in the sixth place: *He commits the common sin, which he finds fault with in others.* <note>original: "Peccat commune peccatum, quod in cæteris arguit."</note> Truly, he wonders that all mortals assert these things so confidently: “*The sand that supports us is firm enough. This alone on which we stand does not move, etc.*”; yet he does not wonder at himself <margin>25</margin> when he says with equal confidence: “*The sand must be rejected, etc.*”<sup>c</sup>

This was no more foolish than what our Author asserts in a similar matter.

He responded in the seventh place: *He commits a sin peculiar to himself.* Truly...

<meta>This page continues the "Seventh Objections," where René Descartes responds to the criticisms of Father Pierre Bourdin. <header>WORKS OF DESCARTES.</header>

What other men hold to be somewhat firm and sufficient—the very earth we stand on, the sand, the stones—this "rule" of his, by a peculiar plan of her own, adopts the opposite: namely, a trench from which the sand, stones, and the rest have been removed. She treats this trench not only as something firm, but as so firm that a most solid chapel <note>original: "sacellum"; Bourdin uses the image of a small chapel to represent a philosophical system built on Descartes's foundations.</note> can be founded within it. She relies on it to such an extent that if you were to remove this support, she would fall flat on her face<sup>a</sup>.

In this, she is no more delusional than our Author <note>Descartes is referring to Father Bourdin here.</note>, while he remains unmindful of his own words: *You shall neither assert nor deny, etc.* <note>original: "Nec pones, nec negabis." This was Bourdin's rule for total skepticism, which Descartes argues Bourdin himself fails to follow.</note>

<margin>128</margin>
He replied in the eighth point: *The imprudent man sins. Truly, he does not notice that the instability of the soil is a two-edged sword: while he flees one edge, he is wounded by the other. Sand is not stable enough for him; therefore<sup>b</sup> he removes it and replaces it with its opposite—namely, a trench empty of sand—and while the imprudent man leans on this trench as if it were a firm thing, he is wounded.*<sup>c</sup>

Here again, one only needs to remember those words: *You shall neither assert nor deny.* And this talk of a sword is more worthy of the wisdom of a Mason than of our Author.

He replied in the ninth point: *The prudent man sins when, knowingly and willingly and despite warnings, he blinds himself; through a voluntary rejection of those things that are necessary for building houses, he allows himself to be deluded by his own rule, achieving not only what he did not intend, but even that which he most dreads.*<sup>d</sup>

How true this might be of the Architect and the construction of his chapel, and how similarly true it is of me, the things I have demonstrated make clear.

### SEVENTH OBJECTIONS.
<note>original: "OBJECTIONES SEPTIMÆ"</note>

ŒUVRES. II. 70

He replied in the tenth point: He sins by *commission* <note>In a legal or moral sense, a "sin of commission" is doing something that is forbidden.</note>, when he returns to old ways against what he forbade in a solemn edict, and, contrary to the laws of excavation <note>original: "fossionis"; the process of digging foundations by clearing away unreliable "sand," or doubtful beliefs</note>, he resumes what he had rejected. You remember this well.<sup>a</sup>

In imitating this, our Author <note>Descartes is referring to Father Bourdin here</note> does not remember the words: *You shall neither assert, nor deny*, etc. <note>original: "Nec pones, nec negabis"; Bourdin’s own rule for total skepticism, which Descartes argues Bourdin is failing to follow.</note> Otherwise, with what face could he pretend that something was forbidden by a solemn edict which he previously said should not even be denied?

He replied in the eleventh point: He sins by *omission* <note>A "sin of omission" is failing to do what is required.</note>, when he disregards what he prescribes as a foundation: « *The greatest care must be taken that we do not admit anything as true which we cannot prove to be true* », a rule he bypasses more than once, assuming with impunity as something most certain and true, without proving it, that: « *Sandy soil is not firm enough to support buildings* », and other things of that kind.<sup>b</sup>
<margin>129</margin>

Where clearly, like our Author, he was hallucinating, applying to excavation (just as our man does to the rejection of doubts) what pertains only to construction, whether of buildings or of Philosophy. For it is very true that nothing should be admitted as true which we cannot prove to be true when the question is about establishing or affirming it; but, when it is only about digging out or casting aside <note>Descartes distinguishes between "affirming a truth" and "suspecting a belief is false enough to be cleared away."</note>, it is enough that we suspect it.

He replied in the twelfth point: That art <note>Descartes's method of doubt.</note> either contains nothing good, or nothing new, and indeed much that is superfluous. For, 1. if he says that by his "rejection of sand" he understands that excavation which all other Architects use—who do not reject sand except insofar as it is not firm enough to sustain the weight of the buildings—he will say something good, but nothing new; and that excavation will not be new, but old, and common to every single Architect.<sup>c</sup>

### WHETHER ARCHITECTURE CAN BE RENEWED

*You ask in the third place, whether...* When he had reached these words, several of his friends—seeing that the extreme envy and hatred with which he was struck had now clearly turned into a sickness—did not allow him to continue ranting in the streets in this way, but immediately led him to a Doctor.

<margin>434</margin>
I certainly would not dare to suspect any such thing about our Author <note>Descartes refers to his opponent, Father Bourdin, as the "Author" of the objections</note>; but I will only proceed to note here how accurately he has imitated that behavior in everything. He plays the judge in exactly the same way—a most upright judge, mind you, and one who is very cautious and religiously careful not to pronounce anything rashly. After he has condemned me eleven times for the sole reason that I rejected doubts in order to establish certainties, and as it were, dug trenches <note>original: "fossas"; referring to the deep excavations needed to reach bedrock for a building's foundation</note> to lay the foundations of a building, he finally examines the matter on the twelfth occasion, and says:

1. If I have understood it as he truly knows me to have understood it—and as is clear from the words, *You shall neither posit nor deny, etc.* <note>original: "Nec pones nec negabis"</note> attributed to me by him—then indeed I have something good, but *nothing new* <note>original: "nihil novi"</note>.

...nothing good. This is especially absurd since he admitted at the start of that same Dissertation that the very person he was reproaching abhorred that opinion so much, he believed it could not even enter the mind of any sane man.

<margin>135</margin> As for the questions that follow (numbers 3, 4, and 5), whether in the work of our Author or the Mason <note>original: "Cæmentarium"; the Mason or Bricklayer character in Bourdin's allegory</note>, they are completely irrelevant to the matter at hand; they were never raised by me, nor by the Architect <note>Descartes refers to himself as the "Architect" within the context of Bourdin's metaphor</note>. It is likely that these questions were first devised by the Mason so that—since he did not dare touch anything the Architect had actually built, for fear of revealing his own ignorance—he might at least appear to be criticizing something more than just the digging of the foundations <note>original: "fossionem"; referring to Descartes’s method of radical doubt as "digging" to find a firm foundation for knowledge</note>. Our Author has imitated him in this regard as well.

3. For when he says that a **thinking thing** <term>res cogitans; Descartes's famous definition of the soul or mind</term> can be understood without the **mind**, the **soul**, or the **body** being understood, he is no better a philosopher than the Mason when he says that someone **skilled in architecture** is no more an **Architect** than he is a **Mason** or a **Porter**, and can be understood without any of them.

4. Likewise, it is surely just as foolish to say that a **thinking thing** exists without a **mind** existing, as it is to say that someone **skilled in architecture** exists without an **Architect** existing (at least when the word **mind** <note>original: "mens"</note> is used as I have indicated I use it, in accordance with common usage). And it is no more contradictory for a thing...

Descartes is now addressing the fifth point of this critique regarding the nature of consciousness and "reflexive" thought.</meta>

<page-num>559</page-num>
### SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

...a thinking thing existing without a body, than a skilled Architect without a Mason <note>original: "Cæmentario"; a bricklayer or stonecutter</note>, or a Laborer <note>original: "Bajulo"; a porter or common carrier of materials</note>.

5. Likewise, when he says it is not enough for some substance to be thinking for it to be placed above matter and be clearly spiritual—which is what he alone wants to be called the **mind** <note>original: "mentem"</note>—but that it is furthermore required that it thinks that it thinks by a **reflexive act** <term>reflexive act: a "bending back" of the mind where it makes its own thought the object of its attention</term>, or that it has consciousness of its own thought, he is hallucinating just as much as the Mason, when the latter says that one skilled in Architecture must, <margin>10</margin> by a reflexive act, consider that he has that skill before he can be an Architect. For although in reality no one is an Architect who has not often considered—or at least been able to consider—that he possesses the skill of building, it is nevertheless obvious that such consideration <margin>136</margin> is not required for him to be an Architect. Nor is a similar consideration or reflection required for a thinking substance to be placed above matter. For any first thought through which we notice something does not differ more from a second thought (through which we notice that we noticed that first thing) than that second differs from a third (through which we notice <margin>20</margin> that we noticed that we noticed). Nor can even the slightest reason be given why, if the first thought were granted to a corporeal thing <note>original: "rei corporeae"; a physical or bodily thing</note>, the second should not also be granted. Wherefore it should be noted that our Author errs much more dangerously in this regard than the Mason: for by removing the true and <margin>25</margin> most intelligible difference between corporeal and incorporeal things—namely, that the latter think and the former do not—and by substituting another in its place which can in no way be seen as essential—namely, that the latter consider that they think, while the former do not—he does everything in his power to prevent the real <margin>30</margin> [distinction...] <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence, likely continuing the thought that Bourdin's definition obscures the "real distinction" between mind and body.</note>

<sig>2</sig> <meta>not a new line.</meta>

<vocab>thought, reflection, consciousness, Architect, Mason, mind, matter, substance</vocab>

<summary>Descartes argues that the defining characteristic of the mind is the simple act of thinking, not the secondary "reflexive" act of thinking about one's own thinking. He asserts that if a physical body were capable of a single thought, it would be logically capable of reflecting on that thought as well, thus making Bourdin's distinction between "thought" and "reflection" useless for defining the soul.</summary>
<keywords>reflexive act, consciousness, mind-body distinction, Pierre Bourdin, substance, spiritual vs. corporeal, architecture metaphor</keywords>
