...the distinction of the human mind from the body is understood.

6. He is even less to be excused for favoring the cause of **brute animals** <note>original: "brutorum animalium"; non-human animals</note>, and for wishing to attribute thought to them no less than to humans, than a Mason would be if he attempted to claim the skill of Architecture for himself and those like him, no less than for Architects.

And finally, it is clear enough in all these matters that both [the Mason and the opponent] have thought in the same way—not about what might be true or plausible, but only about what could be imagined to disparage <margin>137</margin> their enemy. They do this in order to describe him as completely ignorant and foolish to those who do not know him, and who do not care to inquire more carefully into the truth of the matter. Indeed, the Historian of the Mason <note>Descartes refers to Bourdin's writing as a fictional history</note>, to express his insane envy, aptly relates that he praised the Architect's excavation as if it were a magnificent display, but despised the stone revealed by that excavation and the **small chapel** <note>Descartes's metaphor for his metaphysical foundations</note> built upon it as a thing of no importance. Nevertheless, he still gave thanks out of "friendship" and "singular goodwill" toward him, and so on. Likewise, in the conclusion, he brings him in uttering these remarkable **exclamations** <term>exclamations: original "epiphonemata"; a rhetorical device used to summarize or conclude with emphasis</term>: *Furthermore, if he says this, what and how much will remain? What will be redundant? What **babbling** <term>babbling: original "battologia"; repetitive, vain, or nonsensical speech</term>? What machines for show or for **deceptions** <note>original: "præstigias"; tricks or illusions</note>?* etc. And a little later: *In this matter you fear, I believe, for that art of yours which you love, which you embrace; I forgive you* <note>original: "ignosco"</note>, etc. And also: *Do not fear, I am a friend,* etc. For all these things represent the Mason's sickness so graphically that it seems nothing more fitting could have been imagined by any poet.

### SEVENTH OBJECTIONS

But it is truly surprising that our Author [Bourdin] imitates all these things with such great emotion that he does not notice what he himself is doing, and fails to use that **reflective act of thought** <term>reflective act of thought: Latin "cogitatio reflexa"; the mind's ability to turn back upon itself to observe its own operations</term>, which he just claimed was what distinguished humans from the beasts. For he would certainly not say that there is an excess of words in my writings, if he considered how much greater an apparatus he himself has used—I will not say to attack (since he attacks with no reasons), but (let me use a somewhat harsh word, as no other occurs to me that is equally fit <margin>138</margin> to express the truth of the matter) to **bark at** <note>original: "allatrandam"; Descartes suggests Bourdin's criticism is like a dog's bark rather than rational argument</note> the single doubt of which I treated, compared to the effort I took to propose it.

Nor would he have mentioned **pointless repetition** <term>pointless repetition: Latin "battologia"; a rhetorical term for vain or stuttering speech</term> if he noticed how prolix, how superfluous, and how empty a talkativeness he has used throughout his whole Dissertation—at the end of which, nevertheless, he affirms that he has aimed for brevity. Because he says in that same place that he is my friend, I shall treat him in the most friendly manner possible: just as the Mason was led by his friends to the Doctor, so I will recommend this friend of ours to his Superior <note>Father Étienne Dinet, the Jesuit Provincial and Bourdin's superior</note>.

Indeed, as soon as I held that Dissertation in my hands, I rejoiced as if over a great treasure: for nothing is more desirable to me than either to test the certainty of my opinions—if by chance, being examined by great men, they are found to be false in no part—or at least to be warned of my errors, so that I might correct them. And just as in well-constituted bodies there is such a communication and consensus among all the parts that each individual part does not <margin>141</margin> | use its own private strength alone, but there is also a certain common strength of the whole, which supports each part while it acts: so, since I knew how close the union of minds is accustomed to be among all of you <note>Descartes is praising the legendary cohesion and discipline of the Jesuit Order</note>, I believed that I had before me not just the Dissertation of one Reverend Father* <note>original: "R. P." for *Reverendus Pater*, referring here to Pierre Bourdin</note>, but the fair and accurate judgment of the entire Society regarding my opinions.

For surely, if it had proceeded from an author who was governed by the same spirit as your whole Society, there would appear in it a greater—or at least no less—kindness, gentleness, and modesty than is found in the writings of private individuals on the same subject. ## LETTER TO FATHER DINET

**WORKS. II. ; 3**

...they would either immediately overturn it once published, or suffocate it as if in its cradle. I certainly laughed at their efforts in the beginning; indeed, the more I noticed how vehement they were in attacking my views, the more I considered myself to be valued by them. But when I saw their number increasing by the day—and as it happens, they were far more diligent in seeking opportunities to harm me than any well-wishers were in protecting me—I feared that they might achieve something through their secret schemes. I worried they would disturb my peace <note>original: "otium"</note> more if I persisted in my plan not to publish my Philosophy <note>original: "Philosophiam meam"</note> than if I openly opposed them. <gloss>a</gloss> <note>The original text is slightly corrupted here; the editor suggests reading "and" or "but."</note> By delivering exactly what they fear, I will ensure they have nothing left to fear: I have decided to make public all those few things I have thought regarding Philosophy, <margin>165</margin> and to strive so that, if they are true, they may be accepted by as many people as possible.

Therefore, I will not present them in the same order or style in which I previously wrote a large part of them—that is, in the Treatise <note>Descartes refers here to *The World*, a work he withdrew from publication in 1633 after the condemnation of Galileo.</note> whose argument I explained in the *Discourse on Method* <gloss>b</gloss> <note>A reference to the *Discourse*, published in 1637.</note>—but in another style better suited for use in the schools <note>Descartes is referring to the Scholastic university system; he later published this "school-friendly" version as the *Principles of Philosophy*.</note>. Specifically, I will include individual questions in short articles and arrange them in such an order that the proof of what follows depends solely on what came before, bringing them all together into a single body of work. In this way, I hope to set forth the truth of all those matters typically debated in Philosophy so clearly that anyone seeking it will very easily find it there.

For indeed, all young people truly seek the truth,

Rather, they support these institutions only in the hope of truth, which most people persuade themselves will eventually emerge from those very disputes. Or, if they have already been taught by long experience <margin>15</margin> how rarely truth is found in this way, they still value it so much that they do not think even a very small hope of finding it should be neglected. <margin>167</margin> For no nation was ever so fierce or so barbarous, and so averse to the right use of reason—by which alone we are humans—that it wished for opinions to be taught among itself that fought against known <margin>20</margin> truth. And therefore, there is no doubt that truth is to be preferred to all opinions that differ from it, no matter how long-established and widespread they may be; and that all those who teach others are bound to seek it with all their might <margin>25</margin> and to teach it once it is found.

...followed; well-trodden and known paths are always safer than new and unknown ones; especially because of Theology <term>Theology: In the 17th century, Philosophy was expected to serve as a foundation for religious doctrine, and any "new" system was viewed with suspicion.</term>, with <margin>168</margin> which experience over many years has now taught that the old and common Philosophy <note>original: "veterem & vulgarem Philosophiam"; Descartes is referring to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian system taught in universities.</note> agrees perfectly, <margin>5</margin> while the new is uncertain. But I respond, on the contrary, that I certainly claim nothing for myself, nor do I profess to see more than others; but perhaps it has been of benefit to me that, since I do not trust much in my own natural talent, I have followed only plain and easy paths. <margin>15</margin> For, if someone progresses further along these paths than others—even those endowed with much greater talent—who are struggling through those rugged and impenetrable paths which they follow, it is <margin>169</margin> not to be wondered at.

I add that I do not want to be believed regarding the truth of those things <margin>20</margin> which I promise, but to be judged by those Specimens <note>original: "Speciminibus"; Descartes refers to his published works like the *Dioptrics* and *Meteors*, which served as practical "samples" of his method.</note> which I have already given. For there I explained not one or two, but more than six hundred questions, which had been explained by no one before me in such a way; and although many have so far looked at my <margin>25</margin> writings with a sideways glance <note>original: "transversis oculis"; an idiom meaning to look at something with suspicion, hostility, or envy.</note>, and have tried in every way to refute them, no one yet, as far as I know, has been able to find anything not true in them. Let an enumeration be made of all the questions which, in so many centuries in which other Philosophies flourished, were solved by their help, <margin>30</margin> and perhaps they will be found neither so many, nor so illustrious. Indeed, I profess that not even a single question...

...solution of any [problem], given by means of the principles peculiar to Peripatetic Philosophy <term>Peripatetic Philosophy: The school of philosophy following the teachings of Aristotle, which dominated medieval and Renaissance universities.</term>, that I cannot <margin>170</margin> demonstrate to be illegitimate and false. Let a trial be made; let a few choice problems be proposed—not indeed all of them, <margin>5</margin> for I do not think it worth the effort to spend much time on the matter—but a few of the more select ones: I will stand by my promises. And I only warn, so as not to leave room for a quibble, that in speaking of the principles peculiar to Peripatetic Philosophy, I except those questions <margin>10</margin> whose solutions are drawn either from experience alone, common to all men, or from the consideration of figures and motions which is proper to Mathematicians, or finally in Metaphysics from those common notions which it is clear from my *Meditations* are admitted by me, as well <margin>15</margin> as the preceding. <note>original: "ex Meditationibus meis"; referring to his 1641 work *Meditations on First Philosophy*.</note>

I also add what will perhaps seem to be a paradox: that there is nothing in that philosophy, insofar as it is considered Peripatetic and distinct from others, which is not new; and nothing <margin>171</margin> | in mine which is not old. For, as far as principles are <margin>20</margin> concerned, I admit only those which have been common to all philosophers without exception until now, and which are therefore the oldest of all; and those things which I then deduce from them, I show were already previously contained and implied in them so clearly that they appear to be <margin>25</margin> even the most ancient, as if they were implanted by nature in human minds. On the contrary, however, the principles of the common philosophy, at least at the time when they were invented by Aristotle or others, were new, nor should they be thought better now than they were then; <margin>30</margin> and nothing is deduced from them that is not controversial, and which cannot be changed by individual philosophers according to the custom of the schools, and...

...therefore, it is not particularly new, since it is still renewed daily.

<margin>172</margin>
As for Theology, since one truth can never be in opposition to another, it would be a form of impiety to fear that truths discovered in Philosophy might oppose those that are matters of faith. And I absolutely declare that nothing pertains to religion which cannot be explained just as easily, and even more easily, by my principles than by those commonly accepted. I believe I have already given a sufficiently clear example of this at the end of my response to the fourth set of Objections <note>original: "ad quartas Objectiones"; these were the objections to his *Meditations* raised by Antoine Arnauld, a theologian who questioned how Descartes' view of matter could square with the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist.</note>, concerning the very question in which Philosophy is usually most difficult to reconcile with Theology. I am ready to provide the same for any other matters if necessary, and even to show that, on the contrary, there are many things in the common Philosophy <term>Common Philosophy: Refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian system taught in schools.</term> which actually conflict with those certainties in Theology, even if this is commonly concealed by philosophers or goes unnoticed due to a long habit of believing them.

<margin>173</margin>
Nor is it to be feared that my opinions will spread too much by attracting an unlearned crowd eager for novelty; on the contrary, experience shows that they are approved primarily by the more learned. Since these opinions attract people not by novelty, but by truth alone, their growth cannot be excessive. <note>Descartes is arguing that his work appeals to reason and expertise rather than "trendy" or populist impulses.</note>

Nor is it more to be feared that they will disturb the peace of the Schools; but on the contrary, since all philosophers harass one another with so many controversies that they could never be in a greater state of war than they are now, there is no better way...

He, however, did not cease in the meantime; he gathered his Academic Senate every day so that he might share some of that <margin>15</margin> <margin>187</margin> infamy with them. For him, it was a | matter of great importance: reasons had to be sought as to why he wanted the Physician's response and his entire philosophy to be condemned, yet he could find none. ...[undoubtedly the case that the teachings of the schools] are overturned by [my] Philosophy. <note>original: "Philosophiâ evertuntur." This completes the sentence from the previous page where Descartes argues that traditional Scholasticism cannot withstand his method of doubt and reason.</note> But why does it allow itself to be overturned so easily? Why does it not support itself with reasons? And is it not sufficiently shown that those teachings are uncertain, from the fact that nothing certain could be built upon them until now?
<margin>5</margin> The second reason is that youth, by the support of this presumed Philosophy, are unable to understand the technical terms <term>technologemata<gloss>specialized jargon or technical vocabulary used in academic or scientific writing</gloss></term> commonly used in the books of standard authors. As if indeed it were necessary that Philosophy, which was established for the pursuit of truth, should teach any words that it does not itself require! Why does he not
<margin>10</margin> rather condemn Grammar and Rhetoric on those grounds, since it is more their duty to deal with words? Yet they are so far from teaching such terms that they reject them as barbaric. Let him say, then, that for this reason they turn youth <margin>201</margin> away from sound Philosophy, and prevent them from being led to
<margin>15</margin> the peak of erudition; he is no more to be laughed at for saying that than when he says the same of our Philosophy. For the explanation of those terms is not to be sought from Philosophy itself, but from the books of those who use such words.
Finally, the third reason has two parts: one of
<margin>20</margin> which is clearly ridiculous, and the other injurious and false. For what is so true and clear that various false and absurd opinions cannot be easily deduced from it by reckless youth? <margin>25</margin> is plainly false and insulting. Nor will I make use of the excuse that I do not consider his theology to be orthodox...

I think: I have never despised anyone because they thought differently than I do, especially regarding matters of faith; for I know <margin>202</margin> that | faith is a gift of God <note>original: "fidem esse donum Dei"</note>. Indeed, I respect and love many who profess the same religion as he does, including theologians and preachers. But I have already often <margin>5</margin> testified that I never wish to involve myself in any theological controversies; and since in Philosophy I deal only with those things which are most clearly known by <term>natural reason<gloss>the human capacity for logical thought, independent of divine revelation</gloss></term>, they cannot conflict with anyone's theology, unless it be a theology that manifestly opposes the light of reason—<margin>10</margin> something which I know no one would say of their own.

Furthermore, lest I seem to rashly assert that none of the reasons brought forward by the Physician <note>Descartes refers here to Henricus Regius, a professor of medicine and early supporter whose arguments Voetius attacked.</note> can be resolved by the Theologian <note>Gisbertus Voetius</note>, there is already a double or triple proof of this matter. For <margin>15</margin> already two or three pamphlets have been published on this subject, not indeed by the Theologian himself, but on his behalf, and by such persons that, if they contained anything good, it would be attributed to him alone; nor would he have permitted them to put forward such <margin>203</margin> foolish things | while hiding behind their names, if he had anything better to offer.

The first pamphlet was published under the title of *Theses* <margin>20</margin> by his son, a Professor in the same Academy. <note>Paul Voet, son of Gisbertus Voetius.</note> And since in that work only the futile arguments of his father for establishing <term>substantial forms<gloss>a traditional Scholastic concept suggesting that objects have an internal "essence" that determines their behavior; Descartes rejected these in favor of physical, mechanical laws</gloss></term> were repeated, or other even more vacuous ones added, and since no mention at all was made of the Physician's reasons by which <margin>25</margin> all those things had already been refuted, nothing else can be gathered from it except that its author does not understand them, or is certainly not open to learning.

***

11 no new paragraph (*first edition*). — 19 same remark. — 27 *same*.

<page-num>599</page-num>
<header>LETTER TO FATHER DINET.</header>

<margin>5</margin> Another pamphlet—and a double one at that—has appeared under the name of that student who acted as the respondent <note>In a traditional academic debate, the "respondent" was a student who defended a set of theses, though the arguments were often prepared by their professor.</note> in that seditious three-day debate presided over by the Rector <note>original: "Rectore præside"; referring to Gisbertus Voetius.</note>; its title is: *The Forerunner, or a Protective Examination of the Principles of Orthodox Philosophy, etc.* <note>original: "Prodromus sive Examen tutelare orthodoxæ Philosophiæ principiorum &c."</note> <margin>204</margin> And in this work, everything has been collected that its author, or authors, have been able to devise up to now to <margin>10</margin> attack the arguments of the Physician <note>Henricus Regius, Descartes' ally and a professor of medicine.</note>; for even a second part, or a "new *Forerunner*," was joined to the first, so that nothing would be omitted from what occurred to the author while the first part was being printed. Yet, in all of these pages, not one of the Physician's arguments—not even the smallest—has been refuted, I will not say solidly, but not even <margin>15</margin> plausibly. Therefore, that author seems to have cared for nothing else than to stitch together a thick volume of mere nonsense, even titling it a *Forerunner* <note>The word "Prodromus" implies a precursor to a much larger work yet to come.</note> so that even more might be expected. He did this to ensure that no one would deign to respond to him; and in this way, he might triumph, at least in the eyes of the <margin>20</margin> ignorant masses, who believe books are better the thicker they are, and who always judge those who speak most boldly and at greatest length to be the victors.

<margin>205</margin>
<margin>25</margin> But as for me, who do not seek the favor of the common crowd, and care for nothing else but | to protect the truth as much as is in my power—thereby gratifying the upright and the expert while satisfying my own conscience—I hope that I shall make these futile tricks, and all others that my adversaries are accustomed to using, so public that no one will use them in the future, unless they are unashamed to be openly recognized as a slanderer and a hater of the truth. Indeed, thus far it has been of no small help in restraining those who are more modest that, from the beginning...

<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES.</header>

...I requested everyone that, if they had anything with which to challenge those things I proposed as true in my writings, they should deign to write it to me, and I promised I would respond to them <note>original: "responsurum"; referring to his invitation for criticism in the *Discourse on the Method*, part 6.</note>: for they saw that they could say nothing about me in the presence of others that they did not also communicate to me, without by that very act being rightly brought under suspicion of slander. 
But many neglected this, and although they truly found nothing in my writings <margin>206</margin> that they could prove false—and perhaps had not even <margin>10</margin> read them—they nevertheless slandered them in secret. Some did this with such zeal that they wrote entire books on the subject, not to be published to the light of day, but (which I consider much worse) to be read repeatedly in private before the gullible <note>Descartes is targeting Pierre Gassendi here, a rival philosopher who had circulated private objections to Descartes' *Meditations* before they were officially published together.</note>; and they filled these books partly with false reasoning <margin>15</margin> disguised by many verbal evasions, and partly with true arguments, but arguments which only attacked opinions falsely attributed to me.
Now, however, I ask and urge all of them to publish those writings of theirs. For experience has taught me <margin>20</margin> that this will be better than if they send them to me as I previously requested; lest, if I perhaps did not judge them worthy of a response, they might in the meantime falsely boast that I was unable to answer them, or complain that they were being snubbed by me; nor even that some, whose writings I might <margin>207</margin> publish <note>In the 17th century, authors often published their opponents' letters alongside their own rebuttals to ensure the reader saw the whole argument.</note>, should think an injustice was being done to <margin>25</margin> them by me because I added my responses to them—since, as a certain person recently said of himself, they would be deprived in this way of the benefit they could enjoy if they saw to the publication themselves: namely, that their works might be read for several months, and influence and prejudice the minds of many before I could respond to them. And so, to them...

<header>LETTER TO FATHER DINET.</header>
<sig>WORKS. II. 76</sig>

I will not begrudge them the fruit of their labor; moreover, I do not promise that I will respond, except in those instances where I find such arguments that I do not think they can be easily resolved by readers themselves. For as much as concerns quibbles or insults, and any other words <margin>5</margin> foreign to the purpose, I shall consider that they work for me rather than against me, for this reason: I do not think anyone would use such tactics in such a cause, except one who desires to persuade people of more than he can <margin>208</margin> prove with reasons; | and who, by this very act, demonstrates <margin>10</margin> that he does not seek the truth, but wishes to attack it, and consequently reveals that he is not candid and upright.

But I do not doubt that even many sincere and pious men may hold my opinions as suspect, both because they see them being criticized by others, and also for this <margin>15</margin> reason alone: that they are said to be "new," <note>In the 17th century, "novelty" in philosophy or theology was often viewed with extreme suspicion, as it was frequently associated with heresy or the disruption of social order.</note> and have not been understood by many until now. And perhaps there is hardly any assembly of judges to be found in which, if my views were to be deliberated upon, there would not be many more who would think <margin>20</margin> they should be rejected than those who would dare to approve them. For reason and prudence persuade us that, regarding a matter not entirely transparent to us, we should judge only according to what usually happens in similar cases: and so many people until now have brought forth new opinions in Philosophy which have been <margin>25</margin> <margin>209</margin> found to be no better than the common and accepted ones <note>original: "vulgatis & receptis"; referring to the traditional Aristotelian-Scholastic philosophy taught in universities.</note>, | but often more dangerous, so that all those who do not yet clearly perceive my own views would, if asked for their opinion, not without merit say that they should be rejected. And therefore, however true they may be, I would nonetheless think I must fear lest perhaps by your whole Society <note>The "Society" refers to the Society of Jesus (the Jesuits). Descartes had been educated by the Jesuits at La Flèche and was deeply concerned with their official approval of his work.</note>, and generally <margin>30</margin> by all assemblies of those who teach, as recently by...

<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES.</header>

[My opinions] would be condemned by that Academic Senate of which I have already written, were it not for the fact that I believe they will be protected by you, in your exceptional kindness and prudence. But, since you govern that part of the Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits). Father Dinet was the Provincial of the Province of Paris.</note> from which my *Essays* <note>original: *Specimina*. This refers to the *Discourse on Method* and the scientific essays published with it in 1637.</note> <margin>5</margin> can be more easily read than by the others—namely, because the principal part of them was written in French—I am persuaded that you alone have the greatest power in this matter. Nor indeed do I ask any other favor from you here than that you either examine them yourself or, if greater business prevents you, entrust that care not to a single Reverend Father <margin>210 10</margin> <note>original: "R. P. [Bourdin]". This refers to Father Pierre Bourdin, a Jesuit who had been a sharp critic of Descartes.</note>, but to others who are more candid; and just as in legal trials, when two or three trustworthy witnesses affirm they have seen something, more credit is given to them alone than to the entire multitude of other men who, perhaps led by conjectures, think the <margin>15</margin> opposite: so you should believe only those who profess that they perfectly understand the matter about which they will judge; and finally that, if you should have any reasons that ought to recall me from my purpose, you would not find it troublesome to teach them to me.
<margin>20</margin> For truly, in those few *Meditations* <note>Descartes' *Meditations on First Philosophy*, first published in 1641.</note> which I have published, all the principles of the Philosophy I am preparing are contained; while in the *Dioptrics* <note>A treatise on optics.</note> and the *Meteorology* <note>A treatise on atmospheric phenomena.</note>, I have derived many particular conclusions from them which demonstrate what kind of reasoning I use; and therefore, although I do not yet show <margin>25</margin> that entire Philosophy, I think nevertheless that, from those things I have already given, it can easily <margin>211</margin> be understood what it will be like in the future. Nor, in my opinion, without...

<page-num>603</page-num>

# LETTER TO FATHER DINET.

For good reason, I preferred to send out some specimens <note>original: *specimina*. This refers to the essays published with the *Discourse on Method* in 1637, intended as "samples" of his new philosophical system.</note> of my work first, rather than presenting the entire work before it had been requested. For although, to speak freely, I do not doubt its truth, yet because I know how easily even the truth—when attacked by a few envious people under the guise of "novelty" <note>In the 17th century, "novelty" in philosophy or theology was often viewed with suspicion and linked to heresy.</note>—can <margin>5</margin> be condemned by many wise men, I am not certain that it is desired by everyone, nor do I wish to thrust it upon the unwilling. For this reason, I am warning everyone far in advance that I am preparing it: many private individuals desire and expect it; one group of teachers, indeed, judged that it should be rejected; but because I know <margin>10</margin> they were moved to this only by their seditious and inept Rector <note>Descartes refers here to Gisbertus Voetius, the Rector of the University of Utrecht, who led a fierce campaign against Cartesian philosophy.</note>, it holds no authority with me. But if, by chance, many others did not want it, and had more just reasons for their refusal, I would think they should be preferred over private individuals. And <margin>15</margin> <margin>212</margin> I declare altogether that I will do nothing knowingly against the advice of wiser men or the will of those in power. And since I do not doubt that the side toward which your Society <note>The Society of Jesus (the Jesuits).</note> leans must outweigh the other, you will do me the greatest favor if you wish to advise me of your opinion and that of your colleagues: <margin>20</margin> so that, just as in the rest of my life I have always especially honored and respected you, so too in this matter, which I think is of some importance, I may undertake nothing except with your favor. Farewell.

---

->THE END.<-

a. OVIEDO (Francisco de), born in Madrid in 1602, entered the Society of Jesus in 1618. He first taught the humanities, then for five years philosophy, two years moral theology, and five years scholasticism at Alcala and Madrid, where he died on February 9, 1651. He left behind three works: 1st *Complete course of philosophy reduced to a single body* <note>original: "Integer cursus philosophicus ad unum corpus redactus"</note> (vols. I and II, Lyon, 1640; second edition, ibid., 1641), Provincial Approval, August 8, 1638. — 2nd *Theological, Scholastic and Moral Treatises* <note>original: "Tractatus Theologici, Scholastici et Morales"</note> (ibid., 1646). — 3rd *On the virtues of Faith, Hope and Charity* <note>original: "De virtutibus Fide, Spe et Charitate"</note> (ibid., 1651).
